chapter-04-data-link-layer.answer: GBN uses cumulative ACKs; SR uses individual selective ACKs
chapter-04-data-link-layer.explanation: Go-Back-N uses cumulative ACKs, where ACK(n) acknowledges that all frames up to and including n have been received correctly. If a frame has an error, subsequent frames are discarded. Selective Repeat uses selective ACKs, where the receiver acknowledges each frame individually and buffers out-of-order frames, requesting retransmission only of the lost frame via a Negative ACK (NAK).
chapter-04-data-link-layer.examTrick: GBN = Cumulative ACK (all-or-nothing). SR = Selective ACK (buffers out-of-order).
chapter-04-data-link-layer.subject: Computer Networks
chapter-04-data-link-layer.chapterName: Data Link Layer and Transmission Control

chapter-04-data-link-layer.question: In an Ethernet network with bandwidth B = 10 Mbps and propagation speed v = 200,000 km/s, if the distance between the two furthest stations is 2.5 km, what is the minimum Ethernet frame size required to guarantee collision detection?
options: 64 bytes
125 bytes
31.25 bytes
500 bytes
chapter-04-data-link-layer.explanation:
1. Propagation delay Tp = Distance / Speed = 2.5 km / 200,000 km/s = 1.25 * 10^-5 seconds = 12.5 microseconds.
2. Minimum frame transmission time Tt >= 2 * Tp = 2 * 12.5 microseconds = 25 microseconds.
3. Minimum frame size L_min >= 2 * Tp * B = 25 microseconds * 10 Mbps = 250 bits.
4. Convert to bytes: 250 bits / 8 = 31.25 bytes.
chapter-04-data-link-layer.examTrick: Formula: L_min >= 2 * Tp * B. Just compute propagation time, multiply by 2, multiply by bandwidth, then divide by 8 to get bytes!
chapter-04-data-link-layer.subject: Computer Networks
chapter-04-data-link-layer.chapterName: Data Link Layer and Transmission Control

chapter-04-data-link-layer.question: Why is the collision vulnerability window of Slotted ALOHA half that of Pure ALOHA?
options: Because Slotted ALOHA operates at twice the frequency band
Because Slotted ALOHA restricts transmissions to discrete slot boundaries, making the collision window equal to Tt instead of 2 * Tt
Because Slotted ALOHA uses a token ring approach
Because Slotted ALOHA uses carrier sensing before transmitting
chapter-04-data-link-layer.answer: Because Slotted ALOHA restricts transmissions to discrete slot boundaries, making the collision window equal to Tt instead of 2 * Tt
chapter-04-data-link-layer.explanation: In Pure ALOHA, a frame transmitted at time t can collide with any frame transmitted between t - Tt and t + Tt, yielding a collision window of 2 * Tt. In Slotted ALOHA, packets can only be sent at slot boundaries. If a collision occurs, it occurs within that slot, meaning the vulnerability window is reduced to exactly Tt.
chapter-04-data-link-layer.examTrick: Pure ALOHA window = 2 * Tt (starts anytime). Slotted ALOHA window = Tt (starts only on slots). Half the window = Double the efficiency (36.8% vs 18.4%)!
chapter-04-data-link-layer.subject: Computer Networks
chapter-04-data-link-layer.chapterName: Data Link Layer and Transmission Control

chapter-04-data-link-layer.question: In the analysis of ARQ protocols, the parameter 'a' is defined as the ratio of propagation delay (Tp) to transmission delay (Tt). How does a very high value of 'a' (a >> 1) affect the performance of Stop-and-Wait ARQ?
options: It makes Stop-and-Wait extremely efficient (approaching 100%)
It degrades Stop-and-Wait efficiency to near zero, as the channel remains idle during the long propagation delay
It causes routing loops to form
It increases the transmission bandwidth of the link
chapter-04-data-link-layer.answer: It degrades Stop-and-Wait efficiency to near zero, as the channel remains idle during the long propagation delay
chapter-04-data-link-layer.source: CN Reference PDF Section 2.2.1 Stop-and-Wait ARQ
chapter-04-data-link-layer.explanation: The efficiency of Stop-and-Wait is η = 1 / (1 + 2a). When a = Tp / Tt >> 1 (which occurs on links with high bandwidth-delay products, such as satellite links), the denominator becomes very large, and efficiency η approaches 0. The sender spends almost all its time waiting for ACKs rather than transmitting data.
chapter-04-data-link-layer.examTrick: High 'a' (long delay, short transmission) = Stop-and-Wait is terrible! This is why high-latency or high-speed links must use sliding window protocols like Go-Back-N or Selective Repeat.
chapter-04-data-link-layer.subject: Computer Networks
chapter-04-data-link-layer.chapterName: Data Link Layer and Transmission Control

chapter-05-transport-layer.question: In TCP Congestion Control, suppose the current congestion window (cwnd) is 16 KB and the slow start threshold (ssthresh) is 8 KB. If the sender is in the Congestion Avoidance phase and successfully transmits one full window of segments, what will be the new value of cwnd?
options: 17 KB
32 KB
8 KB
24 KB
chapter-05-transport-layer.explanation: During the Slow Start phase (when cwnd < ssthresh), cwnd increases exponentially (doubling every round-trip time, RTT). Once cwnd >= ssthresh, TCP enters the Congestion Avoidance phase. In this phase, cwnd increases linearly by approximately 1 MSS (Maximum Segment Size) for each RTT (i.e., after one full window of successful transmissions). Here, since the sender is in Congestion Avoidance, cwnd increases from 16 KB to 16 + 1 = 17 KB.
chapter-05-transport-layer.examTrick:
Slow Start = Exponential growth (double cwnd per RTT).
Congestion Avoidance = Linear growth (+1 segment size per RTT). Simple but highly tested logic!
chapter-05-transport-layer.subject: Computer Networks

chapter-05-transport-layer.question: A TCP connection is undergoing slow start. Suppose its cwnd is 32 segments and a packet timeout occurs. What are the new values of ssthresh and cwnd respectively (assuming standard TCP Tahoe)?
options: ssthresh = 16, cwnd = 1
ssthresh = 16, cwnd = 1
ssthresh = 32, cwnd = 1
ssthresh = 8, cwnd = 1
chapter-05-transport-layer.explanation:
When a packet loss is detected via a timeout in standard TCP Tahoe/Reno:
1. The slow start threshold (ssthresh) is set to half of the current congestion window: ssthresh = cwnd / 2 = 32 / 2 = 16 segments.
2. The congestion window (cwnd) is reset to 1 segment (cwnd = 1 MSS).
3. The sender then resumes Slow Start from cwnd = 1 up to the new ssthresh = 16.
chapter-05-transport-layer.examTrick: For Timeout: cwnd is always reset to 1 segment. ssthresh becomes half of the cwnd at the time of loss. (In TCP Reno, for 3 duplicate ACKs, cwnd is halved instead of going to 1 - known as Fast Recovery).
chapter-05-transport-layer.subject: Computer Networks

chapter-05-transport-layer.question: Which of the following transport layer phenomena describes 'Silly Window Syndrome' (SWS)?
options: The sender transmits huge chunks of data that overflow the receiver's main buffer.
The receiver continually advertises tiny window sizes (e.g., a few bytes) and the sender transmits tiny segments to match, leading to high header overhead.
The network routers drop packets because the TCP window size is configured too high.
A sequence number wrap-around causes TCP segments to arrive completely out of order.
chapter-05-transport-layer.answer: The receiver continually advertises tiny window sizes (e.g., a few bytes) and the sender transmits tiny segments to match, leading to high header overhead.
chapter-05-transport-layer.explanation: Silly Window Syndrome occurs when either the receiver announces a tiny free buffer space (window) or the sender transmits very small pieces of data. Because a standard TCP/IP packet has a 40-byte header (20 bytes TCP + 20 bytes IP), transmitting 1 byte of data in a 41-byte packet results in massive network overhead. It is resolved using Nagle's Algorithm (sender side) and Clark's Solution or Delayed ACKs (receiver side).
chapter-05-transport-layer.examTrick: Silly Window Syndrome = tiny data segment overhead! Resolved by Nagle's Algorithm on the sender side.
chapter-05-transport-layer.subject: Computer Networks

chapter-05-transport-layer.question: Host A is opening a TCP connection to Host B. Host A sends a SYN segment with Sequence Number = 1000. Host B accepts the connection and responds with a SYN-ACK segment. What is the Acknowledgment Number in Host B's response?
chapter-05-transport-layer.explanation: During the TCP 3-way handshake: 1. Host A sends SYN (Seq = X). 2. Host B responds with SYN-ACK (Seq = Y, Ack = X + 1). Here, Host A sends SYN with Seq = 1000. Therefore, Host B acknowledges receipt by setting Ack = 1000 + 1 = 1001. This indicates that Host B expects Host A's next packet to start with Sequence Number 1001.
chapter-05-transport-layer.examTrick: SYN and FIN control flags consume exactly 1 logical sequence number, even though they contain zero payload bytes! Therefore, the ACK is always Seq + 1.
chapter-05-transport-layer.subject: Computer Networks

chapter-05-transport-layer.question: What is the key difference between User Datagram Protocol (UDP) and Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) headers?
options: UDP headers do not contain any port numbers.
UDP has a fixed 8-byte header size with no options, whereas TCP has a minimum 20-byte header.
UDP headers are dynamic and can expand up to 100 bytes using option fields.
UDP headers do not include a checksum field.
chapter-05-transport-layer.answer: UDP has a fixed 8-byte header size with no options, whereas TCP has a minimum 20-byte header.
chapter-05-transport-layer.explanation: The UDP header is extremely lightweight, containing only four fields: Source Port (2 bytes), Destination Port (2 bytes), Length (2 bytes), and Checksum (2 bytes), giving a fixed size of 8 bytes. The TCP header has a minimum size of 20 bytes and can expand up to 60 bytes to support options (e.g., MSS, Window Scale, Timestamps).
chapter-05-transport-layer.examTrick: UDP header is fixed at 8 bytes. TCP header is minimum 20 bytes (maximum 60 bytes). Keep these numbers memorized for quick PSU questions!
chapter-05-transport-layer.subject: Computer Networks

chapter-05-transport-layer.question: In network socket programming, which system call is used on the server-side to associate a local IP address and port number with a socket descriptor?
options: socket()
listen()
connect()
bind()
chapter-05-transport-layer.explanation: In socket programming, the server-side flow is: socket() -> bind() -> listen() -> accept(). The bind() system call assigns a physical IP address and a port number to the socket descriptor created by socket().
chapter-05-transport-layer.examTrick: Server socket flow: S-B-L-A (Socket, Bind, Listen, Accept). Client socket flow: S-C (Socket, Connect). connect() is purely a client-side call!
chapter-05-transport-layer.subject: Computer Networks

chapter-05-transport-layer.question: In TCP Reno congestion control, what happens to the congestion window (cwnd) and slow start threshold (ssthresh) when a loss is detected via 3 Duplicate ACKs (Fast Retransmit)?
options: cwnd is reset to 1 segment, ssthresh is halved
cwnd is halved, ssthresh is set to this halved value (Fast Recovery), and linear increase resumes
cwnd is doubled, ssthresh remains unchanged
No action is taken; the sender waits for a timeout
chapter-05-transport-layer.answer: cwnd is halved, ssthresh is set to this halved value (Fast Recovery), and linear increase resumes
chapter-05-transport-layer.explanation: When loss is detected via 3 duplicate ACKs (indicating mild congestion), TCP Reno triggers Fast Retransmit (retransmits the missing segment immediately) and Fast Recovery. Under Fast Recovery, instead of resetting cwnd to 1, ssthresh is set to cwnd / 2, and cwnd is set to ssthresh + 3 MSS (to account for the segments that have left the pipe and are buffered at the receiver). The sender then enters Congestion Avoidance directly, avoiding the slow start phase.
chapter-05-transport-layer.examTrick: Reno halving (3 Dup ACKs) vs Tahoe resetting (reset to 1). Timeout ALWAYS resets cwnd to 1 in both Reno and Tahoe! 3 Dup ACKs is mild, so Reno just halves cwnd (Fast Recovery).
chapter-05-transport-layer.subject: Computer Networks

chapter-05-transport-layer.question: Which of the following correctly describes the behavioral difference between a Leaky Bucket traffic shaper and a Token Bucket traffic shaper?
options: Leaky Bucket permits bursty data transmission; Token Bucket releases packets at a strictly constant, uniform rate
Leaky Bucket drops all packets; Token Bucket compresses packets
Leaky Bucket releases packets at a strictly constant, uniform rate; Token Bucket generates tokens at a constant rate, permitting bursty data transmission when tokens are accumulated
There is no functional difference; they are identical traffic shaping models
chapter-05-transport-layer.answer: Leaky Bucket releases packets at a strictly constant, uniform rate; Token Bucket generates tokens at a constant rate, permitting bursty data transmission when tokens are accumulated
chapter-05-transport-layer.explanation: As documented in the Congestion Control reference materials, a Leaky Bucket traffic shaper drops bursty traffic and releases packets at a strictly constant, uniform rate. A Token Bucket traffic shaper generates tokens at a constant rate, accumulating them in a bucket. If tokens are accumulated, a burst of packets can be sent immediately, allowing flexible bursty transmissions while still enforcing a long-term average rate limit.
chapter-05-transport-layer.examTrick: Leaky Bucket = Strict constant rate (No bursts allowed!). Token Bucket = Average rate over time, but permits bursts when bucket is full of tokens!
chapter-05-transport-layer.subject: Computer Networks

chapter-05-transport-layer.question: During a TCP connection teardown (Four-way handshake), why does the host that initiates the active close enter the TIME-WAIT state and wait for 2 * MSL (Maximum Segment Lifetime) before fully closing the socket?
options: To allow any duplicate, delayed packets in the network to die out and to guarantee that the final ACK was received by the peer
To download any remaining payload packets
To calculate the final checksum of the session
To request a new IP address from the DHCP server
chapter-05-transport-layer.answer: To allow any duplicate, delayed packets in the network to die out and to guarantee that the final ACK was received by the peer
chapter-05-transport-layer.explanation: The TIME-WAIT state serves two main purposes: 1. To ensure that the final ACK (Segment 4 of the 4-way teardown) was received by the other peer. If the ACK is lost, the peer will retransmit its FIN, and the host in TIME-WAIT can re-send the ACK. 2. To allow any old, delayed, duplicated packets belonging to this connection to expire in the network, preventing them from corrupting future sessions using the same socket pair.
chapter-05-transport-layer.examTrick: TIME-WAIT = 2 * MSL (usually 4 minutes). It prevents old delayed duplicates from popping up and corrupting a newly opened connection on the same ports.
chapter-05-transport-layer.subject: Computer Networks

chapter-05-transport-layer.question: Which of the following statements is technically accurate regarding the UDP Checksum field in IPv4 vs. IPv6?
options: UDP Checksum is mandatory in both IPv4 and IPv6
UDP Checksum is optional in both IPv4 and IPv6
UDP Checksum is optional in IPv4 (if not calculated, set to all 0s), but is strictly mandatory in IPv6
UDP Checksum is mandatory in IPv4, but is optional in IPv6
chapter-05-transport-layer.answer: UDP Checksum is optional in IPv4 (if not calculated, set to all 0s), but is strictly mandatory in IPv6
chapter-05-transport-layer.explanation: In IPv4, calculating the UDP checksum is optional to reduce processing overhead. If a sender does not calculate it, the checksum field is set to all 0s. In IPv6, however, because intermediate routers no longer verify or compute checksums (which was dropped from the IPv6 header to speed up routing), the UDP checksum is strictly mandatory at the end-nodes for packet integrity.
chapter-05-transport-layer.examTrick: IPv6 has NO header checksum, so UDP checksum becomes MANDATORY in IPv6 to maintain packet integrity! In IPv4, it is optional.
chapter-05-transport-layer.subject: Computer Networks

chapter-05-transport-layer.question: In server-side socket programming, what does the second parameter (backlog) of the listen(int sockfd, int backlog) system primitive represent?
options: The maximum speed of the link in Mbps
The maximum number of fully established, pending connections that can be queued waiting for the application to accept() them
The size of the socket's transmission buffer in bytes
The timeout duration in seconds for receiving packets
chapter-05-transport-layer.answer: The maximum number of fully established, pending connections that can be queued waiting for the application to accept() them
chapter-05-transport-layer.explanation: The backlog parameter in listen() specifies the maximum length to which the queue of pending connections (connection requests that have completed the 3-way handshake but have not yet been accepted by the application via accept()) may grow. If a connection request arrives when the queue is full, the client may receive an error (or TCP ignores the SYN so the client retries).
chapter-05-transport-layer.examTrick: Backlog = Waiting room size! It limits how many fully established connections can queue up waiting for accept() before the server starts turning clients away.
chapter-05-transport-layer.subject: Computer Networks

chapter-05-transport-layer.question: How do TCP and UDP compare in terms of their flow control mechanisms?
options: TCP uses a sliding window size advertised by the receiver; UDP has zero flow control and depends on the application layer to prevent buffer overflow
Both TCP and UDP use identical sliding window flow control
TCP has no flow control; UDP uses credit-based flow control
TCP uses rate-limiting; UDP uses window-based flow control
chapter-05-transport-layer.answer: TCP uses a sliding window size advertised by the receiver; UDP has zero flow control and depends on the application layer to prevent buffer overflow
chapter-05-transport-layer.explanation: TCP has built-in flow control using a sliding window where the receiver advertises its available buffer size in the 'Receiver Window Size' header field, preventing the sender from overwhelming the receiver. UDP is connectionless and has no flow control mechanism whatsoever in its header; it simply pushes packets as fast as possible. If the receiver's buffer overflows, UDP packets are dropped.
chapter-05-transport-layer.examTrick: TCP = Receiver Window flow control (reliable pacing). UDP = No flow control (blast and pray). Applications using UDP must handle pacing themselves if needed!
chapter-05-transport-layer.subject: Computer Networks

chapter-05-transport-layer.question: What is the relationship between the TCP Maximum Segment Size (MSS) and the IP Maximum Transmission Unit (MTU) on a standard link?
options: MSS is always twice the size of the MTU
MSS is equal to the MTU of the link
MSS = MTU - (IP Header Size + TCP Header Size), which is typically MTU - 40 bytes
MSS has no relationship to MTU
chapter-05-transport-layer.answer: MSS = MTU - (IP Header Size + TCP Header Size), which is typically MTU - 40 bytes
chapter-05-transport-layer.explanation: The Maximum Segment Size (MSS) represents the maximum size of the TCP data payload that can be sent in a single segment without causing IP fragmentation. On a typical Ethernet link where the MTU is 1500 bytes, the MSS is calculated as: 1500 - 20 bytes (IP header) - 20 bytes (TCP header) = 1460 bytes.
chapter-05-transport-layer.examTrick: MSS = MTU - 40! It represents data payload size only. For standard Ethernet: MTU is 1500, base headers are 40, so MSS is 1460.
chapter-05-transport-layer.subject: Computer Networks

chapter-05-transport-layer.question: In which of the following scenarios will a host send a TCP segment with the RST (Reset) control flag set to 1?
options: To request the peer to slow down its transmission rate due to network congestion
When a client attempts to connect to a port on a server where no application is listening
During a normal, graceful four-way teardown
To acknowledge the receipt of an urgent out-of-band data segment
chapter-05-transport-layer.answer: When a client attempts to connect to a port on a server where no application is listening
chapter-05-transport-layer.explanation: The RST flag is used to immediately abort a connection. If a host receives a TCP segment (like a SYN) destined for a port on which no application is listening, the host's operating system responds with a segment where RST = 1 and ACK = 1 to explicitly inform the caller that the connection is refused and should not be retried.
chapter-05-transport-layer.examTrick: RST = Hard abort / Connection refused! It is sent when a packet arrives at a closed port or when a connection gets severely desynchronized.
chapter-05-transport-layer.subject: Computer Networks

chapter-05-transport-layer.question: How does the TCP Selective Acknowledgment (SACK) option improve over the standard Cumulative Acknowledgment scheme during multiple packet losses?
options: By encrypting the retransmitted segments
By allowing the receiver to inform the sender of all non-contiguous segments received correctly, preventing the sender from having to retransmit segments that have already arrived
By forcing the sender to use UDP instead of TCP
By increasing the IP packet size to 65,535 bytes
chapter-05-transport-layer.answer: By allowing the receiver to inform the sender of all non-contiguous segments received correctly, preventing the sender from having to retransmit segments that have already arrived
chapter-05-transport-layer.explanation: With standard cumulative ACKs, if segments 1, 3, and 4 arrive but 2 is lost, the receiver can only send ACK 2. The sender does not know if 3 and 4 arrived and may have to retransmit them. SACK is an option that allows the receiver to append blocks of successfully received non-contiguous data ranges, so the sender only retransmits the truly missing segments (segment 2 in this case).
chapter-05-transport-layer.examTrick: SACK = Selective ACK blocks! It prevents redundant retransmissions when multiple packets are lost in a single window.
chapter-05-transport-layer.subject: Computer Networks

chapter-06-application-security.question:
Consider the following statements regarding network firewalls:
I. A Packet Filter Firewall analyzes network traffic at the transport layer.
II. A Circuit Level Firewall operates at the transport and session layers of the OSI Model.
Which of the statements is/are TRUE?
options: Only I
Only II
None
I and II
chapter-06-application-security.explanation:
Let's analyze both statements:
- Statement I is True: Packet filtering firewalls work primarily at the network and transport layers (Layers 3 and 4) by examining source/destination IP addresses, protocol types, and port numbers (TCP/UDP segments).
- Statement II is True: Circuit-level gateways operate at the transport and session layers of the OSI model (Layers 4 and 5) to monitor TCP handshakes and determine whether a requested session is legitimate before establishing a circuit.
chapter-06-application-security.examTrick:
Firewalls summary:
- Packet Filter: Layers 3 & 4 (fastest, stateless)
- Circuit Level: Layers 4 & 5 (monitors handshakes/TCP state)
- Application / Proxy: Layer 7 (deep content inspection, slowest)
chapter-06-application-security.subject: Computer Networks
chapter-06-application-security.chapterName: Application Layer Protocols and Network Security

chapter-06-application-security.question: In the RSA public-key cryptosystem, if the two prime numbers are p = 7 and q = 11, and the encryption key is chosen as e = 13, what is the value of the decryption key d?
chapter-06-application-security.explanation:
Let's perform the RSA mathematical steps:
1. Compute n = p * q = 7 * 11 = 77.
2. Compute Euler's totient function φ(n) = (p - 1) * (q - 1) = 6 * 10 = 60.
3. The decryption key d must satisfy the congruency relation: d * e ≡ 1 (mod φ(n))
   d * 13 ≡ 1 (mod 60)
4. We find d by finding the multiplicative inverse of 13 modulo 60:
   Let's check d = 37: 37 * 13 = 481.
   481 / 60 = 8 with a remainder of 1. Thus, 481 ≡ 1 (mod 60).
Therefore, d = 37.
chapter-06-application-security.examTrick: Decryption key 'd' is calculated as the modular multiplicative inverse of 'e' modulo φ(n). Never use modulo n, always use modulo φ(n) = (p-1)(q-1)!
chapter-06-application-security.subject: Computer Networks
chapter-06-application-security.chapterName: Application Layer Protocols and Network Security

chapter-06-application-security.question: Which of the following is NOT a public key (asymmetric) cryptosystem?
options: El Gamal
Rabin
AES
RSA
chapter-06-application-security.explanation: Asymmetric (public key) algorithms use a pair of keys: a public key for encryption and a private key for decryption. Examples include RSA, El Gamal, Rabin, and Diffie-Hellman. Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) is a symmetric-key block cipher algorithm where the same key is used for both encryption and decryption.
chapter-06-application-security.examTrick: Symmetric algorithms (S-K-D-A): DES, 3DES, AES, RC4, Blowfish. Asymmetric algorithms (A-R-E-D): RSA, Rabin, El Gamal, Diffie-Hellman.
chapter-06-application-security.subject: Computer Networks
chapter-06-application-security.chapterName: Application Layer Protocols and Network Security

chapter-06-application-security.question: In the RSA public-key algorithm, how is the encryption key 'e' selected with respect to the totient function φ(n)?
options: e must be chosen as a relative prime to q
e must be chosen as a relative prime to p
e must be chosen as a relative prime to φ(n)
e must be chosen as a relative prime to n
chapter-06-application-security.answer: e must be chosen as a relative prime to φ(n)
chapter-06-application-security.explanation: In RSA, once φ(n) = (p-1)(q-1) is computed, the public exponent 'e' is chosen such that 1 < e < φ(n) and e is coprime (relatively prime) to φ(n). That is, the greatest common divisor gcd(e, φ(n)) must be exactly 1, guaranteeing that a modular multiplicative inverse d exists.
chapter-06-application-security.examTrick: The selection rule is gcd(e, φ(n)) = 1. If they are not relatively prime, you cannot compute the decryption key 'd'!
chapter-06-application-security.subject: Computer Networks
chapter-06-application-security.chapterName: Application Layer Protocols and Network Security

chapter-06-application-security.question: Which of the following application layer protocol maps well-known default port 53 and uses UDP for standard queries, but can fall back to TCP for large zone transfers?
options: DHCP
DNS
SMTP
FTP
chapter-06-application-security.explanation: Domain Name System (DNS) resolves human-readable domain names (like google.com) to IP addresses. DNS queries are small and speed is vital, so it uses UDP on port 53. However, DNS uses TCP port 53 for reliable connection-oriented actions like zone transfers between primary and secondary DNS servers, or when response sizes exceed 512 bytes.
chapter-06-application-security.examTrick: DNS uses BOTH UDP and TCP on port 53! Queries use UDP, zone transfers/large responses use TCP.
chapter-06-application-security.subject: Computer Networks
chapter-06-application-security.chapterName: Application Layer Protocols and Network Security

chapter-06-application-security.question: In the File Transfer Protocol (FTP), which port numbers are utilized for the Data Connection and the Control Connection respectively in active mode?
options: Port 20 for Control, Port 21 for Data
Port 21 for Control, Port 20 for Data
Port 80 for Control, Port 443 for Data
Port 25 for Control, Port 110 for Data
chapter-06-application-security.answer: Port 21 for Control, Port 20 for Data
chapter-06-application-security.explanation:
FTP is an out-of-band protocol because it uses two separate TCP connections:
1. Control Connection (Port 21): Used for sending commands and receiving server responses (e.g., login, file list requests).
2. Data Connection (Port 20 in active mode): Used for actual file transfers.
chapter-06-application-security.examTrick: Control comes first (21), then Data follows (20). FTP is one of the few protocols that uses TWO separate ports!
chapter-06-application-security.subject: Computer Networks
chapter-06-application-security.chapterName: Application Layer Protocols and Network Security

chapter-06-application-security.question: In a Diffie-Hellman Key Exchange, the public parameters are a prime p = 11 and its primitive root g = 2. If Alice selects private key a = 3 and Bob selects private key b = 4, what is the shared secret key K computed by both?
chapter-06-application-security.explanation:
1. Alice computes her public value A = g^a mod p = 2^3 mod 11 = 8.
2. Bob computes his public value B = g^b mod p = 2^4 mod 11 = 16 mod 11 = 5.
3. Alice computes the shared secret K = B^a mod p = 5^3 mod 11 = 125 mod 11 = 4.
4. Bob computes the shared secret K = A^b mod p = 8^4 mod 11 = 4096 mod 11 = 4 (since 4096 = 11 * 372 + 4). Both calculate the identical shared secret K = 4.
chapter-06-application-security.examTrick: Diffie-Hellman formula for shared secret: K = B^a mod p = A^b mod p. Here, K = 5^3 mod 11 = 125 mod 11 = 4.
chapter-06-application-security.subject: Computer Networks
chapter-06-application-security.chapterName: Application Layer Protocols and Network Security

chapter-06-application-security.question: In a network containing 'N' users, what is the total number of unique keys required for secure pairwise communication under a Symmetric Key Cryptosystem vs. an Asymmetric Key Cryptosystem?
options: N keys for Symmetric, N^2 keys for Asymmetric
N(N-1)/2 keys for Symmetric, 2N keys for Asymmetric
2N keys for Symmetric, N(N-1)/2 keys for Asymmetric
N keys for both cryptosystems
chapter-06-application-security.answer: N(N-1)/2 keys for Symmetric, 2N keys for Asymmetric
chapter-06-application-security.explanation: In a symmetric cryptosystem, every communicating pair requires a distinct shared key. The number of unique pairs among N users is N(N-1)/2. In an asymmetric cryptosystem, each user requires exactly 2 keys (one public, one private), totaling 2N keys for the entire network.
chapter-06-application-security.examTrick: Symmetric = Pairwise = N(N-1)/2 (Scales quadratically!). Asymmetric = 2 per user = 2N (Scales linearly!). This is why asymmetric cryptography is highly scalable for large networks.
chapter-06-application-security.subject: Computer Networks
chapter-06-application-security.chapterName: Application Layer Protocols and Network Security

chapter-06-application-security.question: Which of the following correctly describes the distinct roles of SMTP vs. POP3/IMAP in email communications?
options: SMTP is used to retrieve email from a server; POP3/IMAP are used to push email from a client to a server
SMTP is used to push email from a client to a server and between servers; POP3 and IMAP are pull protocols used by a client to retrieve email from a mail server
SMTP operates over UDP port 25; POP3/IMAP operate over UDP port 80
SMTP encrypts email; POP3/IMAP decrypt email
chapter-06-application-security.answer: SMTP is used to push email from a client to a server and between servers; POP3 and IMAP are pull protocols used by a client to retrieve email from a mail server
chapter-06-application-security.explanation: Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP) is a push protocol operating on TCP port 25, used to transmit mails from clients to mail servers and to relay mail between mail servers. Post Office Protocol (POP3) and Internet Message Access Protocol (IMAP) are pull protocols used by end clients to retrieve their email from mail servers.
chapter-06-application-security.examTrick: SMTP = Send Mail To People (Push, Port 25). POP3/IMAP = Pull protocols to download mail. POP3 downloads and deletes, IMAP keeps emails synced on the server!
chapter-06-application-security.subject: Computer Networks
chapter-06-application-security.chapterName: Application Layer Protocols and Network Security

chapter-06-application-security.question: An HTML web page contains text and 5 embedded images. To download this complete page from a web server with a round-trip time (RTT) of 20 ms, how much total time is required under Non-Persistent HTTP without parallel connections vs. Persistent HTTP with pipelining (ignoring transmission times)?
options: 120 ms for Non-Persistent, 40 ms for Persistent
240 ms for Non-Persistent, 40 ms for Persistent
240 ms for Non-Persistent, 60 ms for Persistent
100 ms for Non-Persistent, 20 ms for Persistent
chapter-06-application-security.answer: 240 ms for Non-Persistent, 60 ms for Persistent
chapter-06-application-security.explanation:
Let's perform the RTT calculations:
1. Non-Persistent HTTP: Each object needs a new connection (1 RTT for handshake, 1 RTT for request/response = 2 RTTs per object).
   - Base HTML file: 2 RTTs.
   - 5 Images: 5 * 2 RTTs = 10 RTTs.
   - Total = 12 RTTs * 20 ms = 240 ms.
2. Persistent HTTP with Pipelining: Uses a single TCP connection for all items.
   - Handshake + HTML file: 1 RTT + 1 RTT = 2 RTTs.
   - All 5 images are requested in parallel / pipelined: 1 RTT.
   - Total = 3 RTTs * 20 ms = 60 ms.
chapter-06-application-security.examTrick: Non-Persistent: 2 * (1 + Images) RTTs. Persistent with Pipelining: 1 RTT (Handshake) + 1 RTT (HTML) + 1 RTT (All Images) = 3 RTTs total! If the connection is already open, it is just 2 RTTs.
chapter-06-application-security.subject: Computer Networks
chapter-06-application-security.chapterName: Application Layer Protocols and Network Security

chapter-06-application-security.question: In symmetric block ciphers, which operation mode processes each block independently, causing identical plaintext blocks to produce identical ciphertext blocks, and making it highly vulnerable to pattern analyses?
options: Cipher Block Chaining (CBC)
Electronic Codebook (ECB)
Cipher Feedback (CFB)
Output Feedback (OFB)
chapter-06-application-security.explanation: Electronic Codebook (ECB) is the simplest mode of operation. Each block of plaintext is encrypted individually using the same key. Therefore, identical plaintext blocks always result in identical ciphertext blocks, which preserves structural patterns. To prevent this, modes like CBC (Cipher Block Chaining) XOR each plaintext block with the previous ciphertext block before encryption.
chapter-06-application-security.examTrick: ECB = Penguin Tux visibility vulnerability! Because identical blocks yield identical ciphertexts, image outlines (like the Linux Tux) remain visible even after encryption. Use CBC or CTR mode to secure structures!
chapter-06-application-security.subject: Computer Networks
chapter-06-application-security.chapterName: Application Layer Protocols and Network Security

chapter-06-application-security.question: How does a sender 'Alice' cryptographically sign an email message to prove non-repudiation and integrity to receiver 'Bob'?
options: Alice encrypts the message with Bob's public key
Alice encrypts a hash of the message with her own private key
Alice encrypts the message with her own public key
Alice hashes the message with Bob's private key
chapter-06-application-security.answer: Alice encrypts a hash of the message with her own private key
chapter-06-application-security.explanation: A digital signature is generated by first hashing the message to a fixed size and then encrypting that hash using the sender's private key. The receiver (Bob) can decrypt the signature using the sender's (Alice's) public key and verify that it matches a freshly computed hash of the received message. Since only Alice possesses her private key, she cannot deny sending the message (non-repudiation) and any modification would break the hash (integrity).
chapter-06-application-security.examTrick: Digital Signature: Sign with SENDER'S PRIVATE key, verify with SENDER'S PUBLIC key! (Confidentiality is opposite: Encrypt with RECEIVER'S PUBLIC key, decrypt with RECEIVER'S PRIVATE key).
chapter-06-application-security.subject: Computer Networks
chapter-06-application-security.chapterName: Application Layer Protocols and Network Security

chapter-06-application-security.question: What is the difference between a recursive DNS query and an iterative DNS query?
options: Recursive queries are encrypted; iterative queries are plaintext
In a recursive query, the DNS client demands the local DNS server resolve the address completely, whereas in an iterative query, the server returns the IP address of the next DNS server to ask
Recursive queries use TCP; iterative queries use UDP
There is no difference; they are synonyms
chapter-06-application-security.answer: In a recursive query, the DNS client demands the local DNS server resolve the address completely, whereas in an iterative query, the server returns the IP address of the next DNS server to ask
chapter-06-application-security.explanation: In a recursive query, the client requests that the DNS server complete the resolution entirely and return either the final IP or an error. In an iterative query, the DNS server returns the IP of the next-level DNS server (Root, TLD, or Authoritative) that is closer to the destination, and the client must query that next server itself.
chapter-06-application-security.examTrick: Recursive = 'Do all the work for me and give me the final answer.' Iterative = 'I don't know the final answer, but here is the IP of the next server you should ask!'
chapter-06-application-security.subject: Computer Networks
chapter-06-application-security.chapterName: Application Layer Protocols and Network Security

chapter-06-application-security.question: During an SSL/TLS session negotiation, what is the role of the 'Server Key Exchange' message, and when is it sent?
options: It is sent by the server to transfer its digital certificate containing its public key
It is sent by the server to deliver temporary key parameters (e.g., Diffie-Hellman parameters) when the server's public key in its certificate is not sufficient for key exchange
It is sent to request the client's credit card credentials
It is sent to compress the HTTP headers
chapter-06-application-security.answer: It is sent by the server to deliver temporary key parameters (e.g., Diffie-Hellman parameters) when the server's public key in its certificate is not sufficient for key exchange
chapter-06-application-security.explanation: In SSL/TLS handshakes, if the negotiated key exchange algorithm is ephemeral (like Ephemeral Diffie-Hellman, DHE/ECDHE), the server's certificate public key is only used to sign the session parameters. The actual temporary key parameters must be sent separately in a 'Server Key Exchange' message so that forward secrecy can be achieved. If static RSA is used (where the client encrypts the pre-master secret using the server's certificate public key directly), this message is omitted.
chapter-06-application-security.examTrick: Server Key Exchange is only sent if the certificate's static public key isn't used for the direct key exchange (e.g., DHE/ECDHE). It contains the ephemeral key parameters.
chapter-06-application-security.subject: Computer Networks
chapter-06-application-security.chapterName: Application Layer Protocols and Network Security

chapter-06-application-security.question: Which SMTP command is sent by the client to gracefully terminate an established SMTP mail exchange session?
options: QUIT
CLOSE
EXIT
BYE
chapter-06-application-security.explanation: The SMTP protocol utilizes simple ASCII commands. To gracefully terminate the TCP connection, the client transmits the QUIT command, and the server responds with a '221 Service closing transmission channel' code before tearing down the connection.
chapter-06-application-security.examTrick: SMTP terminating command is QUIT. Server responds with code 221! Memorize this response code for CIL MT / PSU exams.
chapter-06-application-security.subject: Computer Networks
chapter-06-application-security.chapterName: Application Layer Protocols and Network Security

chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.question: During the 'Instruction Fetch' phase, what is the precise register-transfer sequence that moves an instruction from RAM to the CPU for decoding, and which hardware buses are utilized?
options: PC copies address to MAR -> MAR places it on Address Bus -> Memory places instruction on Data Bus -> MDR stores it -> MDR moves it to IR
PC places address on Data Bus -> MDR copies to MAR -> Memory reads and moves to IR directly
IR copies address to MAR -> MAR places it on Address Bus -> Memory places instruction on Control Bus -> PC stores it
PC copies address to MDR -> MDR places it on Address Bus -> Memory places instruction on Data Bus -> IR copies to MAR
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.answer: PC copies address to MAR -> MAR places it on Address Bus -> Memory places instruction on Data Bus -> MDR stores it -> MDR moves it to IR
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.explanation:
According to the Instruction Fetch Datapath section of the PDF, the physical transfer of an instruction from RAM to the CPU proceeds in four steps:
1. The Program Counter (PC), which holds the address of the next instruction, copies this address to the Memory Address Register (MAR).
2. The MAR places the address on the Address Bus to locate the memory cell in RAM, and a Memory Read control signal is asserted.
3. Main Memory retrieves the instruction and places it on the Data Bus, which carries it to the Memory Data Register (MDR).
4. The MDR copies the instruction to the Instruction Register (IR), where the Control Unit (CU) will decode it in the next cycle.
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.examTrick: Memory Flow Mnemonic: P-M-A-D-M-I. PC -> MAR -> Address Bus -> Data Bus -> MDR -> IR. Address leaves PC, instruction lands in IR!
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.subject: Computer Organization
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.chapterName: Instruction Sets, CPU Design, and Pipelining

chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.question: A CPU has a 0-Address instruction format. Which architectural component does this instruction format heavily rely on for operand retrieval, and how are operations like addition executed?
options: A Stack architecture; addition pops the top two elements, adds them, and pushes the result back onto the stack.
An Accumulator (AC) register; addition adds the memory content directly to the AC.
A General Purpose Register (GPR) file; addition retrieves operands via explicit register index fields.
A FIFO Queue; addition retrieves operands from the front and writes the result to the rear.
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.answer: A Stack architecture; addition pops the top two elements, adds them, and pushes the result back onto the stack.
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.explanation: According to the Instruction Formats section (1.2), a 0-address instruction does not specify any operand addresses in its instruction fields. Instead, it implicitly assumes a Stack architecture. When an operation like 'ADD' is executed, the CPU pops the top two elements from the stack, computes their sum using the ALU, and pushes the resulting sum back onto the top of the stack.
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.examTrick: Zero Address = Zero explicit operands in instruction = Stack (implicit LIFO). All math is done implicitly on the Top-of-Stack (TOS)!
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.subject: Computer Organization
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.chapterName: Instruction Sets, CPU Design, and Pipelining

chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.question: Consider the execution of the statement 'X = (A + B) * C' on a 1-Address (Accumulator-based) CPU architecture. Which of the following represents the correct sequence of assembly instructions to calculate and store the result?
options: LOAD A; ADD B; MULT C; STORE X
LOAD A; ADD B; STORE T; LOAD C; MULT T; STORE X
ADD A, B; MULT X, C
PUSH A; PUSH B; ADD; PUSH C; MULT; POP X
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.answer: LOAD A; ADD B; MULT C; STORE X
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.explanation:
In a 1-address architecture, every instruction has exactly one operand field, and the Accumulator (AC) register acts as the implicit source/destination for all operations:
1. LOAD A: AC = Memory[A]
2. ADD B: AC = AC + Memory[B] (performs A + B and saves to AC)
3. MULT C: AC = AC * Memory[C] (performs AC * C and saves to AC)
4. STORE X: Memory[X] = AC (writes result to variable X)
This matches option 1 and requires no temporary variables.
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.examTrick: 1-Address = One explicit memory address per instruction + implicit Accumulator (AC). Always start by LOADing into AC, execute operations with memory operands, and end with STORE!
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.subject: Computer Organization
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.chapterName: Instruction Sets, CPU Design, and Pipelining

chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.question: An 8-bit Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU) performs subtraction of two signed numbers in 2's complement representation: X = A - B. If A = 01110000 (+112) and B = 10010000 (-112), what is the resulting bit-pattern of X, and what are the statuses of the Carry (C) and Overflow (O/V) flags?
options: X = 00000000; Carry (C) = 1, Overflow (O) = 1
X = 11100000; Carry (C) = 0, Overflow (O) = 1
X = 11100000; Carry (C) = 1, Overflow (O) = 0
X = 00000000; Carry (C) = 0, Overflow (O) = 0
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.explanation:
To perform subtraction A - B, we add the 2's complement of B to A:
1. Given B = 10010000 (-112). Its 2's complement (-B) is: 01110000 (+112).
2. Perform addition A + (-B):
     01110000  (A = +112)
   + 01110000  (-B = +112)
   ------------
     11100000  (Result X = -32 in decimal)
3. Carry Flag (C): No carry out of the MSB addition (the carry out C_out = 0). Thus, Carry = 0.
4. Overflow Flag (O/V): Adding two positive signed numbers (MSB of both is 0) resulted in a negative number (MSB of X is 1). Alternatively, the carry into the MSB (C_in = 1) and carry out of the MSB (C_out = 0) are different: Overflow = C_in XOR C_out = 1 XOR 0 = 1.
Indeed, the correct signed result of 112 - (-112) is +224, which exceeds the maximum representable range of 8-bit signed integers [-128 to +127], triggering an overflow.
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.examTrick: Overflow Quick Rule: Adding two numbers of the same sign that yields a result of the OPPOSITE sign ALWAYS indicates signed overflow! (+112) + (+112) = negative number (-32) -> Overflow (O) = 1. Since no carry-out occurred, C = 0.
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.subject: Computer Organization
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.chapterName: Instruction Sets, CPU Design, and Pipelining

chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.question: Which of the following correct pairings matches the CPU Addressing Mode to its primary practical application and use case in computer systems?
options: Index Mode -> Array Access; Base Register Mode -> Program Relocation; Relative Mode -> Branch Control; Auto-increment -> Stack Push/Pop
Immediate Mode -> Program Relocation; Indirect Mode -> Array Access; Register Mode -> Branch Control; Index Mode -> Stack Push/Pop
Relative Mode -> Program Relocation; Index Mode -> Pointers; Direct Mode -> Branch Control; Base Register -> Stack Push/Pop
Register Indirect -> Program Relocation; Base Register -> Array Access; Relative Mode -> Pointers; Auto-decrement -> Branch Control
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.answer: Index Mode -> Array Access; Base Register Mode -> Program Relocation; Relative Mode -> Branch Control; Auto-increment -> Stack Push/Pop
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.explanation:
According to the Addressing Modes table (2.1) in the PDF:
1. Index Mode: EA = Index Register + Base Address. Base is constant (start of array), index changes. Used for Array Implementation.
2. Displacement / Base Register Mode: EA = Base Register + Offset. Offset is constant, base register changes when program is loaded. Used for Program Relocation in OS.
3. Relative Mode: EA = PC + Offset. Used for Branching and Loop control (IF/WHILE).
4. Auto-increment/decrement: Used for Pushing/Popping from Stacks and sequential processing.
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.examTrick:
A-B-C-D of modes:
- Index = Arrays (Index pointer incremented)
- Base = Relocation (Moving code bases around)
- Relative = Branches (Target is relative to PC)
- Auto-Inc = Stacks (Push/pop adjustments)
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.subject: Computer Organization
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.chapterName: Instruction Sets, CPU Design, and Pipelining

chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.question: If an operand is located in memory, what is the exact difference in the number of memory accesses required to fetch the operand under Direct Addressing Mode versus Indirect Addressing Mode?
options: Direct Mode requires 1 memory access; Indirect Mode requires 2 memory accesses.
Direct Mode requires 2 memory accesses; Indirect Mode requires 1 memory access.
Direct Mode requires 0 memory accesses; Indirect Mode requires 1 memory access.
Both modes require identical numbers of memory accesses.
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.answer: Direct Mode requires 1 memory access; Indirect Mode requires 2 memory accesses.
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.explanation:
Let's analyze the memory accesses needed to fetch the actual operand (excluding the initial fetch of the instruction itself):
- Under Direct Addressing Mode, the Effective Address (EA) is directly embedded in the instruction. The CPU performs exactly 1 memory access to read the operand from that address: EA = Address field.
- Under Indirect Addressing Mode, the address field of the instruction contains the address of the memory location that holds the Effective Address. Thus, the CPU must first access memory to fetch the EA, and then perform a 2nd memory access using that EA to fetch the actual operand: EA = Memory[Address field].
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.examTrick: Indirect = Double dereference = Double memory access! Each level of indirection adds 1 additional memory fetch. Direct is single memory access.
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.subject: Computer Organization
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.chapterName: Instruction Sets, CPU Design, and Pipelining

chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.question: A loop is accessing an array starting at base memory address 1000. Under Index Addressing Mode, if the constant Base Address field in the instruction is set to 1000 and the Index Register currently contains the value 2, how does the CPU compute the Effective Address, and does it modify the original instruction?
options: Effective Address is calculated as 1000 + 2 = 1002 using hardware adder; the original instruction remains unchanged.
Effective Address is calculated as 1000 * 2 = 2000; the base address in the instruction is dynamically overwritten with 2000.
Effective Address is calculated as 1000 - 2 = 998; the index register is reset to 0 in memory.
Effective Address is calculated as Memory[1002]; the instruction's opfield is modified to direct mode.
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.answer: Effective Address is calculated as 1000 + 2 = 1002 using hardware adder; the original instruction remains unchanged.
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.explanation: According to the Index Mode Scenario of the PDF (page 7), in Index Addressing Mode, the instruction contains the constant Base Address (1000). The Index Register dynamically stores the index value (i = 2). A hardware adder computes the Effective Address: EA = Base Address + Index Register = 1000 + 2 = 1002. This calculation is done 'on the fly' during address evaluation, leaving the original instruction code in the Instruction Register (IR) completely unmodified.
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.examTrick: Index addressing computes EA on the fly! The hardware ALU/adder combines them, leaving the base address instruction field pristine for subsequent loop iterations.
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.subject: Computer Organization
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.chapterName: Instruction Sets, CPU Design, and Pipelining

chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.question: A Program Counter (PC) relative branch instruction is stored in memory at address 1000. The branch instruction has an offset field containing the signed value -24. Assuming that the PC is automatically incremented by 2 bytes during the instruction fetch phase (before the branch offset is evaluated), what is the correct branch target address computed by the CPU?
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.explanation:
Let's perform the relative address trace step-by-step:
1. The branch instruction is fetched from memory address 1000.
2. During the instruction fetch phase, the PC is automatically incremented to point to the next sequential instruction: PC = Current Address + Instruction Size = 1000 + 2 = 1002.
3. In the Address Evaluation phase, the branch target (Effective Address) is computed relative to the updated PC: EA = PC_updated + Offset.
4. Substituting values: EA = 1002 + (-24) = 978.
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.examTrick: PC-Relative branch target trap! Always increment the PC first (PC = Branch_Addr + Instruction_Size) BEFORE adding the signed offset. Forgetting the PC increment is a classic off-by-one/two trap!
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.subject: Computer Organization
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.chapterName: Instruction Sets, CPU Design, and Pipelining

chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.question: What are the fundamental architectural differences between a 'Hardwired Control Unit' and a 'Microprogrammed Control Unit' in terms of implementation hardware, speed, and instruction set flexibility?
options: Hardwired uses combinational logic (decoders, flip-flops) and is extremely fast but rigid (RISC); Microprogrammed stores control signals in ROM (Control Memory) and is slower but highly flexible (CISC).
Hardwired stores control micro-instructions in high-speed RAM; Microprogrammed uses pure mechanical logic gates and is faster.
Hardwired is flexible and easily reprogrammed via firmware updates; Microprogrammed requires physical redesign of silicon to add instructions.
Hardwired is commonly used in CISC processors due to instruction complexity; Microprogrammed is used in RISC because of speed requirements.
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.answer: Hardwired uses combinational logic (decoders, flip-flops) and is extremely fast but rigid (RISC); Microprogrammed stores control signals in ROM (Control Memory) and is slower but highly flexible (CISC).
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.explanation:
According to the PDF section 3.1, the two control unit architectures differ as follows:
- Hardwired Control: Built using pure combinational logic (logic gates, decoders, state machines). Since signals propagate through physical silicon paths, it is extremely fast. However, it is rigid because modifying the instruction set requires physically redesigning and manufacturing the chip. Commonly used in RISC architectures.
- Microprogrammed Control: Control signals are stored as binary 'microinstructions' in a special high-speed ROM called Control Memory. Executing an instruction involves running a microprogram. It is slower due to memory read latency but highly flexible, allowing instructions to be added or modified via firmware updates. Commonly used in CISC architectures.
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.examTrick: Hardwired = Hard physical logic gates (RISC, Fast, Rigid). Microprogrammed = Programmed ROM memory (CISC, Slower, Flexible). Easy way to remember the trade-offs!
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.subject: Computer Organization
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.chapterName: Instruction Sets, CPU Design, and Pipelining

chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.question: In a Microprogrammed Control Unit, what is the distinction between 'Horizontal' and 'Vertical' microinstruction formats with respect to control signal encoding, execution speed, and control memory width?
options: Horizontal uses no encoding (one bit per control line), leading to wide memory formats and fastest execution; Vertical encodes mutually exclusive signals, requiring decoders which adds propagation delay but saves significant memory space.
Horizontal encodes signals to save memory; Vertical uses one bit per line and is faster.
Horizontal requires external decoders; Vertical directly controls hardware lines without decoders.
Both formats have identical memory footprints and execution speeds.
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.answer: Horizontal uses no encoding (one bit per control line), leading to wide memory formats and fastest execution; Vertical encodes mutually exclusive signals, requiring decoders which adds propagation delay but saves significant memory space.
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.explanation:
According to the Horizontal vs Vertical Microprogramming section (3.2) in the PDF:
- Horizontal Microprogramming: Every bit in the microinstruction directly corresponds to a specific control line. It features the fastest execution because no decoding delay is introduced. However, this yields very wide (long) microinstructions, consuming massive amounts of Control Memory.
- Vertical Microprogramming: Control signals are grouped into fields and encoded (e.g., using 3 bits to represent 8 signals). It requires an external decoder to unpack these bits to active hardware control lines, causing slower execution due to decoder gate propagation delay, but it drastically reduces the required Control Memory width.
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.examTrick: Horizontal = 1 bit per line = Wide/Fat = Unencoded = No Decoder = Fast. Vertical = Encoded = Narrow/Thin = Needs Decoder = Slower. Remember: Vertical saves money/space, Horizontal saves time!
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.subject: Computer Organization
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.chapterName: Instruction Sets, CPU Design, and Pipelining

chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.question: A microprogrammed control unit must generate 36 control signals. These signals are divided into 6 mutually exclusive groups containing 6, 8, 4, 7, 5, and 6 signals respectively. If vertical microprogramming is used, what is the minimum number of bits required in the microinstruction control field to represent these signals?
options: 19 bits
22 bits
36 bits
12 bits
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.explanation:
In vertical microprogramming, mutually exclusive control signals can be encoded into groups. 
- Important: Each group must also include a 'no-operation' (NOP) state to represent that none of the signals in that group are active. Thus, a group of N signals requires (N + 1) distinct states.
- The number of bits required to encode G states is ceil(log2(G)).
Let's calculate the bits for each of the 6 groups:
1. Group 1 (6 signals + 1 NOP = 7 states): ceil(log2(7)) = 3 bits.
2. Group 2 (8 signals + 1 NOP = 9 states): ceil(log2(9)) = 4 bits.
3. Group 3 (4 signals + 1 NOP = 5 states): ceil(log2(5)) = 3 bits.
4. Group 4 (7 signals + 1 NOP = 8 states): ceil(log2(8)) = 3 bits.
5. Group 5 (5 signals + 1 NOP = 6 states): ceil(log2(6)) = 3 bits.
6. Group 6 (6 signals + 1 NOP = 7 states): ceil(log2(7)) = 3 bits.
Total control field bits = 3 + 4 + 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 19 bits.
Wait, let's re-verify the question. If NOP is not implicitly required for groups or if options are given: Let's calculate the sum of ceil(log2(N+1)) which is 19. Wait, is there any other calculation? Let's check: 
- G1: 6 signals -> 7 states -> 3 bits
- G2: 8 signals -> 9 states -> 4 bits
- G3: 4 signals -> 5 states -> 3 bits
- G4: 7 signals -> 8 states -> 3 bits
- G5: 5 signals -> 6 states -> 3 bits
- G6: 6 signals -> 7 states -> 3 bits
Sum = 3 + 4 + 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 19 bits.
Let's check if we don't add NOP (some textbooks omit NOP, though GATE strictly requires it):
- G1: ceil(log2(6)) = 3 bits
- G2: ceil(log2(8)) = 3 bits
- G3: ceil(log2(4)) = 2 bits
- G4: ceil(log2(7)) = 3 bits
- G5: ceil(log2(5)) = 3 bits
- G6: ceil(log2(6)) = 3 bits
Sum = 3 + 3 + 2 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 17 bits. Since 19 is in the options and is technically rigorous, let's write 19 as the answer and explain both.
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.examTrick: Vertical encoding rule: For N signals in a group, we need ceil(log2(N + 1)) bits because we must reserve one code (all zeros usually) to represent 'No Operation' (active idle). Always add 1 before taking the ceiling log2!
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.subject: Computer Organization
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.chapterName: Instruction Sets, CPU Design, and Pipelining

chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.question: A 5-stage instruction pipeline has stage delays of 150 ns, 120 ns, 180 ns, 140 ns, and 110 ns. Interface latches between stages introduce an additional delay of 10 ns. What is the clock cycle time of this pipelined processor, and how much time does it take to execute 100 independent instructions?
options: Clock cycle = 190 ns; Total execution time = 19,760 ns
Clock cycle = 180 ns; Total execution time = 18,720 ns
Clock cycle = 190 ns; Total execution time = 19,000 ns
Clock cycle = 180 ns; Total execution time = 19,000 ns
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.answer: Clock cycle = 190 ns; Total execution time = 19,760 ns
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.explanation:
Let's perform the pipelining calculations:
1. Clock Cycle Time (Tp): The clock period is determined by the slowest stage plus any interface latch delay (overhead):
   Tp = max(Stage Delays) + Latch Delay
   Tp = max(150, 120, 180, 140, 110) + 10 ns = 180 ns + 10 ns = 190 ns.
2. Total execution time for n instructions in a k-stage pipeline is given by:
   Total Time = [k + (n - 1)] * Tp
   Where k = 5 stages, n = 100 instructions, Tp = 190 ns.
   Total Time = [5 + (100 - 1)] * 190 ns = [5 + 99] * 190 = 104 * 190 = 19,760 ns.
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.examTrick: Pipelining Delay Rule: Clock Cycle is bounded by 'Slowest Stage + Latch Overhead'. Do NOT forget the latch delay! Total cycles to finish N instructions in a K-stage pipe is K + N - 1. Multiply by clock period for final answer.
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.subject: Computer Organization
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.chapterName: Instruction Sets, CPU Design, and Pipelining

chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.question: A non-pipelined processor takes 12 ns to execute a single instruction. The same processor is redesigned with an 8-stage pipeline running at a clock period of 1.8 ns. What is the actual speedup achieved by the pipelined processor for executing 1000 instructions?
options: Speedup = 6.62
Speedup = 8.00
Speedup = 5.43
Speedup = 4.88
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.explanation:
Let's calculate the speedup (S):
1. Time taken by non-pipelined processor (T_nonpipe) to execute n = 1000 instructions:
   T_nonpipe = n * Execution_Time = 1000 * 12 ns = 12,000 ns.
2. Time taken by k = 8 stage pipelined processor (T_pipe) to execute n = 1000 instructions at clock period Tp = 1.8 ns:
   T_pipe = [k + (n - 1)] * Tp
   T_pipe = [8 + (1000 - 1)] * 1.8 = 1007 * 1.8 = 1812.6 ns.
3. Speedup (S) is the ratio of non-pipelined time to pipelined time:
   S = T_nonpipe / T_pipe = 12,000 / 1812.6 = 6.6203.
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.examTrick: Speedup formula: S = (n * t_n) / ((k + n - 1) * t_p). If n approaches infinity, speedup reaches its theoretical limit which is t_n / t_p (12 / 1.8 = 6.67). Since 1000 is a large number, the speedup is very close to this limit: 6.62!
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.subject: Computer Organization
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.chapterName: Instruction Sets, CPU Design, and Pipelining

chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.question: An instruction pipeline experiences a 'Structural Hazard'. What is the physical cause of this hazard type, and what is the standard architectural solution used in modern CPUs?
options: Resource conflict where multiple stages attempt to access the same physical hardware simultaneously; solved by Harvard Architecture (separating Instruction Cache and Data Cache).
Data dependency where an instruction reads a register before a previous one writes it; solved by branch prediction.
A conditional branch instruction changing the target PC; solved by inserting multiple NOP bubbles.
Clock signal skew where latches fail to synchronize; solved by reducing clock speed.
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.answer: Resource conflict where multiple stages attempt to access the same physical hardware simultaneously; solved by Harvard Architecture (separating Instruction Cache and Data Cache).
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.explanation:
According to the Pipeline Hazards section of the PDF (page 12):
- Structural Hazards occur due to resource conflicts where the hardware cannot support all possible combinations of instructions in simultaneous execution. For example, if a single memory bus is shared, the Instruction Fetch (IF) stage (fetching code) and the Memory/Write (MEM) stage (writing data) will clash when trying to access memory in the same clock cycle.
- The standard solution is to split the physical memory interface or cache into separate Instruction Cache (I-Cache) and Data Cache (D-Cache). This separate routing architecture is known as the Harvard Architecture.
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.examTrick: Structural Hazard = Hardware Collision (Memory/ALU clash). Solution = Dual Ports, Register File replication, or Harvard Architecture (Split I-Cache and D-Cache)!
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.subject: Computer Organization
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.chapterName: Instruction Sets, CPU Design, and Pipelining

chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.question: Which of the following describes a 'Read-After-Write' (RAW) data hazard in a pipelined processor, and what is the standard hardware optimization that eliminates execution stall cycles?
options: An instruction attempts to read a source register before a preceding instruction writes to it; resolved by Operand Forwarding (bypassing the result directly from execution latches to ALU inputs).
An instruction writes to a register before a subsequent instruction reads it; resolved by delayed branching.
Multiple instructions attempt to read from the memory bus concurrently; resolved by Harvard Architecture.
An instruction reads a register after it has been written; resolved by inserting a standard hardware stall.
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.answer: An instruction attempts to read a source register before a preceding instruction writes to it; resolved by Operand Forwarding (bypassing the result directly from execution latches to ALU inputs).
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.explanation:
According to the Pipeline Hazards section of the PDF, RAW (Read-After-Write) is the most common data hazard. It occurs when Instruction I2 tries to read a register that is yet to be written back by preceding Instruction I1. 
- Without optimization, I2 must stall until I1 reaches the Write-Back (WB) stage.
- Modern processors solve this using Operand Forwarding (or Bypassing). As soon as the result is computed in the ALU at the end of the Execute (EX) stage of I1, it is directly routed over a bypass bus to the ALU input for the EX stage of I2, completely bypassing the register write-back step and eliminating stall cycles.
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.examTrick: RAW = True Dependency (Read before Write). Solution = Operand Forwarding. The ALU result is grabbed directly from intermediate registers/latches, avoiding waiting for Register File updates!
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.subject: Computer Organization
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.chapterName: Instruction Sets, CPU Design, and Pipelining

chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.question: Consider three instructions in execution: I1: ADD R1, R2, R3; I2: SUB R4, R1, R5; I3: ADD R1, R6, R7. Which of the following correctly identifies the hazard types existing between these instructions?
options: RAW hazard between I1 and I2 on register R1; WAW hazard between I1 and I3 on register R1.
WAR hazard between I1 and I2 on register R1; RAW hazard between I2 and I3 on register R4.
Structural hazard between I1 and I3 on ALU; Control hazard between I2 and I3.
RAW hazard between I2 and I3 on register R1; WAR hazard between I1 and I2 on register R4.
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.answer: RAW hazard between I1 and I2 on register R1; WAW hazard between I1 and I3 on register R1.
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.explanation:
Let's inspect the register dependencies:
- I1 writes to R1 (destination is first in this assembly convention: ADD dest, src1, src2).
- I2 reads R1 (SUB dest, src1, src2). Thus, I2 is reading a register written by I1. This is a Read-After-Write (RAW) data hazard.
- I3 writes to R1. Since both I1 and I3 write to the same register R1, and their order of writing must be preserved, there is a Write-After-Write (WAW) hazard between I1 and I3.
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.examTrick:
Dependency Mapping:
- I1 (Write R1) -> I2 (Read R1) = RAW (True dependency)
- I2 (Read R1) -> I3 (Write R1) = WAR (Anti-dependency)
- I1 (Write R1) -> I3 (Write R1) = WAW (Output dependency)
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.subject: Computer Organization
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.chapterName: Instruction Sets, CPU Design, and Pipelining

chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.question: A pipeline processor has a branch instruction frequency of 20%. The branch predictor is 80% accurate. If a branch is predicted correctly, there is 0 stall cycles. If a branch is mispredicted, the pipeline experiences a 3-cycle branch penalty. If the base CPI under ideal execution is 1.0, what is the average CPI of this processor?
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.explanation:
Let's calculate the average CPI:
1. The processor executes instructions. Under ideal conditions, CPI = 1.0.
2. Branches occur with a frequency of P_branch = 20% = 0.20.
3. The branch predictor mispredicts with a rate of: P_mispredict = 1 - Accuracy = 1 - 0.80 = 20% = 0.20.
4. When a misprediction occurs, there is an additional branch penalty of 3 cycles.
5. The average stall cycles per instruction is calculated as:
   Stalls = Frequency of branch * Misprediction rate * Misprediction penalty
   Stalls = 0.20 * 0.20 * 3 = 0.04 * 3 = 0.12 cycles.
6. Average CPI = Ideal CPI + Stall cycles = 1.0 + 0.12 = 1.12.
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.examTrick: Stall Formula: Branch_Freq * Mispredict_Rate * Penalty. Here, 0.20 * (1 - 0.80) * 3 = 0.12. Add to base CPI (1.0) to get 1.12. Keep it clean and structured!
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.subject: Computer Organization
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.chapterName: Instruction Sets, CPU Design, and Pipelining

chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.question: In a pipeline processor, what does a 'Control Hazard' refer to, and which of the following is a compiler-level software technique used to resolve or minimize it?
options: A delay caused by branch/jump instructions changing the Program Counter; minimized by 'Delayed Branching' where the compiler fills branch delay slots with useful independent instructions.
A clash over hardware buses; resolved by inserting NOP bubbles manually in the assembly file.
A register dependency; resolved by using an out-of-order execution register renaming technique.
An interrupt service routine call; resolved by disabling CPU interrupts during loop execution.
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.answer: A delay caused by branch/jump instructions changing the Program Counter; minimized by 'Delayed Branching' where the compiler fills branch delay slots with useful independent instructions.
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.explanation:
According to the Pipeline Hazards section of the PDF (page 12):
- Control Hazards (Branch Hazards) occur when branch or jump instructions change the value of the Program Counter (PC). Since the next instruction cannot be fetched with certainty until the branch condition is evaluated and the target address is calculated, fetched instructions might become invalid and must be flushed, causing pipeline bubbles.
- Delayed Branching is a software technique where the compiler rearranges code to place one or more independent, useful instructions in 'branch delay slots' immediately following the branch instruction. These slot instructions are executed regardless of whether the branch is taken or not, preventing empty stalls.
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.examTrick: Control Hazard = Branch/Jump PC change. Compiler solution = Delayed Branching (filling delay slots with NOPs or useful independent instructions) so the CPU pipeline never sits idle!
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.subject: Computer Organization
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.chapterName: Instruction Sets, CPU Design, and Pipelining

chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.question: Which of the following represents the correct sequential order of the phases of a complete instruction cycle as executed inside a central processing unit?
options: Fetch -> Decode -> Evaluate Address -> Execute -> Store
Fetch -> Evaluate Address -> Decode -> Execute -> Store
Decode -> Fetch -> Evaluate Address -> Execute -> Store
Fetch -> Decode -> Execute -> Evaluate Address -> Store
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.answer: Fetch -> Decode -> Evaluate Address -> Execute -> Store
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.explanation:
According to Section 1.1 of the PDF (page 3), the execution of every machine instruction involves a sequence of phases called the Instruction Cycle. The exact chronological order is:
1. Fetch: Read the next instruction from memory into the Instruction Register (IR).
2. Decode: The Control Unit determines the operation to be performed and the addressing mode.
3. Evaluate Address: Compute the effective address of the operand if indirect addressing is used.
4. Execute: The Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU) performs the actual operation.
5. Store: Write the computed result back to a register or memory location.
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.examTrick: Classic chronological flow of instructions: F-D-A-E-S (Fetch, Decode, Address, Execute, Store). Standard PSU exam question!
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.subject: Computer Organization
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.chapterName: Instruction Sets, CPU Design, and Pipelining

chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.question: What is the theoretical maximum speedup that an 8-stage instruction pipeline can achieve over a non-pipelined processor under ideal conditions as the number of instructions (n) approaches infinity, and why can this maximum speedup never be physically reached in practice?
options: Maximum speedup is 8; cannot be reached due to pipeline hazards (structural, data, control) and latch register overheads.
Maximum speedup is infinity; cannot be reached because CPU clock speeds are physically limited by heat dissipation.
Maximum speedup is 1; cannot be reached because pipelined execution is inherently slower.
Maximum speedup is 4; cannot be reached because memory bus widths restrict data transfers.
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.answer: Maximum speedup is 8; cannot be reached due to pipeline hazards (structural, data, control) and latch register overheads.
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.explanation:
According to the Speedup Calculation section (4.1) of the PDF:
- Speedup (S) is given by: S = Time(non-pipeline) / Time(pipeline) = (n * k) / (k + n - 1).
- As the number of instructions (n) approaches infinity:
  Lim (n -> inf) of S = k (number of pipeline stages). For an 8-stage pipeline, the theoretical maximum speedup is exactly 8.
- In physical processors, this ideal limit is never reached due to:
  1. Pipeline Hazards (stalls/bubbles caused by structural resource conflicts, data dependencies, and branch flushes).
  2. Interface Latch Delays (the propagation overhead of register latches between stages, which makes the clock period of the pipeline larger than the ideal fraction of non-pipelined execution).
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.examTrick: Theoretical Speedup Max = k (number of stages). Practical Speedup is ALWAYS < k due to: Hazards (Stalls) + Latch Overhead (setup/propagation time)!
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.subject: Computer Organization
chapter-01-instruction-pipelining.chapterName: Instruction Sets, CPU Design, and Pipelining

chapter-02-memory-io-dma.question: Arrange the following storage devices of the memory hierarchy in increasing order of speed and cost per byte, and in decreasing order of capacity and latency.
options: Secondary Storage (Magnetic/SSD) < Main Memory (DRAM) < Cache Memory (SRAM) < Registers
Registers < Cache Memory (SRAM) < Main Memory (DRAM) < Secondary Storage (Magnetic/SSD)
Main Memory (DRAM) < Secondary Storage (Magnetic/SSD) < Cache Memory (SRAM) < Registers
Secondary Storage (Magnetic/SSD) < Cache Memory (SRAM) < Main Memory (DRAM) < Registers
chapter-02-memory-io-dma.answer: Secondary Storage (Magnetic/SSD) < Main Memory (DRAM) < Cache Memory (SRAM) < Registers
chapter-02-memory-io-dma.explanation:
According to the classical Memory Hierarchy Pyramid in the PDF (page 13):
- As you move UP the pyramid (from Secondary Storage to Registers), the speed and cost per byte INCREASE. Registers are the fastest and most expensive per byte, followed by Cache (SRAM), Main Memory (DRAM), and Secondary Storage (SSD/Magnetic).
- As you move DOWN the pyramid (from Registers to Secondary Storage), the storage capacity and access latency INCREASE (which is the same as decreasing capacity and latency in the reverse order).
chapter-02-memory-io-dma.examTrick: Memory Pyramid Rule: Higher up = Faster, Costlier, Smaller, Lower Latency. Bottom = Slower, Cheaper, Larger, Higher Latency. SRAM is Cache, DRAM is Main Memory!
chapter-02-memory-io-dma.subject: Computer Organization
chapter-02-memory-io-dma.chapterName: Memory Hierarchy, Cache, and I/O DMA Control

chapter-02-memory-io-dma.question: Which of the following describes how the 'Principle of Locality' is exploited by system designers to successfully operate Cache Memory?
options: Temporal Locality is exploited by keeping recently accessed variables in Cache; Spatial Locality is exploited by fetching data as larger 'Blocks' rather than single bytes.
Temporal Locality is exploited by bringing adjacent memory cells into the registers; Spatial Locality is exploited by running multiple loops concurrently.
Both temporal and spatial locality are exploited by bypassing the cache memory entirely and writing directly to magnetic disks.
Temporal Locality is exploited by increasing the physical size of RAM; Spatial Locality is exploited by reducing the CPU clock period.
chapter-02-memory-io-dma.answer: Temporal Locality is exploited by keeping recently accessed variables in Cache; Spatial Locality is exploited by fetching data as larger 'Blocks' rather than single bytes.
chapter-02-memory-io-dma.explanation:
According to the Principle of Locality section of the PDF (page 14):
1. Temporal Locality: If a memory location is accessed, it is highly likely to be accessed again soon (e.g., variables in a loop). The cache exploits this by retaining recently accessed data blocks.
2. Spatial Locality: If a memory location is accessed, locations adjacent to it are likely to be accessed soon (e.g., array traversal, sequential instructions). Spatial locality is exploited by bringing data into the cache as larger 'Blocks' (or Cache Lines) rather than fetching single isolated bytes.
chapter-02-memory-io-dma.examTrick: Temporal = Time (re-accessing same variable in a loop). Spatial = Space (accessing neighbors, solved by bringing whole memory blocks into cache lines)!
