chapter-03-subagent-invocation-and-conte.explanation: Subagents start with isolated context and do not automatically inherit parent conversation history. The coordinator must explicitly inject prior findings into the subagent's spawn prompt.
chapter-03-subagent-invocation-and-conte.examTrick: Subagents DO NOT inherit parent context. Coordinator must explicitly pass required facts in prompt.
chapter-03-subagent-invocation-and-conte.subject: Claude CCAF: Agentic Architecture & Orchestration
chapter-03-subagent-invocation-and-conte.chapterName: 1.3 Subagent Invocation, Task Tool & Context Isolation

chapter-03-subagent-invocation-and-conte.question: A "database-migration-writer" subagent that only needs to read schema and write migration files currently has full parent tool access, including production deploys and database deletion. No incidents yet. Most important reason to fix this before launch?
options: Scoping the subagent's tools to only what its task requires limits the blast radius of a reasoning error or prompt injection, independent of whether one has happened yet.
Broad tool access makes responses slower because more tools must be considered per turn.
Broad tool access increases token cost since more tool definitions are included in context.
Other engineers reviewing the config will be confused about what it's supposed to do.
chapter-03-subagent-invocation-and-conte.answer: Scoping the subagent's tools to only what its task requires limits the blast radius of a reasoning error or prompt injection, independent of whether one has happened yet.
chapter-03-subagent-invocation-and-conte.source: QD1-15 | Claude Code subagents — tool restrictions · Settings and permissions
chapter-03-subagent-invocation-and-conte.explanation: Least privilege bounds the worst-case blast radius. If a subagent is manipulated via prompt injection or suffers a reasoning error, it structurally cannot execute deploy or delete actions.
chapter-03-subagent-invocation-and-conte.examTrick: Tool access scoping = Least privilege to bound blast radius against injection & reasoning errors.
chapter-03-subagent-invocation-and-conte.subject: Claude CCAF: Agentic Architecture & Orchestration
chapter-03-subagent-invocation-and-conte.chapterName: 1.3 Subagent Invocation, Task Tool & Context Isolation

chapter-03-subagent-invocation-and-conte.question: Which fields best support a reliable research -> writing subagent handoff?
options: Just the raw text output of the research subagent's final response.
Only a success/failure flag plus a pointer to where full logs can be found.
The entire research subagent's tool-call history, so the writer can re-derive anything it needs.
Structured fields for the specific findings/data produced, the original task's relevant constraints, and an explicit statement of what's still unresolved/uncertain.
chapter-03-subagent-invocation-and-conte.answer: Structured fields for the specific findings/data produced, the original task's relevant constraints, and an explicit statement of what's still unresolved/uncertain.
chapter-03-subagent-invocation-and-conte.source: QD1-31 | Multi-agent research system — handoffs · Structured outputs
chapter-03-subagent-invocation-and-conte.explanation: A reliable handoff schema contains: (1) Findings/data payload, (2) Task constraints (audience, tone, length), and (3) Unresolved/uncertain items to prevent presenting gaps as settled facts.
chapter-03-subagent-invocation-and-conte.examTrick: Reliable handoff schema = Findings payload + Task constraints + Unresolved uncertainties.
chapter-03-subagent-invocation-and-conte.subject: Claude CCAF: Agentic Architecture & Orchestration
chapter-03-subagent-invocation-and-conte.chapterName: 1.3 Subagent Invocation, Task Tool & Context Isolation

chapter-03-subagent-invocation-and-conte.question: A web-search subagent's fetched content contains an embedded prompt injection. What limits the damage?
options: The coordinator's own prompt tells it to ignore any instructions found in fetched content.
The subagent's output is logged, so damage can be detected after the fact.
Prompt injections can't affect subagents because they only process search results, not user instructions.
The subagent's context is isolated and its tool access is scoped narrowly, so even if it's manipulated, it can't take actions or access data outside what it was already permitted to touch.
chapter-03-subagent-invocation-and-conte.answer: The subagent's context is isolated and its tool access is scoped narrowly, so even if it's manipulated, it can't take actions or access data outside what it was already permitted to touch.
chapter-03-subagent-invocation-and-conte.source: QD1-35 | Claude Code subagents — tool restrictions · Claude Code security
chapter-03-subagent-invocation-and-conte.explanation: Prompt injection cannot be prevented by instructions alone. Isolated context and narrow tool permissions bound the blast radius — a compromised subagent holds no credentials or destructive tools.
chapter-03-subagent-invocation-and-conte.examTrick: Defense against indirect injection in subagents = Context isolation + Narrow tool permissions.
chapter-03-subagent-invocation-and-conte.subject: Claude CCAF: Agentic Architecture & Orchestration
chapter-03-subagent-invocation-and-conte.chapterName: 1.3 Subagent Invocation, Task Tool & Context Isolation

chapter-03-subagent-invocation-and-conte.question: A coordinator's attempt to spawn a document-analysis subagent fails; its allowedTools is missing an entry. What's missing?
options: "Spawn"
Nothing is missing; subagent spawning doesn't require any tool permission.
The subagent's own AgentDefinition must list "Task" in its allowedTools.
"Task"
chapter-03-subagent-invocation-and-conte.source: QD1S-13 | Claude Code subagents · Claude Agent SDK
chapter-03-subagent-invocation-and-conte.explanation: Delegation and subagent spawning occur via the Task tool. The coordinator must include "Task" in its allowedTools configuration to invoke subagents.
chapter-03-subagent-invocation-and-conte.examTrick: Coordinator allowedTools must include 'Task' to spawn subagents.
chapter-03-subagent-invocation-and-conte.subject: Claude CCAF: Agentic Architecture & Orchestration
chapter-03-subagent-invocation-and-conte.chapterName: 1.3 Subagent Invocation, Task Tool & Context Isolation

chapter-03-subagent-invocation-and-conte.question: Coordinator prompts to subagents read like step-by-step procedural checklists ("First call search_web with X, then Y, then stop"), and subagents rarely adapt to unexpected findings. Most likely design issue?
options: The subagents are missing tool access needed to adapt their procedures.
The coordinator should switch to fork_session so each subagent can explore divergent procedures.
This is expected and correct behavior.
The coordinator prompts specify rigid procedures rather than research goals and quality criteria, which limits the subagent's ability to adapt as it discovers new information.
chapter-03-subagent-invocation-and-conte.answer: The coordinator prompts specify rigid procedures rather than research goals and quality criteria, which limits the subagent's ability to adapt as it discovers new information.
chapter-03-subagent-invocation-and-conte.source: QD1S-17 | Multi-agent research system — delegating goals, not procedures
chapter-03-subagent-invocation-and-conte.explanation: Procedural checklists convert agents into rigid workflow executors. Delegating research goals and quality criteria (breadth, recency, contradiction checks) gives subagents latitude to adapt.
chapter-03-subagent-invocation-and-conte.examTrick: Delegate goals and quality criteria, not rigid procedural step checklists.
chapter-03-subagent-invocation-and-conte.subject: Claude CCAF: Agentic Architecture & Orchestration
chapter-03-subagent-invocation-and-conte.chapterName: 1.3 Subagent Invocation, Task Tool & Context Isolation

chapter-03-subagent-invocation-and-conte.question: A firm wants to use compaction in subagents as well as the parent. Which design consideration BEST applies?
options: Subagents cannot be compacted at all.
Subagents should compact more aggressively than parents, since tighter scope means heavier summarization does less damage.
Subagents typically have shorter lifespans and tighter scope, so compaction is often unnecessary.
Require compaction for every subagent as a universal context-hygiene rule.
chapter-03-subagent-invocation-and-conte.answer: Subagents typically have shorter lifespans and tighter scope, so compaction is often unnecessary.
chapter-03-subagent-invocation-and-conte.source: BU1-001 (§1.3) | Context windows and compaction · Effective context engineering
chapter-03-subagent-invocation-and-conte.explanation: Subagents are scoped to bounded tasks and short lifespans, rarely generating context pressure. Compacting short-lived subagents wastes summarization passes and risks losing task-dense details.
chapter-03-subagent-invocation-and-conte.examTrick: Subagent compaction is usually unnecessary due to short lifespans and curated narrow scope.
chapter-03-subagent-invocation-and-conte.subject: Claude CCAF: Agentic Architecture & Orchestration
chapter-03-subagent-invocation-and-conte.chapterName: 1.3 Subagent Invocation, Task Tool & Context Isolation

chapter-03-subagent-invocation-and-conte.question: An orchestrator dispatches refunds to a refund-subagent that holds the refund API tool — but the orchestrator also has the refund API tool registered for emergency direct refunds. What concrete cost does this duplication impose?
options: The orchestrator's tool registry consumes roughly twice the memory.
Duplicate registrations cause the MCP protocol to reject the session at startup.
The subagent's calls will be routed to the orchestrator's tool handler instead of its own.
The orchestrator may invoke the refund tool directly for routine cases, bypassing the audit logging and review steps the refund-subagent layer adds.
chapter-03-subagent-invocation-and-conte.answer: The orchestrator may invoke the refund tool directly for routine cases, bypassing the audit logging and review steps the refund-subagent layer adds.
chapter-03-subagent-invocation-and-conte.source: BU1-006 (§1.3) | Claude Code subagents — tool restrictions · Settings and permissions
chapter-03-subagent-invocation-and-conte.explanation: The subagent is a control layer adding audit logging, validation, and policy checks. Registering the same tool on the orchestrator provides a bypass path that skips those controls.
chapter-03-subagent-invocation-and-conte.examTrick: Duplicate tool registration on orchestrator risks bypassing subagent-level policy & audit controls.
chapter-03-subagent-invocation-and-conte.subject: Claude CCAF: Agentic Architecture & Orchestration
chapter-03-subagent-invocation-and-conte.chapterName: 1.3 Subagent Invocation, Task Tool & Context Isolation

chapter-03-subagent-invocation-and-conte.question: A Claude Code-driven literature review where the parent must keep its context clean for final synthesis. Which architecture BEST combines Claude Code's execution model with context isolation?
options: Parent reads every source itself sequentially so synthesis has full provenance.
Parent spawns one subagent that reads all sources for all topics in one giant pass.
Parent issues Agent tool calls per topic; subagents read sources in their own contexts and return only structured summaries, keeping parent context lean for synthesis.
Parent uses Bash grep across the corpus and pipes raw matches into its own reasoning.
chapter-03-subagent-invocation-and-conte.answer: Parent issues Agent tool calls per topic; subagents read sources in their own contexts and return only structured summaries, keeping parent context lean for synthesis.
chapter-03-subagent-invocation-and-conte.source: BU1-007 (§1.3) | Claude Code subagents · Effective context engineering
chapter-03-subagent-invocation-and-conte.explanation: Heavy reading occurs in isolated subagent contexts. Only distilled structured summaries cross back to the parent, preserving the parent's context window for high-level synthesis.
chapter-03-subagent-invocation-and-conte.examTrick: High-volume literature review = Subagents per topic read in isolation -> return structured summaries.
chapter-03-subagent-invocation-and-conte.subject: Claude CCAF: Agentic Architecture & Orchestration
chapter-03-subagent-invocation-and-conte.chapterName: 1.3 Subagent Invocation, Task Tool & Context Isolation

chapter-04-workflow-enforcement-and-hand.question: A support agent processes refunds without verifying account ownership in 8% of cases despite a system prompt saying "always verify customer before refunds." Which architectural fix provides a deterministic guarantee for financial operations?
options: Improve the system prompt with stronger instructions and more examples.
Add few-shot examples showing get_customer before every refund.
Implement a programmatic prerequisite hook blocking process_refund until get_customer completes successfully.
Deploy a separate classifier routing refund requests through identity verification.
chapter-04-workflow-enforcement-and-hand.answer: Implement a programmatic prerequisite hook blocking process_refund until get_customer completes successfully.
chapter-04-workflow-enforcement-and-hand.source: UD1-008 | Claude Code hooks — PreToolUse · Building effective agents
chapter-04-workflow-enforcement-and-hand.explanation: Prompts are probabilistic. Financial operations requiring deterministic guarantees must use code-level PreToolUse hooks that block execution unless prerequisite conditions (e.g. verified get_customer) are satisfied.
chapter-04-workflow-enforcement-and-hand.examTrick: Deterministic financial/policy guarantee = PreToolUse programmatic prerequisite hook.
chapter-04-workflow-enforcement-and-hand.subject: Claude CCAF: Agentic Architecture & Orchestration

chapter-04-workflow-enforcement-and-hand.question: A support agent must compile a self-contained handoff summary when escalating; the human has no transcript access. What must be included?
options: Escalation reason only, as the human will investigate independently.
References to conversation turn numbers for the human to look up.
A brief summary assuming the human has full conversation context.
Customer ID, conversation summary, root cause, refund amount, recommended action.
chapter-04-workflow-enforcement-and-hand.answer: Customer ID, conversation summary, root cause, refund amount, recommended action.
chapter-04-workflow-enforcement-and-hand.source: UD1-016 | Building effective agents — human handoff
chapter-04-workflow-enforcement-and-hand.explanation: A self-contained handoff must provide all necessary facts directly (Customer ID, root cause, amounts, attempted actions, recommended next steps) without requiring transcript access.
chapter-04-workflow-enforcement-and-hand.examTrick: Self-contained handoff: Customer ID + Root cause + Amounts/Details + Attempted steps + Recommended action.
chapter-04-workflow-enforcement-and-hand.subject: Claude CCAF: Agentic Architecture & Orchestration

chapter-04-workflow-enforcement-and-hand.question: A customer asks to speak with a human manager after one unsuccessful troubleshooting attempt. The agent has more steps it could try. What should the agent do?
options: Ask the customer if they'd like to try one more troubleshooting step before escalating.
Escalate but first run diagnostic checks to provide the human with context.
Honor the customer's explicit request for a human representative immediately.
Attempt the remaining troubleshooting steps since the agent may resolve the issue.
chapter-04-workflow-enforcement-and-hand.answer: Honor the customer's explicit request for a human representative immediately.
chapter-04-workflow-enforcement-and-hand.explanation: An explicit customer request for a human is a hard escalation trigger. Overriding it damages user trust. Escalate immediately with the context already gathered.
chapter-04-workflow-enforcement-and-hand.examTrick: Explicit customer request for human = Immediate escalation without delaying for extra diagnostic calls.
chapter-04-workflow-enforcement-and-hand.subject: Claude CCAF: Agentic Architecture & Orchestration

chapter-04-workflow-enforcement-and-hand.question: Policy requires human approval for refunds above $500; a customer requests $847. An emphatic system prompt still yields a 3% failure rate. What fix provides zero tolerance?
options: A separate classifier model evaluating each refund request first.
A self-check step where the agent validates the amount before calling process_refund.
An application-layer hook intercepting process_refund, blocking it server-side when the amount exceeds $500, and triggering human escalation.
Strengthen the system prompt with more emphatic language and examples.
chapter-04-workflow-enforcement-and-hand.answer: An application-layer hook intercepting process_refund, blocking it server-side when the amount exceeds $500, and triggering human escalation.
chapter-04-workflow-enforcement-and-hand.source: UD1-076 | Claude Code hooks · Building effective agents
chapter-04-workflow-enforcement-and-hand.explanation: Threshold comparisons are deterministic numbers. Server-side PreToolUse hooks enforce numerical thresholds at code level (amount > 500 -> block & escalate), providing 0% bypass.
chapter-04-workflow-enforcement-and-hand.examTrick: Zero-tolerance policy threshold = Server-side hook intercepting tool call and enforcing threshold.
chapter-04-workflow-enforcement-and-hand.subject: Claude CCAF: Agentic Architecture & Orchestration

chapter-04-workflow-enforcement-and-hand.question: A payment call times out, the agent retries, and a duplicate charge occurs. What pattern prevents duplicate transactions?
options: Increase the timeout to prevent timeouts from occurring.
Add a 30-second delay between retries so the first request completes or fails.
Use idempotency keys with each payment request so retries produce the same result as the original call.
Check the account balance before retrying to see if the first charge went through.
chapter-04-workflow-enforcement-and-hand.answer: Use idempotency keys with each payment request so retries produce the same result as the original call.
chapter-04-workflow-enforcement-and-hand.source: UD1-078 | Implement tool use — error handling and retries · API errors
chapter-04-workflow-enforcement-and-hand.explanation: Timeouts are ambiguous (network drop vs processing success). Idempotency keys ensure payment providers deduplicate retries and return existing transaction records without double charging.
chapter-04-workflow-enforcement-and-hand.examTrick: Prevent duplicate charges on timeout retry = Client-generated Idempotency Keys.
chapter-04-workflow-enforcement-and-hand.subject: Claude CCAF: Agentic Architecture & Orchestration

chapter-04-workflow-enforcement-and-hand.question: In Claude Code's permission model, what is the correct evaluation order?
options: Allow -> Ask -> Deny
Ask -> Allow -> Deny
Deny -> Ask -> Allow
Allow -> Deny -> Ask
chapter-04-workflow-enforcement-and-hand.source: UD1-098 | Claude Code settings — permission rule precedence
chapter-04-workflow-enforcement-and-hand.explanation: Deny is evaluated first so prohibitions cannot be overridden by broad allows. Ask is evaluated second. Allow is evaluated last.
chapter-04-workflow-enforcement-and-hand.examTrick: Claude Code permission precedence order: Deny -> Ask -> Allow.
chapter-04-workflow-enforcement-and-hand.subject: Claude CCAF: Agentic Architecture & Orchestration

chapter-04-workflow-enforcement-and-hand.question: The refund flow works end to end, but 3% of sessions refund without a fresh identity check — traced to a session-cache race condition under load, not an agent reasoning error. Most effective fix?
options: Add a hook-based prerequisite that blocks process_refund unless a fresh, cache-validated get_customer result exists for this turn.
Add few-shot examples reinforcing "always verify identity first."
Reduce the session cache TTL to shrink the race window.
Add a retry loop that re-runs get_customer whenever process_refund is called.
chapter-04-workflow-enforcement-and-hand.answer: Add a hook-based prerequisite that blocks process_refund unless a fresh, cache-validated get_customer result exists for this turn.
chapter-04-workflow-enforcement-and-hand.explanation: Because the defect is a session-cache race rather than agent reasoning, prompt changes are irrelevant. A PreToolUse hook validating fresh, verified identity check for the current turn closes the race condition.
chapter-04-workflow-enforcement-and-hand.examTrick: Cache race condition / state staleness = PreToolUse hook validating freshness on current turn.
chapter-04-workflow-enforcement-and-hand.subject: Claude CCAF: Agentic Architecture & Orchestration

chapter-04-workflow-enforcement-and-hand.question: A tool result passes schema validation but refund_amount is negative, which is nonsensical here. What does this reveal?
options: The schema itself is broken and needs a type change from number to string.
This is purely a reasoning error, fixable via prompt instructions rather than validation.
Schema validation is redundant once semantic validation exists, so it can be dropped.
Schema validation alone isn't sufficient.
chapter-04-workflow-enforcement-and-hand.source: QD1-39 | Structured outputs and strict tool use · Implement tool use
chapter-04-workflow-enforcement-and-hand.explanation: Schema validation verifies structure and types (e.g. number), but cannot verify domain semantics (e.g. amount >= 0, date not in future). Semantic validation gates are complementary and required.
chapter-04-workflow-enforcement-and-hand.examTrick: Schema validation enforces structure/type; Semantic validation enforces domain business logic.
chapter-04-workflow-enforcement-and-hand.subject: Claude CCAF: Agentic Architecture & Orchestration

chapter-04-workflow-enforcement-and-hand.question: An agent occasionally uses an overly casual tone in customer-facing summaries. No safety, financial, or irreversible consequence — a style preference. Best fix?
options: Add a validation gate rejecting any output not matching a strict tone template.
This requires the same programmatic enforcement as a payment threshold, since any behavior can theoretically drift.
A prompt instruction/style guide is sufficient here.
Add a hook blocking any response containing casual phrasing.
chapter-04-workflow-enforcement-and-hand.answer: A prompt instruction/style guide is sufficient here.
chapter-04-workflow-enforcement-and-hand.source: QD1-42 | Prompt engineering — system prompts and style · Building effective agents
chapter-04-workflow-enforcement-and-hand.explanation: Controls should be proportional to risk. Stylistic and tone preferences are low-stakes and subjective, best handled via prompt instructions and style guides without heavyweight hooks.
chapter-04-workflow-enforcement-and-hand.examTrick: Low-stakes style/tone preference = Prompt instruction/style guide (do not over-engineer with hooks).
chapter-04-workflow-enforcement-and-hand.subject: Claude CCAF: Agentic Architecture & Orchestration

chapter-04-workflow-enforcement-and-hand.question: A Bash tool is exposed via MCP; security wants destructive shell commands refused. An engineer adds "You are a careful DevOps expert; never run destructive commands." A red-team request still elicits one. MOST accurate architectural assessment?
options: The persona grants authority to block destructive commands; the failure must stem from a malformed prompt section.
Setting temperature to 0 will make refusals deterministic.
More forceful language and capitalized warnings will make the constraint reliable enough to serve as the control.
Prompt-based guardrails are probabilistic and can fail under adversarial input; the destructive-command block belongs in the MCP tool's deterministic permission layer.
chapter-04-workflow-enforcement-and-hand.answer: Prompt-based guardrails are probabilistic and can fail under adversarial input; the destructive-command block belongs in the MCP tool's deterministic permission layer.
chapter-04-workflow-enforcement-and-hand.source: BU1-001 (§1.4) | Claude Code hooks and permissions · Claude Code security · MCP
chapter-04-workflow-enforcement-and-hand.explanation: Personas and prompt instructions are probabilistic and susceptible to adversarial prompt injection. Destructive command restrictions must be enforced in the tool's deterministic permission/command-allowlist layer.
chapter-04-workflow-enforcement-and-hand.examTrick: Adversarial security / destructive actions = Enforce in code/MCP permission layer, never prompts.
chapter-04-workflow-enforcement-and-hand.subject: Claude CCAF: Agentic Architecture & Orchestration

chapter-05-agent-sdk-hooks-and-security.question: A compliance workflow must verify identity before financial operations; a system prompt saying "verify first" is insufficient. Which Agent SDK hook enforces verification?
options: PostToolUse hook validating tool results after execution for compliance.
Hooks cannot enforce compliance; programmatic checks required separately.
Agent reasoning hook guiding decision making toward compliant behavior.
PreToolUse hook checking conditions before tool execution, blocking violations.
chapter-05-agent-sdk-hooks-and-security.answer: PreToolUse hook checking conditions before tool execution, blocking violations.
chapter-05-agent-sdk-hooks-and-security.source: UD1-001 | Claude Code hooks — PreToolUse · Hooks guide
chapter-05-agent-sdk-hooks-and-security.explanation: PreToolUse intercepts the call before execution and can return exit code 2 / deny to prevent the unauthorized financial action.
chapter-05-agent-sdk-hooks-and-security.examTrick: PreToolUse = Gating before execution. PostToolUse = Inspecting/transforming after execution.
chapter-05-agent-sdk-hooks-and-security.subject: Claude CCAF: Agentic Architecture & Orchestration
chapter-05-agent-sdk-hooks-and-security.chapterName: 1.5 Agent SDK Hooks, Lifecycle Events & Policy Enforcement

chapter-05-agent-sdk-hooks-and-security.question: Multiple MCP tools return timestamps as Unix epochs, ISO 8601, and locale-specific strings; the agent struggles with cross-format comparison. Where should timestamp normalization occur?
options: Fix the timestamp format at source in all MCP tools, returning a consistent format.
The agent should flexibly handle all common formats without normalization.
PostToolUse hook normalizing all timestamps to ISO 8601 before processing.
Agent system prompt with instructions for handling multiple formats.
chapter-05-agent-sdk-hooks-and-security.answer: PostToolUse hook normalizing all timestamps to ISO 8601 before processing.
chapter-05-agent-sdk-hooks-and-security.source: UD1-032 | Claude Code hooks — PostToolUse · Writing tools for agents
chapter-05-agent-sdk-hooks-and-security.explanation: When consuming third-party or heterogeneous MCP tools you cannot modify at source, a PostToolUse hook normalizes tool outputs into canonical ISO 8601 before the model reasons over them.
chapter-05-agent-sdk-hooks-and-security.examTrick: Normalizing heterogeneous third-party tool outputs = PostToolUse transformation hook.
chapter-05-agent-sdk-hooks-and-security.subject: Claude CCAF: Agentic Architecture & Orchestration
chapter-05-agent-sdk-hooks-and-security.chapterName: 1.5 Agent SDK Hooks, Lifecycle Events & Policy Enforcement

chapter-05-agent-sdk-hooks-and-security.question: Extracted services must use com.company.service.<service-name>; subagents sometimes write com.company.app.<name> or com.company.<name>. A teammate proposes stronger system-prompt instructions. Correct approach?
options: Add the naming convention to the system prompt with three concrete examples.
Implement a PostToolUse hook that inspects written files and normalises package declarations to the correct format.
Create a separate validation subagent reviewing written files after each batch.
Use tool_choice to restrict the agent to a custom write_java_file tool that enforces the convention.
chapter-05-agent-sdk-hooks-and-security.answer: Implement a PostToolUse hook that inspects written files and normalises package declarations to the correct format.
chapter-05-agent-sdk-hooks-and-security.source: UD1-088 | Claude Code hooks — PostToolUse · Hooks guide
chapter-05-agent-sdk-hooks-and-security.explanation: A mechanically checkable regex/string pattern is best enforced mechanically. A PostToolUse hook on Edit/Write checks the written file and automatically normalizes package headers.
chapter-05-agent-sdk-hooks-and-security.examTrick: Mechanical syntax/package normalization on write = PostToolUse hook.
chapter-05-agent-sdk-hooks-and-security.subject: Claude CCAF: Agentic Architecture & Orchestration
chapter-05-agent-sdk-hooks-and-security.chapterName: 1.5 Agent SDK Hooks, Lifecycle Events & Policy Enforcement

chapter-05-agent-sdk-hooks-and-security.question: A hard rule: never push to main. Where should it live so Claude cannot skip it?
options: In the project CLAUDE.md as an "IMPORTANT" rule.
In the local CLAUDE.md so it is scoped to you.
In a pre-tool use hook that stops the push.
In a skill's reference.md file.
chapter-05-agent-sdk-hooks-and-security.answer: In a pre-tool use hook that stops the push.
chapter-05-agent-sdk-hooks-and-security.source: UD1-089 | Claude Code hooks · Claude Code memory
chapter-05-agent-sdk-hooks-and-security.explanation: A PreToolUse hook inspecting Bash commands and blocking git push origin main executes in deterministic code outside the LLM context, making it impossible to bypass via prompt phrasing.
chapter-05-agent-sdk-hooks-and-security.examTrick: Non-negotiable hard constraint (e.g. block push to main) = PreToolUse hook.
chapter-05-agent-sdk-hooks-and-security.subject: Claude CCAF: Agentic Architecture & Orchestration
chapter-05-agent-sdk-hooks-and-security.chapterName: 1.5 Agent SDK Hooks, Lifecycle Events & Policy Enforcement

chapter-05-agent-sdk-hooks-and-security.question: A PreToolUse hook meant to validate a precondition throws an unexpected exception due to a bug in the hook's own code. Safest default?
options: Disable the hook automatically after its first error
Fail closed
Fail open
Retry the hook indefinitely until it stops erroring
chapter-05-agent-sdk-hooks-and-security.source: QD1-45 | Claude Code hooks — exit codes · Claude Code security
chapter-05-agent-sdk-hooks-and-security.explanation: Failing closed (blocking the tool call when the validator errors) preserves safety invariants. Failing open would allow unchecked execution whenever a hook crashes.
chapter-05-agent-sdk-hooks-and-security.examTrick: Safety-critical hook exceptions MUST fail closed (deny/block execution).
chapter-05-agent-sdk-hooks-and-security.subject: Claude CCAF: Agentic Architecture & Orchestration
chapter-05-agent-sdk-hooks-and-security.chapterName: 1.5 Agent SDK Hooks, Lifecycle Events & Policy Enforcement

chapter-05-agent-sdk-hooks-and-security.question: A compliance rule prevents refund processing above $500 without manager approval. Which hook configuration correctly implements this?
options: A PreToolUse hook on process_refund with exit code 2 and JSON output containing a deny decision when the amount exceeds $500.
A SessionStart hook setting a global $500 limit for all financial operations.
A PostToolUse hook on process_refund that reverses transactions over $500.
A system prompt instruction specifying the $500 threshold with examples.
chapter-05-agent-sdk-hooks-and-security.answer: A PreToolUse hook on process_refund with exit code 2 and JSON output containing a deny decision when the amount exceeds $500.
chapter-05-agent-sdk-hooks-and-security.source: UD2-022 | Claude Code hooks — PreToolUse, matchers, exit codes, and JSON output
chapter-05-agent-sdk-hooks-and-security.explanation: PreToolUse scoped to process_refund uses exit code 2 with JSON decision output {"decision": "deny", "reason": "..."} to block the call and return a clear rationale to the model.
chapter-05-agent-sdk-hooks-and-security.examTrick: PreToolUse blocking: Exit code 2 + JSON deny decision to block tool execution.
chapter-05-agent-sdk-hooks-and-security.subject: Claude CCAF: Agentic Architecture & Orchestration
chapter-05-agent-sdk-hooks-and-security.chapterName: 1.5 Agent SDK Hooks, Lifecycle Events & Policy Enforcement

chapter-05-agent-sdk-hooks-and-security.question: Every Bash command issued by the agent must appear in a central audit log with the user identity. Which mechanism BEST supports this?
options: A CLAUDE.md instruction asking the agent to log each command itself.
Manual review of session transcripts after each session.
A PostToolUse hook (or PreToolUse for pre-execution capture) firing on every Bash invocation, writing command + arguments + user identity to the central audit log.
Enable verbose logging on the underlying system shell.
chapter-05-agent-sdk-hooks-and-security.answer: A PostToolUse hook (or PreToolUse for pre-execution capture) firing on every Bash invocation, writing command + arguments + user identity to the central audit log.
chapter-05-agent-sdk-hooks-and-security.source: BU1-005 (§1.5) | Claude Code hooks · Monitoring and usage
chapter-05-agent-sdk-hooks-and-security.explanation: Hooks fire deterministically at the harness level on every matching tool invocation, capturing structured command parameters, timestamp, and user context without relying on model compliance.
chapter-05-agent-sdk-hooks-and-security.examTrick: Central audit logging of tool commands = PostToolUse/PreToolUse hook firing on tool matchers.
chapter-05-agent-sdk-hooks-and-security.subject: Claude CCAF: Agentic Architecture & Orchestration
chapter-05-agent-sdk-hooks-and-security.chapterName: 1.5 Agent SDK Hooks, Lifecycle Events & Policy Enforcement

chapter-06-task-decomposition-and-planni.question: Decomposition creates a fixed 4 subtopics for all topics: simple topics are over-decomposed, complex ones under-decomposed. How do you improve the approach?
options: Increase to a fixed 8 subtopics.
Dynamic decomposition assessing topic complexity to determine the appropriate subtopic count.
Reduce to a single comprehensive subtopic.
Predefined topic taxonomy with mappings to fixed subtopic structures.
chapter-06-task-decomposition-and-planni.answer: Dynamic decomposition assessing topic complexity to determine the appropriate subtopic count.
chapter-06-task-decomposition-and-planni.source: UD1-043 | Multi-agent research system · Building effective agents
chapter-06-task-decomposition-and-planni.explanation: Fixed subtopic counts are inherently flawed. Sizing must be dynamic and complexity-proportional: assess breadth first, then spawn the right number of subtasks.
chapter-06-task-decomposition-and-planni.examTrick: Dynamic adaptive decomposition sizes subtasks to query complexity; avoid fixed subtopic counts.
chapter-06-task-decomposition-and-planni.subject: Claude CCAF: Agentic Architecture & Orchestration

chapter-06-task-decomposition-and-planni.question: A team writes tests first, then uses Claude to implement code passing those tests, iterating by sharing test failures. Which workflow pattern is this?
options: The test-driven iteration pattern: write tests first, then iterate by sharing failures.
Plan mode followed by direct execution.
Prompt chaining with separate steps for testing and implementation.
The interview pattern: have Claude ask questions before implementing.
chapter-06-task-decomposition-and-planni.answer: The test-driven iteration pattern: write tests first, then iterate by sharing failures.
chapter-06-task-decomposition-and-planni.source: UD1-058 | Claude Code best practices — test-driven development
chapter-06-task-decomposition-and-planni.explanation: Test-driven iteration uses tests as executable specifications, feeding failing assertions back into the loop as an objective correction signal.
chapter-06-task-decomposition-and-planni.examTrick: Write tests first -> share failure output in loop = Test-Driven Iteration Pattern.
chapter-06-task-decomposition-and-planni.subject: Claude CCAF: Agentic Architecture & Orchestration

chapter-06-task-decomposition-and-planni.question: Adding comprehensive test coverage to a legacy codebase with unclear module boundaries and undocumented dependencies. Most appropriate decomposition strategy?
options: Adaptive decomposition: first map the codebase structure, identify high-impact areas, then create a prioritized plan that adapts as dependencies are discovered.
Fixed sequential prompt chaining: tests for each file in alphabetical order, one per turn.
Decompose by test type: all unit tests, then integration, then end-to-end.
Give Claude the entire codebase and a single instruction to "add comprehensive tests."
chapter-06-task-decomposition-and-planni.answer: Adaptive decomposition: first map the codebase structure, identify high-impact areas, then create a prioritized plan that adapts as dependencies are discovered.
chapter-06-task-decomposition-and-planni.source: QD1-06 | Claude Code best practices — explore, plan, code
chapter-06-task-decomposition-and-planni.explanation: You cannot plan what you have not mapped. With unknown boundaries, discovery is the mandatory first phase, followed by a prioritized adaptive plan that adjusts as dependencies surface.
chapter-06-task-decomposition-and-planni.examTrick: High architectural uncertainty / legacy code = Adaptive decomposition (Explore -> Plan -> Code).
chapter-06-task-decomposition-and-planni.subject: Claude CCAF: Agentic Architecture & Orchestration

chapter-06-task-decomposition-and-planni.question: Auth extraction and billing extraction are independent; "wire up service mesh config" depends on both. One engineer, limited time. Most reliable decomposition structure?
options: Fan-out the two independent extractions in parallel, then fan-in to a single sequential subtask that only starts once both extractions are verified complete.
Run all three subtasks in parallel to save the most time.
Run all three strictly sequentially in the order mentioned.
Decompose into a single subtask doing the entire migration.
chapter-06-task-decomposition-and-planni.answer: Fan-out the two independent extractions in parallel, then fan-in to a single sequential subtask that only starts once both extractions are verified complete.
chapter-06-task-decomposition-and-planni.source: QD1-10 | Building effective agents — parallelization and orchestrator-workers
chapter-06-task-decomposition-and-planni.explanation: Express the DAG accurately: parallel fan-out for independent nodes, with an explicit synchronization barrier ensuring dependent nodes execute only after upstream completion is verified.
chapter-06-task-decomposition-and-planni.examTrick: DAG schedule: Parallel fan-out for independent tasks -> Verification barrier -> Sequential fan-in.
chapter-06-task-decomposition-and-planni.subject: Claude CCAF: Agentic Architecture & Orchestration

chapter-06-task-decomposition-and-planni.question: "Clean up the auth module" — it contains dead code, inconsistent naming, and a non-constant-time token comparison. Time-boxed to one turn. What FIRST?
options: Ask the user to clarify exactly what "clean up" means before doing anything.
Fix everything found, including the security issue.
Only fix the security issue since it's highest severity, leaving the rest for a separate task.

Proceed with the unambiguous, low-risk cleanup (dead code, naming) immediately, but pause and explicitly flag the security issue for confirmation before touching it, since fixing it changes security-relevant behavior.
chapter-06-task-decomposition-and-planni.answer: Proceed with the unambiguous, low-risk cleanup (dead code, naming) immediately, but pause and explicitly flag the security issue for confirmation before touching it, since fixing it changes security-relevant behavior.
chapter-06-task-decomposition-and-planni.source: QD1-14 | Building effective agents — human-in-the-loop · Claude Code best practices
chapter-06-task-decomposition-and-planni.explanation: Split work by risk profile: execute unambiguous, reversible cleanup immediately while explicitly pausing and gating the security-relevant behaviour change for user confirmation.
chapter-06-task-decomposition-and-planni.examTrick: Ambiguous task with security implications: Execute safe cleanup + Flag security changes for confirmation.
chapter-06-task-decomposition-and-planni.subject: Claude CCAF: Agentic Architecture & Orchestration

chapter-06-task-decomposition-and-planni.question: Translate 200 nearly-identical product templates into 5 languages each, with a fixed, well-understood structure. Best decomposition?
options: Fixed prompt chaining: a predictable sequence applied uniformly across all templates.
Adaptive decomposition: explore the templates first, then build a plan that adapts.
A coordinator that decides template by template whether translation is needed.
Spawn one subagent per language with full isolated context.
chapter-06-task-decomposition-and-planni.answer: Fixed prompt chaining: a predictable sequence applied uniformly across all templates.
chapter-06-task-decomposition-and-planni.source: QD1-48 | Building effective agents — prompt chaining
chapter-06-task-decomposition-and-planni.explanation: Zero structural uncertainty and uniform work fits fixed prompt chaining. It is cheap, predictable, easily parallelized, and avoids adaptive overhead.
chapter-06-task-decomposition-and-planni.examTrick: Uniform, repetitive, known structure = Fixed Prompt Chaining.
chapter-06-task-decomposition-and-planni.subject: Claude CCAF: Agentic Architecture & Orchestration

chapter-06-task-decomposition-and-planni.question: Three replans into an open-ended investigation, the current plan no longer clearly serves the original goal. What should happen?
options: Escalate to a human on every replan, regardless of how minor.

Explicitly re-check the current plan against the original goal before continuing to replan, rather than letting each incremental replan drift the objective without ever validating against the original ask.
Continue replanning since adaptive decomposition is designed to evolve freely.
Revert to the very first plan, since the original plan was presumably correct.
chapter-06-task-decomposition-and-planni.answer: Explicitly re-check the current plan against the original goal before continuing to replan, rather than letting each incremental replan drift the objective without ever validating against the original ask.
chapter-06-task-decomposition-and-planni.source: QD1-49 | Building effective agents — planning · Multi-agent research system
chapter-06-task-decomposition-and-planni.explanation: Goal drift occurs when incremental replanning evaluates only against the previous drifted plan. Periodically re-validating the plan against the original objective reference prevents drift.
chapter-06-task-decomposition-and-planni.examTrick: Prevent goal drift = Re-validate replanned actions against original root goal & constraints.
chapter-06-task-decomposition-and-planni.subject: Claude CCAF: Agentic Architecture & Orchestration

chapter-06-task-decomposition-and-planni.question: "Rename this variable across the codebase" split into 6 subagents (one per file type), each with coordinator hand-off overhead, for one mechanical low-risk operation. Best assessment?
options: Correctly decomposed, since parallelizing by file type is always more efficient.
Six subagents is appropriate as long as the token budget allows.
The decomposition is fine, but it should use peer-to-peer topology.
This is over-decomposition.
chapter-06-task-decomposition-and-planni.source: QD1-51 | Building effective agents — start simple
chapter-06-task-decomposition-and-planni.explanation: Decomposition is only justified by parallelism gains, context isolation, or specialization. Spawning 6 subagents for a mechanical variable rename introduces coordination overhead that exceeds the work.
chapter-06-task-decomposition-and-planni.examTrick: Over-decomposition: Adding subagent overhead to mechanical single-pass tasks adds latency and divergence.
chapter-06-task-decomposition-and-planni.subject: Claude CCAF: Agentic Architecture & Orchestration

chapter-06-task-decomposition-and-planni.question: Designing a general-purpose orchestration layer handling both sequential and parallel execution uniformly. MOST consistent design strategy?
options: Force everything strictly sequential to keep the orchestrator simple.
Express subtasks with explicit dependencies in a DAG; the orchestrator runs independent nodes in parallel and dependent nodes sequentially.
Force everything parallel to maximize speed.
Let each subagent decide its own execution pattern.
chapter-06-task-decomposition-and-planni.answer: Express subtasks with explicit dependencies in a DAG; the orchestrator runs independent nodes in parallel and dependent nodes sequentially.
chapter-06-task-decomposition-and-planni.explanation: A DAG (Directed Acyclic Graph) is the universal representation: nodes with no incoming edges execute concurrently in parallel; dependent nodes execute sequentially upon predecessor completion.
chapter-06-task-decomposition-and-planni.examTrick: Universal orchestration = DAG dependency graph with automatic parallel/sequential scheduling.
chapter-06-task-decomposition-and-planni.subject: Claude CCAF: Agentic Architecture & Orchestration

chapter-06-task-decomposition-and-planni.question: An extraction agent must store audited records. A source API returns a permanent schema-change error; the agent replans to a looser scraping path, succeeds, but the records now skip mandatory audit validation. MOST accurate diagnosis of the replanning defect?
options: The agent should never replan after a tool error; it should halt and escalate every failure.
The replan satisfied the immediate obstacle but was not validated against the original goal constraint requiring audited records.
The agent misclassified the error; a permanent schema-change error should have been retried with exponential backoff.
The agent used in-context memory for the audit records when it should have used semantic memory.
chapter-06-task-decomposition-and-planni.answer: The replan satisfied the immediate obstacle but was not validated against the original goal constraint requiring audited records.
chapter-06-task-decomposition-and-planni.source: BU1-008 (§1.6) | Building effective agents — planning and guardrails
chapter-06-task-decomposition-and-planni.explanation: The replan solved the local obstacle ('get the data') while silently discarding a non-negotiable constraint ('records must be audited'). Replans must be validated against all original constraints.
chapter-06-task-decomposition-and-planni.examTrick: Replanning failure: Overcoming local obstacle while dropping global security/audit constraints.
chapter-06-task-decomposition-and-planni.subject: Claude CCAF: Agentic Architecture & Orchestration

chapter-07-session-state-resumption-and-.question: Explore two distinct refactoring approaches from the same codebase analysis without context contamination. Which session technique?
options: Resume the same session and clearly label each approach in the prompts.
Use fork_session to create two independent branches from the shared analysis baseline.
Use a single session but instruct the agent to keep the approaches in separate mental namespaces.
Start two completely fresh sessions, repeating the codebase analysis in each.
chapter-07-session-state-resumption-and-.answer: Use fork_session to create two independent branches from the shared analysis baseline.
chapter-07-session-state-resumption-and-.source: UD1-051 | Claude Agent SDK — session forking
chapter-07-session-state-resumption-and-.explanation: fork_session branches from a completed baseline analysis, giving both explorations identical starting context with zero cross-contamination.
chapter-07-session-state-resumption-and-.examTrick: Divergent exploration from common baseline = fork_session.
chapter-07-session-state-resumption-and-.subject: Claude CCAF: Agentic Architecture & Orchestration

chapter-07-session-state-resumption-and-.question: What does the --resume flag do in Claude Code?
options: It continues a specific named prior conversation session.
It restores the last auto-saved scratchpad file.
It reloads all CLAUDE.md configuration files.
It re-runs the last command with fresh context.
chapter-07-session-state-resumption-and-.answer: It continues a specific named prior conversation session.
chapter-07-session-state-resumption-and-.explanation: --resume <session-name> loads and continues a specific named session. In contrast, --continue picks up the most recent session.
chapter-07-session-state-resumption-and-.examTrick: --resume <name> = Target specific session. --continue = Pick up latest session.
chapter-07-session-state-resumption-and-.subject: Claude CCAF: Agentic Architecture & Orchestration

chapter-07-session-state-resumption-and-.question: After 45 minutes, several early file reads are stale because a colleague pushed changes, and the agent is making recommendations from outdated contents. Best recovery strategy?
options: Continue in the current session and ask the agent to re-read the changed files.
Start a completely new session with no context from the previous one.
Start a fresh session with a summary of the key findings and decisions, then read the changed files for current state.
Use fork_session to create a new branch that excludes the stale tool results.
chapter-07-session-state-resumption-and-.answer: Start a fresh session with a summary of the key findings and decisions, then read the changed files for current state.
chapter-07-session-state-resumption-and-.source: UD1-085 | Effective context engineering for AI agents · Claude Code CLI
chapter-07-session-state-resumption-and-.explanation: When context contains broad stale reads and contaminated reasoning, starting fresh with an injected summary of durable decisions sheds stale baggage and re-establishes clean state.
chapter-07-session-state-resumption-and-.examTrick: Broad context staleness / contaminated reasoning = Fresh session + injected summary + re-read.
chapter-07-session-state-resumption-and-.subject: Claude CCAF: Agentic Architecture & Orchestration

chapter-07-session-state-resumption-and-.question: A multi-agent pipeline crashes at subagent 7 of 12. How should the system recover without reprocessing the first 6?
options: Re-run the full pipeline with a faster model.
Store the full conversation history in memory and replay it on restart.
Log all intermediate results to a database and query it on restart.
Have each agent export structured state to a known file location; the coordinator loads a manifest on resume and injects agent states into prompts.
chapter-07-session-state-resumption-and-.answer: Have each agent export structured state to a known file location; the coordinator loads a manifest on resume and injects agent states into prompts.
chapter-07-session-state-resumption-and-.source: UD1-059 | Effective context engineering for AI agents · Multi-agent research system
chapter-07-session-state-resumption-and-.explanation: State durability requires: (1) each agent persisting structured outputs, (2) coordinator reading a completion manifest, and (3) injecting completed state into downstream prompts.
chapter-07-session-state-resumption-and-.examTrick: Crash recovery = Persisted structured state files + Coordinator manifest loading + Prompt injection.
chapter-07-session-state-resumption-and-.subject: Claude CCAF: Agentic Architecture & Orchestration

chapter-07-session-state-resumption-and-.question: Resuming a session where only one specific file changed and the rest of the prior findings are still valid. Most efficient reliable approach?
options: Resume without mentioning the change at all.
Use fork_session to create a branch specifically to handle the changed file.
Inform the resumed session about the specific file change for targeted re-analysis, rather than requiring full re-exploration.
Discard the entire session and start fresh.
chapter-07-session-state-resumption-and-.answer: Inform the resumed session about the specific file change for targeted re-analysis, rather than requiring full re-exploration.
chapter-07-session-state-resumption-and-.source: QD1S-40 | Claude Code CLI reference · Effective context engineering
chapter-07-session-state-resumption-and-.explanation: When staleness is narrow and known (one file), resuming the session and explicitly informing Claude of the changed file scopes the re-read while preserving all still-valid architectural context.
chapter-07-session-state-resumption-and-.examTrick: Narrow, isolated file change = Resume session + explicitly prompt about the changed file.
chapter-07-session-state-resumption-and-.subject: Claude CCAF: Agentic Architecture & Orchestration

chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.question: A subagent named 'code-reviewer' is defined in managed settings, in .claude/agents/, in ~/.claude/agents/, and in an enabled plugin. Which definition wins?
options: The managed settings definition — subagent scope precedence runs managed > --agents flag > project > user > plugin.
The project definition in .claude/agents/, because project configuration is closest to the work.
The user definition in ~/.claude/agents/, because personal configuration is most specific.
The plugin definition, because plugin components are namespaced and load last.
chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.answer: The managed settings definition — subagent scope precedence runs managed > --agents flag > project > user > plugin.
chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Subagents: file locations and scope precedence
chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.explanation:
The documented priority order is: 1 managed settings (organization-wide), 2 the --agents CLI flag (current session), 3 .claude/agents/ (project), 4 ~/.claude/agents/ (all projects), 5 a plugin's agents/ directory. Subagents override BY NAME — one definition wins outright rather than merging.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** Project sits third, below managed and the CLI flag.
- **C.** User sits fourth, above only plugins.
- **D.** Plugin agents are the lowest priority of the five.

Note the contrast with SKILLS, whose precedence is managed > user > project — the opposite ordering of project and user. The exam likes this asymmetry.
chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.examTrick: Subagents: managed > --agents > project > user > plugin. Skills: managed > user > project. The middle two swap.
chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.subject: Claude CCAF: Agentic Architecture & Orchestration

chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.question: Which two frontmatter fields are required in a subagent definition file?
options: name and description.
name and tools.
description and model.
name, description, and tools.
chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.answer: name and description.
chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Subagents: frontmatter fields
chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.explanation:
'Only name and description are required.' name is a unique lowercase identifier; description tells Claude when to delegate to this subagent. Everything else — tools, disallowedTools, model, permissionMode, skills, memory, isolation, maxTurns, background, hooks, mcpServers — is optional.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B, D.** tools is optional; omitting it gives the subagent the full available tool set.
- **C.** model is optional and defaults to 'inherit'.

The description carries real weight: it is what Claude matches your task against when deciding whether to delegate, so a vague description means the subagent never gets used or gets used wrongly.
chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.examTrick: Only name + description required. description is the delegation trigger, so write it as when-to-use text.
chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.subject: Claude CCAF: Agentic Architecture & Orchestration

chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.question: What is the difference between the tools and disallowedTools frontmatter fields?
options: tools is an allowlist — only the listed tools work; disallowedTools is a denylist — everything except the listed tools works.
tools applies to built-in tools and disallowedTools applies only to MCP tools.
tools grants permission without prompting; disallowedTools triggers a prompt instead of blocking.
They are equivalent; disallowedTools is the deprecated older spelling.
chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.answer: tools is an allowlist — only the listed tools work; disallowedTools is a denylist — everything except the listed tools works.
chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Subagents: tool restrictions
chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.explanation:
The docs present both approaches: an allowlist such as 'tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash' means only those tools are available, while a denylist such as 'disallowedTools: Write, Edit' means everything except those. disallowedTools also accepts MCP patterns: 'mcp__github' removes all tools from that server, and 'mcp__*' removes every MCP tool.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** Both fields handle built-in and MCP tools.
- **C.** These fields shape the tool POOL, not permission prompting. Pre-approving tools without prompting is what a skill's allowed-tools field does.
- **D.** Both are current and serve opposite purposes.

A further documented form restricts which subagents this one may spawn: 'tools: Agent(worker, researcher), Read, Bash'.
chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.examTrick: tools = allowlist. disallowedTools = denylist. Both accept mcp__server and mcp__* patterns.
chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.subject: Claude CCAF: Agentic Architecture & Orchestration

chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.question: Which of these does NOT load into a normal (non-fork) subagent at startup?
options: The main conversation's history and its auto memory.
The system prompt from the subagent file's markdown body.
CLAUDE.md files and a git status snapshot.
Skills listed in the subagent's skills field.
chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.answer: The main conversation's history and its auto memory.
chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Subagents: what loads at startup
chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.explanation:
A non-fork subagent starts with: its own system prompt from the file body, the task delegation message Claude wrote, CLAUDE.md files, a git status snapshot, preloaded skills from the skills field, and the sibling roster of named agents. What never reaches subagents: output style settings, the main conversation's auto memory, and conversation history — 'except forks'.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B, C, D.** All three are documented as loading.

This is why a subagent needs everything it must know stated in the delegation prompt. It cannot see what you discussed with the lead agent. A vague delegation like 'review that' fails because there is no 'that' in the subagent's context.
chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.examTrick: Subagent gets CLAUDE.md + git status + its own prompt + preloaded skills. It does NOT get the conversation. Forks get the conversation.
chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.subject: Claude CCAF: Agentic Architecture & Orchestration

chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.question: What does a fork inherit that a normal subagent does not?
options: The entire parent conversation history, the same system prompt, the same tools, and the same model.
Only the parent's tool set; the conversation is still isolated.
The parent's auto memory but not its conversation history.
Nothing extra; a fork is another name for a subagent with inherit as its model.
chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.answer: The entire parent conversation history, the same system prompt, the same tools, and the same model.
chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Subagents: fork the current conversation
chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.explanation:
'For a fork, Claude Code loads the parent's conversation so far, system prompt, and tools instead.' The fork also shares the prompt cache with the parent, stays in the background, and returns its result as a message. Use a fork 'when the side task needs extensive context'; use a subagent when the task produces verbose output or needs constrained tools.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B, C.** The defining property of a fork is inheriting the conversation.
- **D.** They differ fundamentally in what loads.

A skill can also run forked via 'context: fork' in its frontmatter, which is how a skill gets isolation without you writing a subagent file.
chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.examTrick: Fork = full parent conversation + same prompt/tools/model + shared prompt cache. Subagent = fresh context, own definition.
chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.subject: Claude CCAF: Agentic Architecture & Orchestration

chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.question: What is distinctive about the built-in Explore and Plan subagents?
options: They are read-only, they omit CLAUDE.md and the git status snapshot, they don't count toward spawn depth limits, and they can't be resumed.
They run on a fixed small model regardless of the session model.
They have write access but are restricted to the working directory.
They inherit the parent conversation like forks do.
chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.answer: They are read-only, they omit CLAUDE.md and the git status snapshot, they don't count toward spawn depth limits, and they can't be resumed.
chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Subagents: built-in subagents
chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.explanation:
Explore handles file discovery and codebase exploration; Plan handles codebase research during plan mode. Both are read-only, both inherit the session model (Explore capped at Opus on the Claude API), and both 'omit CLAUDE.md and git status'. They also 'don't count toward spawn depth limits and can't be resumed.' The general-purpose agent, by contrast, inherits the model and has all available tools.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** They inherit rather than pin a small model.
- **C.** Both are read-only; no write access.
- **D.** Only forks inherit the parent conversation.

The CLAUDE.md omission is deliberate: these agents are pure search workers, and project conventions would be context they never act on.
chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.examTrick: Explore/Plan: read-only, no CLAUDE.md, no git status, exempt from depth limits, not resumable.
chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.subject: Claude CCAF: Agentic Architecture & Orchestration

chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.question: Which invocation guarantees that a specific named subagent runs, rather than leaving the decision to Claude?
options: An @-mention such as @"code-reviewer (agent)".
Natural language: 'Use the code-reviewer subagent to suggest improvements.'
Setting model: inherit in the subagent's frontmatter.
Adding the subagent name to CLAUDE.md.
chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.answer: An @-mention such as @"code-reviewer (agent)".
chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Subagents: invoking subagents
chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.explanation:
The docs describe three escalating patterns: natural language names the subagent and 'Claude decides whether to delegate'; an @-mention 'Guarantees that specific subagent runs'; and 'claude --agent code-reviewer' or the agent key in .claude/settings.json makes the whole session use that subagent's configuration.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** Naming it in prose is a suggestion Claude weighs, not a guarantee.
- **C.** model: inherit controls which model runs, not whether the agent is chosen.
- **D.** CLAUDE.md is advisory context and cannot force delegation.

The escalation ladder mirrors the enforcement-versus-guidance theme across the whole exam: prose suggests, syntax guarantees, configuration pins.
chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.examTrick: Prose = Claude decides. @-mention = guaranteed. --agent flag = whole session.
chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.subject: Claude CCAF: Agentic Architecture & Orchestration

chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.question: What are the default limits on subagent nesting and concurrency?
options: Up to 3 layers deep and a maximum of 20 subagents running simultaneously, both configurable by environment variable.
Unlimited nesting, with a maximum of 5 concurrent subagents.
One layer only — subagents cannot spawn other subagents.
Up to 10 layers deep with no concurrency limit.
chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.answer: Up to 3 layers deep and a maximum of 20 subagents running simultaneously, both configurable by environment variable.
chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Subagents: key behaviors
chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.explanation:
'Subagents can spawn other subagents up to 3 layers deep by default (configurable via CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_DEPTH)' and 'max 20 subagents running simultaneously (configurable via CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONCURRENT_SUBAGENTS).' Explore and Plan do not count toward the depth limit.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B, D.** Depth is bounded at 3 by default; concurrency is bounded at 20.
- **C.** Nesting is explicitly allowed.

The limits exist because each subagent is a full context window with its own token cost — unbounded fan-out is expensive and hard to reason about.
chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.examTrick: 3 layers deep, 20 concurrent, both env-var configurable. Explore/Plan are exempt from depth.
chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.subject: Claude CCAF: Agentic Architecture & Orchestration

chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.question: A subagent should keep notes across invocations in a directory separate from the main conversation's memory. Which frontmatter field enables that?
options: memory, set to user, project, or local.
autoMemoryDirectory, set to a path.
context, set to persist.
skills, listing a memory skill.
chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.answer: memory, set to user, project, or local.
chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Subagents: enable persistent memory
chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.explanation:
The subagent frontmatter includes 'memory: project  # Optional: user, project, or local'. The memory docs confirm the isolation: 'The main conversation's auto memory isn't loaded into subagents... A subagent's own auto memory, enabled with the subagent memory field, is a separate directory.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** autoMemoryDirectory is a settings.json key that relocates the whole auto-memory directory; it is not subagent frontmatter.
- **C.** context accepts fork, not persist.
- **D.** skills preloads skill content; it has nothing to do with persistence.

The separation matters: a subagent's learnings do not leak into the main conversation's memory, and vice versa.
chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.examTrick: Subagent memory is a SEPARATE directory from the main conversation's. Enabled by the memory: frontmatter field.
chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.subject: Claude CCAF: Agentic Architecture & Orchestration

chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.question: Which frontmatter field gives a subagent its own git worktree so its edits stay isolated from the main checkout?
options: isolation: worktree
worktree: true
sandbox: worktree
permissionMode: plan
chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.answer: isolation: worktree
chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Subagents: frontmatter fields; worktrees
chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.explanation:
The frontmatter reference lists 'isolation: worktree  # Optional: git worktree isolation'. This pairs with the worktree.sparsePaths setting, which the large-codebase docs describe as 'particularly useful for subagent worktree isolation' — each subagent that runs in a worktree gets a lightweight checkout instead of the full tree, and all worktrees in a session share the same sparsePaths.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B, C.** Neither is a documented field name.
- **D.** permissionMode controls whether Claude asks before acting; it does not isolate the filesystem.

Note the pairing to remember: isolation: worktree on the agent, worktree.sparsePaths and symlinkDirectories in settings to keep those checkouts cheap.
chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.examTrick: isolation: worktree on the agent + worktree.sparsePaths in settings = cheap isolated parallel work.
chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.subject: Claude CCAF: Agentic Architecture & Orchestration

chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.question: Which frontmatter field caps how many agentic turns a subagent may take before it must return?
options: maxTurns
effort
background
permissionMode
chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.answer: maxTurns
chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Subagents: frontmatter fields
chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.explanation:
The frontmatter reference lists 'maxTurns: 10  # Optional: agentic turn limit'. It is a bound on the subagent's loop, which matters for cost control and for guaranteeing that a delegated task terminates.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** effort sets the reasoning effort level (low/medium/high/xhigh/max), not a turn count.
- **C.** background: true controls whether the subagent runs in the background.
- **D.** permissionMode sets the subagent's permission baseline (default, acceptEdits, auto, plan).

maxTurns is one of the orchestration-layer safeguards the exam asks about: it guarantees the loop ends, so the coordinator always gets control back.
chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.examTrick: maxTurns bounds the agentic loop. It is a termination guarantee, which is why it appears in orchestration-safeguard questions.
chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.subject: Claude CCAF: Agentic Architecture & Orchestration

chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.question: How can a non-fork subagent be given more work after it has already returned a result?
options: Resume it with full context using the SendMessage tool; non-fork subagents are resumable.
It cannot be resumed; spawn a new subagent with the accumulated context in its prompt.
Re-invoke it by name, which automatically restores its prior context.
Only forks can be resumed, because only they carry conversation history.
chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.answer: Resume it with full context using the SendMessage tool; non-fork subagents are resumable.
chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Subagents: key behaviors
chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.explanation:
'Resumable: non-fork subagents can be resumed with full context via SendMessage.' The exceptions are the built-in Explore and Plan agents, which 'can't be resumed'. Resuming preserves the subagent's accumulated context, which is the difference between continuing an investigation and restarting one from cold.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** Resumption exists precisely so you do not have to re-derive context.
- **C.** A fresh Agent call starts a cold context; only SendMessage continues an existing one.
- **D.** Reversed — non-fork subagents are the resumable ones.

This is the session-resumption principle applied within a single session: restore state rather than repeat prior work.
chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.examTrick: SendMessage resumes an existing subagent with its context. A new Agent call starts cold. Explore/Plan cannot be resumed at all.
chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.subject: Claude CCAF: Agentic Architecture & Orchestration

chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.question: A side task needs everything discussed so far in the conversation but will produce a lot of intermediate output. Which is the better choice and why?
options: A fork — it inherits the full conversation the task depends on, and its work still happens outside the main thread.
A subagent — its fresh context prevents the verbose output from polluting the conversation.
A skill with allowed-tools set, run inline.
A dynamic workflow, since verbose output always warrants a script.
chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.answer: A fork — it inherits the full conversation the task depends on, and its work still happens outside the main thread.
chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Subagents: forks vs subagents
chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.explanation:
The documented split: use a fork 'when the side task needs extensive context'; use a subagent 'when the task produces verbose output or needs constraints'. Here the task NEEDS the accumulated context, which a fresh subagent cannot see. The fork still runs in the background and returns its result as a message, so the verbose intermediate work stays out of the main thread either way.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** A subagent's fresh context is a liability when the task depends on the conversation; you would have to re-explain everything in the prompt.
- **C.** Running inline puts all the verbose output into the main context.
- **D.** Workflows are for jobs that 'outgrow a handful of subagents' — a codebase-wide audit or a large migration, not one side task.
chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.examTrick: Needs the conversation → fork. Needs isolation or tool constraints → subagent. Outgrows a handful of agents → workflow.
chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.subject: Claude CCAF: Agentic Architecture & Orchestration

chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.question: How does a subagent's permission handling work relative to the main session?
options: Subagents inherit parent permissions, and permission prompts raised by a background subagent surface in the main session.
Subagents run without permissions and must request each tool from the parent explicitly.
Subagents always run in bypassPermissions mode so they are not interrupted.
Subagent permission prompts are auto-denied because the subagent runs in the background.
chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.answer: Subagents inherit parent permissions, and permission prompts raised by a background subagent surface in the main session.
chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Subagents: key behaviors
chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.explanation:
'Subagents inherit parent permissions' and 'subagents run in background by default in interactive mode; permission prompts surface in the main session.' A subagent can also set its own permissionMode in frontmatter (default, acceptEdits, auto, plan) to tighten or loosen its baseline.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** There is no per-tool request protocol back to the parent; inheritance plus the frontmatter fields govern access.
- **C.** bypassPermissions is not the subagent default, and the docs caution about it specifically.
- **D.** Prompts are surfaced to you, not silently denied.

The practical consequence: a permission rule you set for the session also constrains what your subagents can do, which is how you keep a fan-out of 20 agents safe.
chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.examTrick: Permissions inherit downward; prompts bubble upward to the main session. permissionMode in frontmatter adjusts the baseline.
chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.subject: Claude CCAF: Agentic Architecture & Orchestration

chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.question: Which frontmatter field preloads specific skill content into a subagent at launch?
options: skills — listed skills are fully preloaded into the subagent's context at launch, rather than loaded on demand.
allowed-tools — which also grants the skills' tools.
context — set to the skill name.
mcpServers — skills are delivered as MCP resources.
chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.answer: skills — listed skills are fully preloaded into the subagent's context at launch, rather than loaded on demand.
chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Subagents: preload skills; Extend Claude Code
chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.explanation:
'Skills work differently in subagents. Instead of on-demand loading, skills listed in the subagent's skills field are fully preloaded into its context at launch. Subagents can still discover and invoke unlisted project, user, and plugin skills through the Skill tool.' Note the interaction with disable-model-invocation: that flag 'Also prevents the skill from being preloaded into subagents.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** allowed-tools is a SKILL frontmatter field for pre-approving tools, not a subagent field for loading skills.
- **C.** context accepts fork.
- **D.** mcpServers scopes MCP servers to the subagent.
chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.examTrick: In the main session skills load on demand. In a subagent, listed skills are PRELOADED at launch. disable-model-invocation blocks preloading.
chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.subject: Claude CCAF: Agentic Architecture & Orchestration

chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.question: A subagent should be restricted so it can only spawn two specific worker agents. Which syntax expresses that?
options: tools: Agent(worker, researcher), Read, Bash
allowedAgents: worker, researcher
subagents: [worker, researcher]
disallowedTools: Agent(*), plus tools: Agent(worker), Agent(researcher)
chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.answer: tools: Agent(worker, researcher), Read, Bash
chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Subagents: tool restrictions
chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.explanation:
The docs show 'Restrict spawnable subagents (only these can be spawned): tools: Agent(worker, researcher), Read, Bash'. The Agent tool takes a parenthesised list in the same way permission rules scope a tool, so the allowlist entry both grants the Agent tool and constrains which agent types it may launch.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B, C.** Neither field name exists.
- **D.** Over-complicated and self-contradictory: a bare deny of the Agent tool would remove it entirely, and the allowlist form already expresses the constraint in one entry.

This matters for orchestration design: a coordinator that can spawn anything is hard to reason about, while a coordinator restricted to two named workers has a bounded delegation graph.
chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.examTrick: Agent(name1, name2) inside tools: constrains WHICH agents can be spawned, not just whether spawning is allowed.
chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.subject: Claude CCAF: Agentic Architecture & Orchestration

chapter-08-subagents-configuration-and-i.question: Which statement about the model field in subagent frontmatter is correct?
options: It accepts sonnet, opus, haiku, fable, or inherit, and inherit is the default.
It is required, and there is no inherit option.
It accepts only a full model id such as claude-opus-5.
It is ignored for background subagents, which always use the fastest available model.
