chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.question: You answer 'Yes, and don't ask again' to a permission prompt for a Bash command. Where does Claude Code write that approval, and who does it affect?
options: To .claude/settings.local.json as an allow rule, affecting only you in that repository.
To .claude/settings.json as an allow rule, affecting everyone who clones the repository.
To ~/.claude/settings.json as an allow rule, affecting you in every project on the machine.
To ~/.claude.json under the project's path, the same file MCP local-scoped servers use.
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.answer: To .claude/settings.local.json as an allow rule, affecting only you in that repository.
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Settings: project local settings; Permissions
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.explanation:
The docs state that when Claude asks permission to run a Bash command and you choose 'Yes, and don't ask again', Claude Code saves that approval as an allow rule in .claude/settings.local.json. If you started in a subdirectory or a worktree of a git repository, it reads and writes that file at the repository root, so the approval applies across the whole repository. Claude Code also adds the file to your global git excludes the first time it writes it, so it stays out of commits.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** The CLI never writes the shared project file on your behalf; that would silently change permissions for the whole team. (The VS Code extension's approval card does let you pick the shared file explicitly.)
- **C.** User settings hold personal preferences you set, not per-repository approvals captured from prompts.
- **D.** ~/.claude.json is the MCP local-scope and project-state file, not a settings file. Confusing .claude/settings.local.json with ~/.claude.json is a deliberate exam trap.
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.examTrick: Prompt-captured approvals land in .claude/settings.local.json. Never in the shared file, never in user settings.
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.question: A settings file contains a deny rule Bash(aws *) and an allow rule Bash(aws s3 ls). Claude attempts to run 'aws s3 ls'. What happens?
options: The call is blocked; a deny rule cannot carry allowlist exceptions, and deny beats a more specific allow.
The call runs, because the more specific allow rule wins over the broader deny rule.
Claude Code prompts the user to resolve the conflict between the two rules.
The call runs, because allow rules are evaluated before deny rules.
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.answer: The call is blocked; a deny rule cannot carry allowlist exceptions, and deny beats a more specific allow.
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Configure permissions
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.explanation:
The docs are explicit: 'A broad deny rule like Bash(aws *) blocks every matching call, including calls that also match a narrower allow rule like Bash(aws s3 ls), so a deny rule can't carry allowlist exceptions.' The same precedence applies between ask and allow: a matching ask rule prompts even when a more specific allow rule also matches.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** Specificity does not override rule type. This is the single most common wrong instinct, because it is how firewall and IAM rules often behave.
- **C.** There is no interactive conflict resolution; the precedence is fixed and deterministic.
- **D.** Evaluation order is not the mechanism. Deny simply outranks allow, and ask also outranks allow.
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.examTrick: deny > ask > allow, regardless of specificity. To carve an exception, narrow the deny rule itself.
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.question: What is the difference between a deny rule written as 'Bash' and one written as 'Bash(rm *)'?
options: A bare tool name removes the tool from Claude's context entirely so Claude never sees it; a scoped rule leaves the tool available and blocks only matching calls.
They are equivalent; the bare form is shorthand that Claude Code expands to a wildcard pattern.
The bare form only blocks interactive sessions, while the scoped form also applies in headless -p runs.
The bare form triggers a permission prompt, while the scoped form denies silently.
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.answer: A bare tool name removes the tool from Claude's context entirely so Claude never sees it; a scoped rule leaves the tool available and blocks only matching calls.
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Configure permissions
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.explanation:
Per the docs: 'A bare tool name like Bash removes the tool from Claude's context entirely, so Claude never sees it... A scoped rule like Bash(rm *) leaves the tool available and blocks matching calls when Claude attempts them.' Bare-name removal applies to every tool except EndConversation. Note that Bash(*) is equivalent to Bash, and as a deny rule both forms remove the tool.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** They differ in kind, not just in breadth: one is tool removal, the other is call-time blocking.
- **C.** Neither form is session-mode dependent; deny rules apply in every mode.
- **D.** Deny never prompts. Prompting is what an 'ask' rule does.
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.examTrick: Bare name in deny = tool is invisible to Claude. Scoped pattern = tool visible, specific calls blocked.
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.question: A team commits .claude/settings.json containing both permissions.allow and permissions.deny rules. A teammate clones the repo and starts a session but has not yet accepted the workspace trust dialog. Which rules are in effect?
options: The deny and ask rules apply right away; the allow rules wait until the teammate trusts the folder.
No rules apply until the folder is trusted, so the teammate is prompted for everything.
All rules apply immediately, because they are committed to the repository.
The allow rules apply immediately; the deny rules wait until the folder is trusted.
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.answer: The deny and ask rules apply right away; the allow rules wait until the teammate trusts the folder.
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Settings: 'The key waits for trust'; Permissions: workspace trust
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.explanation:
The docs state that permissions.allow rules, permissions.additionalDirectories, extraKnownMarketplaces, and most env values apply only after each teammate trusts the folder. Until then they still see prompts. Deny and ask rules apply right away. The asymmetry is a security design: a repository you have not trusted can restrict Claude but cannot grant it new powers.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** Restrictive rules are honoured immediately; a hostile repo cannot be made safer by withholding trust, so there is no reason to delay deny.
- **C.** Applying committed allow rules before trust would let any cloned repository silently pre-approve commands.
- **D.** Exactly backwards, and dangerously so.
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.examTrick: Untrusted folder: restrictions (deny/ask) live, grants (allow) dormant. Grants need trust; restrictions never do.
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.question: A platform team wants every developer in one repository to get the same lint/test permission allowlist and the same PostToolUse formatting hook, shared through source control. Which file?
options: Commit them to .claude/settings.json at the repository root.
Put them in ~/.claude/settings.json and ask each developer to copy it.
Put them in .claude/settings.local.json so each developer's copy stays personal.
Put them in CLAUDE.md so they load into every session automatically.
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.answer: Commit them to .claude/settings.json at the repository root.
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Settings: settings files and who they affect
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.explanation:
The docs describe .claude/settings.json as affecting 'Everyone who starts Claude Code in the folder that contains it. In a git repository, commit it so teammates get it', and list its typical use as 'Team permissions, hooks, plugins, and the environment variables the project needs.' Each teammate can still override for themselves in .claude/settings.local.json.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** User settings are per-machine and per-person; a copy-this-file instruction is exactly the drift the shared file exists to prevent.
- **C.** The local file is gitignored by design and is for personal overrides, so nothing would be shared.
- **D.** CLAUDE.md cannot contain permission rules or hooks at all; it is prose context, not configuration.
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.examTrick: Shared team tooling = project-level .claude/settings.json (committed). Personal/experimental = user or local.
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.question: Which permission rule correctly blocks Claude's file tools from reading .env files anywhere at or under the current directory?
options: "deny": ["Read(.env)"] — bare filenames follow gitignore semantics and match at any depth.
"deny": ["Write(.env)"] — the Write tool is what creates and modifies the file.
"deny": ["Glob(**/.env)"] — Glob is the tool that discovers the files.
"deny": ["Bash(cat .env)"] — blocking the shell read is what matters.
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.answer: "deny": ["Read(.env)"] — bare filenames follow gitignore semantics and match at any depth.
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Permissions: Read and Edit
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.explanation:
The docs state that Read and Edit rules use gitignore pattern syntax, and that 'Bare filenames follow gitignore semantics and match at any depth, so Read(.env) and Read(**/.env) are equivalent.' Deny rules also cover recognised Bash file commands such as cat, head, grep, and find when a denied path is passed as an argument.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** Claude Code checks file permissions against Edit(path) and Read(path) rules only. A path rule written for Write is accepted but never consulted, and warns at startup. Use Edit(...) instead of Write(...).
- **C.** Same problem: a Glob path rule is never consulted. Use Read(docs/**) in place of Glob(docs/**).
- **D.** It blocks one exact command string and nothing else — not the Read tool, not 'head .env', not a different quoting.
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.examTrick: Only Read(path) and Edit(path) are consulted for file paths. Write/Glob/NotebookEdit path rules are silently ignored.
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.question: Which statement about the Bash rule pattern Bash(ls *) is correct?
options: It matches 'ls -la' but not 'lsof', because a space before the trailing * enforces a word boundary.
It matches both 'ls -la' and 'lsof', because * matches any sequence of characters.
It matches only the exact command 'ls *' with a literal asterisk argument.
It matches 'ls -la' and also 'ls -la && rm -rf /', because * spans the whole command line.
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.answer: It matches 'ls -la' but not 'lsof', because a space before the trailing * enforces a word boundary.
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Permissions: Bash rules
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.explanation:
Per the docs: 'When * appears at the end with a space before it (like Bash(ls *)), it enforces a word boundary, requiring the prefix to be followed by a space or end-of-string. For example, Bash(ls *) matches ls -la but not lsof. In contrast, Bash(ls*) without a space matches both.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** That describes Bash(ls*), written without the space. The space is load-bearing.
- **C.** The asterisk is a wildcard in permission patterns, not a literal.
- **D.** Claude Code is shell-operator aware. A rule must match each subcommand independently; recognised separators are &&, ||, ;, |, |&, &, and newlines. So Bash(safe-cmd *) does not authorise 'safe-cmd && other-cmd'.
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.examTrick: 'ls *' (with space) = word boundary. 'ls*' (no space) = prefix match, catches lsof. And && always splits into independently-matched subcommands.
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.question: An engineer writes the permission rule Bash(command:rm *) intending to block deletions. What does Claude Code do?
options: Ignores the rule and emits a startup warning; the correct form is Bash(rm *).
Applies it exactly as written, blocking any rm command.
Applies it only to the PowerShell tool, since 'command' is a PowerShell field name.
Treats 'command:' as a literal prefix and matches commands that start with the text 'command:'.
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.answer: Ignores the rule and emits a startup warning; the correct form is Bash(rm *).
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Permissions: matching tool input fields
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.explanation:
The docs state you cannot match a tool's primary content field this way — command for Bash and PowerShell, file_path for Read/Edit/Write, path for Grep and Glob, notebook_path for NotebookEdit, url for WebFetch. 'A rule like Bash(command:rm *) would be bypassable by a compound command, so Claude Code ignores it and emits a startup warning. Use Bash(rm *), Read(./path), or WebFetch(domain:host) instead.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** A silently-accepted rule that looks like it blocks rm but does not would be worse than no rule; the docs specify the warning precisely to avoid that.
- **C.** Both Bash and PowerShell use 'command' as their primary field, and neither can be matched this way.
- **D.** There is no literal-prefix fallback; the rule is discarded.
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.examTrick: field:value syntax works for secondary fields (WebFetch(domain:...), Bash(run_in_background:true)) but never for the primary content field.
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.question: Match each requirement to the correct mechanism: (i) block Claude from ever reading production credentials, (ii) tell Claude the project uses 2-space indentation, (iii) run ESLint after every file edit.
options: (i) permissions.deny, (ii) CLAUDE.md, (iii) PostToolUse hook.
(i) CLAUDE.md, (ii) CLAUDE.md, (iii) CLAUDE.md.
(i) PreToolUse hook, (ii) settings.json, (iii) a /lint slash command.
(i) permissions.deny, (ii) a skill, (iii) a .claude/rules/ file with paths frontmatter.
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.answer: (i) permissions.deny, (ii) CLAUDE.md, (iii) PostToolUse hook.
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Memory: managed settings vs managed CLAUDE.md table; Extend Claude Code
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.explanation:
The docs give this split as a table: 'Block specific tools, commands, or file paths' → Managed settings: permissions.deny. 'Code style and quality guidelines' → Managed CLAUDE.md. And for automation: 'Use a hook when the action must happen the same way every time and doesn't need Claude to think... Run ESLint after every file edit.' Settings rules are enforced by the client regardless of what Claude decides; CLAUDE.md shapes behaviour but is not an enforcement layer.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** Puts a hard security boundary and a deterministic automation into advisory prose. Neither is guaranteed.
- **C.** A slash command must be invoked by a human, so it cannot satisfy 'after every file edit'. And indentation style is not a settings key.
- **D.** A skill loads on demand, so an always-applicable convention like indentation belongs in CLAUDE.md. A path-scoped rule is context, not an executed action, so it cannot run ESLint.
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.examTrick: Three buckets: hard boundary = permissions/hooks; always-on convention = CLAUDE.md; must-run-every-time action = hook.
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.question: An organization wants behavioural instructions ('Always run make lint before committing') applied on every machine, deployed centrally, and not excludable by individual developers. What is the supported mechanism?
options: A managed CLAUDE.md at the managed policy location, or the claudeMd key inside managed-settings.json.
A CLAUDE.md committed to every repository, enforced by a pre-commit hook in CI.
The claudeMd key in each developer's ~/.claude/settings.json, distributed by MDM.
A .claude/rules/ file symlinked from a company-standards directory on each machine.
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.answer: A managed CLAUDE.md at the managed policy location, or the claudeMd key inside managed-settings.json.
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Memory: Deploy organization-wide CLAUDE.md
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.explanation:
Managed policy CLAUDE.md lives at /Library/Application Support/ClaudeCode/CLAUDE.md (macOS), /etc/claude-code/CLAUDE.md (Linux and WSL), or C:\Program Files\ClaudeCode\CLAUDE.md (Windows). The claudeMd key lets you put that content directly inside managed-settings.json instead. It loads before user and project CLAUDE.md, and the docs state 'Managed policy CLAUDE.md files cannot be excluded' by claudeMdExcludes.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** A per-repository file is excludable and drifts; CI enforcement happens after the fact, not in the session.
- **C.** The docs are explicit that claudeMd is honoured in managed and policy settings only — 'Setting claudeMd in user, project, or local settings has no effect.'
- **D.** Symlinked rules are a sharing convenience for an individual, not an organization-wide policy, and they can be removed locally.
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.examTrick: 'Cannot be excluded / organization-wide' = managed policy tier. claudeMd only works in managed/policy settings.
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.question: A developer adds a // comment and a trailing comma to .claude/settings.json to document a rule. What happens at the next session start?
options: Claude Code reports a Settings Error, because settings files are strict JSON.
The file loads normally; Claude Code strips comments the way it strips HTML comments from CLAUDE.md.
The comment is preserved and injected into Claude's context as documentation.
Claude Code auto-repairs the file and writes back valid JSON.
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.answer: Claude Code reports a Settings Error, because settings files are strict JSON.
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Settings: change a setting
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.explanation:
The docs say: 'Settings files are strict JSON: a // comment or a trailing comma is a syntax error, and Claude Code reports the file as a Settings Error at the next start.' Add a $schema line instead to get autocomplete and inline validation in your editor.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** Block-level HTML comment stripping is a CLAUDE.md feature (markdown), not a JSON settings feature. The two are being deliberately conflated here.
- **C.** Settings are configuration read by the client; they never enter Claude's context as prose.
- **D.** Claude Code does auto-recover a corrupted ~/.claude.json from backups, but it does not rewrite a malformed settings file for you.
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.examTrick: settings.json = strict JSON, no comments. CLAUDE.md = markdown, HTML comments stripped before injection.
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.question: Which permission mode automatically accepts file edits and common filesystem commands such as mkdir, touch, mv, and cp within the working directory?
options: acceptEdits
bypassPermissions
plan
default
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.answer: acceptEdits
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Permissions: permission modes
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.explanation:
The docs define acceptEdits as the mode that 'Automatically accepts file edits and common filesystem commands such as mkdir, touch, mv, and cp for paths in the working directory or additionalDirectories.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** bypassPermissions skips permission prompts entirely, including writes to protected paths such as .git and .claude — far broader, and the docs restrict it to isolated environments like containers or VMs.
- **C.** plan mode is the opposite: Claude reads and analyses without making changes.
- **D.** default asks before actions that might modify your system.
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.examTrick: acceptEdits = edits + benign filesystem commands. bypassPermissions = everything, containers only.
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.question: A security team must ensure developers cannot use bypassPermissions mode. Where should the setting go and what is it?
options: Set permissions.disableBypassPermissionsMode to "disable" in managed settings, where it cannot be overridden.
Set permissions.deny to ["bypassPermissions"] in the project's .claude/settings.json.
Add 'Never use bypassPermissions mode' to the managed policy CLAUDE.md.
Set defaultMode to "default" in ~/.claude/settings.json on each machine.
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.answer: Set permissions.disableBypassPermissionsMode to "disable" in managed settings, where it cannot be overridden.
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Permissions: permission modes
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.explanation:
The docs state: 'To prevent bypassPermissions or auto mode from being used, set permissions.disableBypassPermissionsMode or permissions.disableAutoMode to "disable" in any settings file. These are most useful in managed settings where they can't be overridden.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** deny rules name tools and patterns, not permission modes; a mode is not a tool.
- **C.** A CLAUDE.md line is advisory. A developer can still press the keys that switch modes — the model's cooperation is not what gates a mode.
- **D.** A default mode is a starting point the developer can change, and a user-level setting is theirs to edit.
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.examTrick: Prevent a capability = a settings key at the managed tier, not a deny rule and not a CLAUDE.md sentence.
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.question: You want to restrict Claude's network access to a small set of approved documentation domains. What is the recommended configuration?
options: Deny curl, wget and similar Bash commands, then allow the WebFetch tool per domain with WebFetch(domain:github.com).
Allow only Bash(curl https://github.com/ *) so curl is restricted to the approved host.
Deny the WebFetch tool entirely and let Claude use curl, which is easier to audit in shell history.
Add the approved domain list to CLAUDE.md and instruct Claude to fetch nothing else.
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.answer: Deny curl, wget and similar Bash commands, then allow the WebFetch tool per domain with WebFetch(domain:github.com).
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Permissions: restrict Bash network tools
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.explanation:
The docs recommend exactly this pairing: 'use deny rules to block curl, wget, and similar commands, then use the WebFetch tool with WebFetch(domain:github.com) permission for allowed domains.' The reason is given alongside: Bash permission patterns that try to constrain command arguments are fragile.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** The docs use this exact pattern as the cautionary example: Bash(curl http://github.com/ *) 'won't match variations' — a different scheme, an extra flag before the URL, or a redirect all slip past it.
- **C.** Backwards. WebFetch is the tool with real domain-level matching; curl arguments are what cannot be constrained reliably.
- **D.** Advisory text is not a network boundary.
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.examTrick: Domain restriction is a WebFetch(domain:...) job. Constraining URLs inside Bash arguments is documented as fragile.
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.question: In user settings (~/.claude/settings.json) you write the deny rule Read(/secrets/**), expecting it to block a secrets directory inside every project. What does it actually block?
options: ~/.claude/secrets/**, because a /path pattern is relative to the settings source, which for user settings is the config directory.
/secrets/** at the filesystem root on every machine.
<project root>/secrets/** in whichever project is open.
Nothing; a leading slash is invalid in Read rules and the rule is discarded.
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.answer: ~/.claude/secrets/**, because a /path pattern is relative to the settings source, which for user settings is the config directory.
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Permissions: Read and Edit pattern types
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.explanation:
There are four pattern types: //path (absolute from filesystem root), ~/path (from home), /path (relative to the settings source), and path or ./path (relative to current directory). The docs give this case directly: 'A deny rule such as Read(/secrets/**) in user settings blocks ~/.claude/secrets/**, not a secrets directory in your project. To write a rule in user settings that applies inside every project, use a // absolute path or a ~/ home-relative path instead.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** That is what // means. A single leading slash is source-relative, not root-absolute — the exam's favourite distinction here.
- **C.** That is what /path means in PROJECT settings, where the settings source is the project root. The same pattern resolves differently depending on which file it lives in.
- **D.** The rule is valid; it just anchors somewhere the author did not expect.
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.examTrick: Four anchors: // = filesystem root, ~/ = home, / = settings source, ./ or bare = cwd. Same pattern, different file, different target.
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.question: A rule allows Bash(npm test *). Which invocations does it also cover?
options: 'timeout 30 npm test' and 'NODE_ENV=test npm test', because a fixed set of wrappers and known-safe env assignments are stripped before matching.
Only the literal string 'npm test ...'; any prefix causes the rule to miss.
'devbox run npm test', because environment runners are stripped like other wrappers.
'npm test && npm run lint', because the allow rule covers the whole command line.
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.answer: 'timeout 30 npm test' and 'NODE_ENV=test npm test', because a fixed set of wrappers and known-safe env assignments are stripped before matching.
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Permissions: wrapper stripping
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.explanation:
The docs list the stripped wrappers as timeout, time, nice, nohup, and stdbuf, plus the shell builtins command and builtin, and zsh's noglob — each runs its argument as the actual command. Claude Code also strips a leading assignment of certain known-safe environment variables, so Bash(npm test *) matches NODE_ENV=test npm test.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** Too strict; the wrapper list exists precisely so ordinary invocations are not blocked.
- **C.** The docs call this out as a hazard: development environment runners such as devbox run, mise exec, npx, and docker exec are NOT in the strip list, because Bash(devbox run *) would match 'devbox run rm -rf .'. Write a rule naming both the runner and the inner command.
- **D.** && splits the command; each subcommand must match a rule independently.
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.examTrick: Stripped: timeout/time/nice/nohup/stdbuf/command/builtin/noglob/bare xargs. NOT stripped: npx, docker exec, devbox run, mise exec.
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.question: A teammate chose 'Yes, and don't ask again' for a Bash command but is still prompted for it every session. What is the most likely cause?
options: A project or managed file has a matching ask rule, and an allow rule in the local file does not outrank ask.
The local settings file was not committed, so the approval was discarded at session end.
Allow rules expire after a fixed retention period set by cleanupPeriodDays.
The approval was written to user settings, which are read only at install time.
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.answer: A project or managed file has a matching ask rule, and an allow rule in the local file does not outrank ask.
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Settings: common cases
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.explanation:
The docs describe this symptom verbatim: 'You chose "Yes, and don't ask again" on a permission prompt but still get prompted for the same tool. That choice saved an allow rule to your local file, and an allow rule there doesn't outrank an ask rule from a project or managed file.' The related possibility is that the folder is not yet trusted, which keeps allow rules dormant.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** The local file is deliberately gitignored and persists on disk; committing it is not required for it to work.
- **C.** cleanupPeriodDays governs session transcript retention, not permission rules.
- **D.** The approval goes to .claude/settings.local.json, not user settings, and settings files are watched and reloaded live.
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.examTrick: Still prompted after 'don't ask again' = an ask rule upstream, or the folder is untrusted. Rule type beats file locality.
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.question: Which allow-rule glob is valid and will actually auto-approve MCP tools?
options: "mcp__github__get_*" — allow globs are accepted only after a literal, glob-free mcp__<server>__ prefix.
"mcp__*" — it names the MCP namespace, so every MCP tool is approved.
"*" — the universal glob approves all tools including MCP ones.
"mcp__*__get_*" — wildcards in the server segment let one rule cover every server's getters.
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.answer: "mcp__github__get_*" — allow globs are accepted only after a literal, glob-free mcp__<server>__ prefix.
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Permissions: tool-name globs
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.explanation:
Per the docs: 'Allow rules accept tool-name globs only after a literal mcp__<server>__ prefix. The server segment must be glob-free so the rule names a specific server you configured. mcp__puppeteer__* matches every tool from the puppeteer server, and mcp__github__get_* matches its get_ tools. An unanchored allow glob such as "*", "B*", or "mcp__*" is skipped with a warning and doesn't auto-approve anything.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B, C, D.** All three are unanchored or have a globbed server segment, so all three are skipped with a warning and approve nothing. Note the asymmetry that makes this a good exam question: deny and ask rules DO accept globs in the tool-name position, so "mcp__*" is a perfectly valid way to deny every MCP tool. It is only allow that requires the literal server name.
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.examTrick: Deny/ask: globs anywhere, including "*" and "mcp__*". Allow: must anchor on a literal mcp__<server>__ prefix.
chapter-08-settings-permissions-and-enfo.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.question: A developer needs Claude to consider one specific config file while answering a single question in this session only. Which mechanism fits?
options: An @ reference to the file in the prompt — Claude reads it before responding, with no cross-session cost.
An entry in CLAUDE.md, so the file is always available.
A .claude/rules/ file with a paths glob matching that config file.
A skill containing the file's contents, invoked with /<name>.
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.answer: An @ reference to the file in the prompt — Claude reads it before responding, with no cross-session cost.
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Best practices: provide rich content; Memory
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.explanation:
The three-way decision turns on reusability, specificity, and cross-session need. This case is one file, one question, one session — so an @ reference is right: 'Reference files with @ instead of describing where code lives. Claude reads the file before responding.' Nothing is added to any persistent file, so no future session pays for it.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** CLAUDE.md loads its FULL content into every session's context window. Paying that cost forever for a one-off question is the documented anti-pattern: 'only include things that apply broadly.'
- **C.** A path-scoped rule is for conventions that should apply whenever matching files are touched, across sessions — not for a single question.
- **D.** A skill is for reusable reference material or a repeatable workflow, not a one-time file read.
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.examTrick: One-off, this session = @ reference. Every session = CLAUDE.md. Sometimes, on demand = skill. When matching files are touched = .claude/rules/.
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.chapterName: 3.9 Context Provisioning: @ References, CLAUDE.md Imports & Mechanism Selection

chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.question: Which content belongs in CLAUDE.md rather than a skill?
options: Build and test commands, code style rules that differ from defaults, and 'always do X' conventions the project needs every session.
The team's full API style guide and endpoint reference documentation.
A multi-step deployment checklist triggered before a release.
A debugging playbook used a few times a month.
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.answer: Build and test commands, code style rules that differ from defaults, and 'always do X' conventions the project needs every session.
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Extend Claude Code: CLAUDE.md vs Skill
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.explanation:
The docs' rule: 'Put it in CLAUDE.md if Claude should always know it: coding conventions, build commands, project structure, never do X rules. Put it in a skill if it's reference material Claude needs sometimes (API docs, style guides) or a workflow you trigger with /<name> (deploy, review, release).' The load difference drives it — CLAUDE.md loads every session automatically; skills load on demand.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B, C, D.** All three are the docs' own examples of skill content: reference material needed sometimes, and invocable workflows. Putting them in CLAUDE.md spends context every session on material most sessions never use.

The stated rule of thumb: 'Keep CLAUDE.md under 200 lines. If it's growing, move reference content to skills or split into .claude/rules/ files.'
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.examTrick: CLAUDE.md = always needed. Skill = sometimes needed, or /invoked. The test is 'would removing this cause Claude to make mistakes?'
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.chapterName: 3.9 Context Provisioning: @ References, CLAUDE.md Imports & Mechanism Selection

chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.question: What is the maximum import depth for @path imports in CLAUDE.md, and how do relative paths resolve?
options: Imported files can recursively import others up to a maximum depth of four hops; relative paths resolve relative to the file containing the import.
Imports are not recursive at all; only the top-level CLAUDE.md may use @.
Depth is unlimited; relative paths resolve against the working directory.
Maximum depth is two hops; relative paths resolve against the project root.
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.answer: Imported files can recursively import others up to a maximum depth of four hops; relative paths resolve relative to the file containing the import.
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Memory: import additional files
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.explanation:
'Both relative and absolute paths are allowed. Relative paths resolve relative to the file containing the import, not the working directory. Imported files can recursively import other files, with a maximum depth of four hops.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** Recursive imports are explicitly supported.
- **C.** Both halves are wrong: depth is capped at four, and resolution is relative to the importing file, not the cwd.
- **D.** Two is the wrong number, and project-root resolution is the wrong anchor.
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.examTrick: Four hops max. Relative to the IMPORTING FILE, not the working directory.
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.chapterName: 3.9 Context Provisioning: @ References, CLAUDE.md Imports & Mechanism Selection

chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.question: You want to mention the path @README in CLAUDE.md as documentation, without importing the file. How?
options: Wrap it in backticks; import parsing skips Markdown code spans and fenced code blocks.
Escape it as \@README.
Prefix it with a hash: #@README.
It is not possible; any @ followed by a path is always imported.
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.answer: Wrap it in backticks; import parsing skips Markdown code spans and fenced code blocks.
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Memory: import additional files
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.explanation:
'Import parsing skips Markdown code spans and fenced code blocks. To mention a path in your CLAUDE.md without importing it, wrap it in backticks: writing `@README` keeps the text literal, while @README outside backticks imports the file.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** No backslash escape is documented for imports.
- **C.** A hash prefix makes it a markdown heading; the @ would still be parsed.
- **D.** Directly contradicted by the code-span rule.
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.examTrick: Backticks make @paths literal. This is why a CLAUDE.md documenting its own import syntax does not import everything it mentions.
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.chapterName: 3.9 Context Provisioning: @ References, CLAUDE.md Imports & Mechanism Selection

chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.question: Does splitting a large CLAUDE.md into @path imports reduce context usage?
options: No — imported files still load and enter the context window at launch; use path-scoped rules in .claude/rules/ to actually reduce context.
Yes — imports are lazy and load only when Claude needs the referenced content.
Yes — imported files are summarized before entering context.
No — imports are never loaded at all, so the content is simply lost.
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.answer: No — imported files still load and enter the context window at launch; use path-scoped rules in .claude/rules/ to actually reduce context.
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Memory: write effective instructions; my CLAUDE.md is too large
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.explanation:
The docs say it twice. 'You can also split content into imports for organization, though imported files still load and enter the context window at launch.' And: 'Splitting into @path imports helps organization but doesn't reduce context, since imported files load at launch.' The mechanism that genuinely reduces context is path-scoped rules, which 'only load when Claude works with matching files.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** Skills are the on-demand mechanism; imports are eager.
- **C.** No summarization occurs; content is expanded and loaded.
- **D.** They are loaded — that is precisely the problem.
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.examTrick: Imports = organization only, zero context savings. Real savings = .claude/rules/ with paths frontmatter, or skills.
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.chapterName: 3.9 Context Provisioning: @ References, CLAUDE.md Imports & Mechanism Selection

chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.question: Claude Code is launched in foo/bar/. In what order does CLAUDE.md content appear in context?
options: foo/CLAUDE.md before foo/bar/CLAUDE.md — content is ordered from the filesystem root down to your working directory, and within a directory CLAUDE.local.md is appended after CLAUDE.md.
foo/bar/CLAUDE.md before foo/CLAUDE.md — the most specific file loads first so it takes precedence.
Only foo/bar/CLAUDE.md loads; parent directory files are ignored unless imported.
Files load in alphabetical order by absolute path, regardless of depth.
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.answer: foo/CLAUDE.md before foo/bar/CLAUDE.md — content is ordered from the filesystem root down to your working directory, and within a directory CLAUDE.local.md is appended after CLAUDE.md.
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Memory: how CLAUDE.md files load
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.explanation:
'All discovered files are concatenated into context rather than overriding each other. Across the directory tree, content is ordered from the filesystem root down to your working directory. For the foo/bar/ example, foo/CLAUDE.md appears in context before foo/bar/CLAUDE.md, so instructions closer to where you launched Claude are read last. Within each directory, CLAUDE.local.md is appended after CLAUDE.md.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** Reversed. Note also that CLAUDE.md files are ADDITIVE, not overriding — 'When instructions conflict, Claude uses judgment to reconcile them, with more specific instructions typically taking precedence.' That is judgement, not a precedence rule.
- **C.** Ancestor files load at launch; subdirectory files below the cwd load on demand when Claude reads files there.
- **D.** Order is by tree position, not alphabetical.
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.examTrick: Root → down to cwd. Additive concatenation, NOT override. CLAUDE.local.md always after CLAUDE.md in the same directory.
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.chapterName: 3.9 Context Provisioning: @ References, CLAUDE.md Imports & Mechanism Selection

chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.question: Which CLAUDE.md location is shared with the team via source control?
options: ./CLAUDE.md or ./.claude/CLAUDE.md — project instructions.
~/.claude/CLAUDE.md — user instructions.
./CLAUDE.local.md — local instructions.
/etc/claude-code/CLAUDE.md — managed policy.
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Memory: choose where to put CLAUDE.md files
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.explanation:
The table lists four scopes in load order, broadest to most specific: Managed policy (OS-specific system paths, all users in the organization), User instructions at ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md (just you, all projects), Project instructions at ./CLAUDE.md or ./.claude/CLAUDE.md (shared with 'Team members via source control'), and Local instructions at ./CLAUDE.local.md (just you, current project, add to .gitignore).

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** Personal preferences across all your projects, shared with nobody.
- **C.** Explicitly personal and gitignored: 'For private per-project preferences that shouldn't be checked into version control.'
- **D.** Distributed by MDM or configuration management, not source control, and it applies machine-wide rather than per repository.
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.examTrick: Four scopes: managed policy > user > project > local. Only PROJECT travels through source control.
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.chapterName: 3.9 Context Provisioning: @ References, CLAUDE.md Imports & Mechanism Selection

chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.question: You work across several git worktrees of one repository and want the same personal instructions in each. Why does CLAUDE.local.md fail, and what is the documented alternative?
options: A gitignored CLAUDE.local.md only exists in the worktree where you created it; instead import a file from your home directory, such as @~/.claude/my-project-instructions.md.
CLAUDE.local.md is deprecated in worktrees; use .claude/CLAUDE.md instead.
Worktrees do not load any CLAUDE.md files; use --add-dir to reach the main checkout.
CLAUDE.local.md loads fine in worktrees; the correct fix is to commit it.
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.answer: A gitignored CLAUDE.local.md only exists in the worktree where you created it; instead import a file from your home directory, such as @~/.claude/my-project-instructions.md.
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Memory: import additional files
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.explanation:
'If you work across multiple git worktrees of the same repository, a gitignored CLAUDE.local.md only exists in the worktree where you created it. To share personal instructions across worktrees, import a file from your home directory instead.' The docs show '# Individual Preferences\n- @~/.claude/my-project-instructions.md'.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** .claude/CLAUDE.md is the shared project file; putting personal preferences there exposes them to the team.
- **C.** Worktrees load CLAUDE.md normally.
- **D.** Committing a personal file defeats its purpose and shares it with everyone.

Related warning worth knowing: an import in a project-level memory file whose path resolves OUTSIDE the working directory is an 'external' import. The first time Claude Code encounters external imports in a project it shows an approval dialog; if you decline, they stay disabled.
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.examTrick: Worktree-portable personal instructions = a home-directory import (@~/...). External imports from a PROJECT file trigger a one-time approval dialog.
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.chapterName: 3.9 Context Provisioning: @ References, CLAUDE.md Imports & Mechanism Selection

chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.question: A repository already uses AGENTS.md for another coding agent. What is the documented way to make Claude Code read the same instructions without duplicating them?
options: Create a CLAUDE.md that imports it with @AGENTS.md, optionally adding Claude-specific instructions below the import.
Rename AGENTS.md to CLAUDE.md, since Claude Code reads only that filename.
Set an agentsMdCompat flag in settings.json.
Claude Code reads AGENTS.md automatically when no CLAUDE.md is present.
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.answer: Create a CLAUDE.md that imports it with @AGENTS.md, optionally adding Claude-specific instructions below the import.
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Memory: AGENTS.md
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.explanation:
'Claude Code reads CLAUDE.md, not AGENTS.md. If your repository already uses AGENTS.md for other coding agents, create a CLAUDE.md that imports it so both tools read the same instructions without duplicating them. You can also add Claude-specific instructions below the import.' A symlink also works if you do not need Claude-specific content — but on Windows creating a symlink requires Administrator privileges or Developer Mode, so use the @AGENTS.md import instead.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** Renaming breaks the other agent that depends on AGENTS.md.
- **C.** No such setting exists.
- **D.** Explicitly contradicted: 'Claude Code reads CLAUDE.md, not AGENTS.md.'
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.examTrick: @AGENTS.md import inside CLAUDE.md. Symlink is the alternative, but not on Windows without admin/Developer Mode.
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.chapterName: 3.9 Context Provisioning: @ References, CLAUDE.md Imports & Mechanism Selection

chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.question: What is the documented target size for a CLAUDE.md file, and what happens above the hard limit?
options: Target under 200 lines; Claude Code loads a CLAUDE.md of up to 4 MiB in full and skips a larger file.
Target under 200 lines; anything above 200 lines is truncated at load.
Target under 25KB; anything larger is summarized before injection.
There is no size guidance; CLAUDE.md files are always loaded in full.
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.answer: Target under 200 lines; Claude Code loads a CLAUDE.md of up to 4 MiB in full and skips a larger file.
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Memory: write effective instructions; how it works
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.explanation:
'Size: target under 200 lines per CLAUDE.md file. Longer files consume more context and reduce adherence.' And separately: 'Claude Code loads a CLAUDE.md file of up to 4 MiB in full and skips a larger file. Shorter files produce better adherence.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** 200 lines is a guideline for adherence, not a truncation point.
- **C.** The 200-line / 25KB pair is the AUTO MEMORY limit — 'The first 200 lines of MEMORY.md, or the first 25KB, whichever comes first, are loaded at the start of every conversation.' The docs state that limit 'applies only to MEMORY.md.' Confusing the two limits is a deliberate trap.
- **D.** Both a guideline and a hard limit are documented.
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.examTrick: CLAUDE.md: 200-line TARGET, 4 MiB hard skip. MEMORY.md: 200 lines OR 25KB, whichever first — a real load cutoff.
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.chapterName: 3.9 Context Provisioning: @ References, CLAUDE.md Imports & Mechanism Selection

chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.question: Which item does the documentation say to EXCLUDE from CLAUDE.md?
options: File-by-file descriptions of the codebase and detailed API documentation.
Bash commands Claude cannot guess.
Developer environment quirks such as required environment variables.
Repository etiquette such as branch naming and PR conventions.
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.answer: File-by-file descriptions of the codebase and detailed API documentation.
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Best practices: write an effective CLAUDE.md
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.explanation:
The Exclude column lists: anything Claude can figure out by reading code, standard language conventions Claude already knows, detailed API documentation (link to docs instead), information that changes frequently, long explanations or tutorials, file-by-file descriptions of the codebase, and self-evident practices like 'write clean code'. The test given is: 'For each line, ask: Would removing this cause Claude to make mistakes? If not, cut it.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B, C, D.** All three appear verbatim in the Include column.

The consequence of ignoring this: 'If Claude keeps doing something you don't want despite having a rule against it, the file is probably too long and the rule is getting lost.'
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.examTrick: Exclude anything derivable from the code. /doctor proposes exactly these cuts for a checked-in CLAUDE.md.
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.chapterName: 3.9 Context Provisioning: @ References, CLAUDE.md Imports & Mechanism Selection

chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.question: Terraform conventions should load only when Claude edits .tf files. Which configuration achieves this?
options: A .claude/rules/ markdown file with YAML frontmatter paths: ['terraform/**/*'], which activates only when Claude works with matching files.
A section in the root CLAUDE.md headed '# Terraform'.
A CLAUDE.md placed inside the terraform/ directory.
A /terraform slash command that loads the conventions on demand.
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.answer: A .claude/rules/ markdown file with YAML frontmatter paths: ['terraform/**/*'], which activates only when Claude works with matching files.
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Memory: path-specific rules
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.explanation:
'Rules can be scoped to specific files using YAML frontmatter with the paths field. These conditional rules only apply when Claude is working with files matching the specified patterns.' Rules WITHOUT a paths field are loaded unconditionally at launch, with the same priority as .claude/CLAUDE.md.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** A root CLAUDE.md section loads in every session regardless of whether any .tf file is touched — the context cost the question is trying to avoid.
- **C.** A per-directory CLAUDE.md is a valid alternative and the docs compare the two, but it is tied to directory placement. A path-scoped rule is the right answer when conventions should be centralized or apply to scattered paths; the question's phrasing ('.tf files', not 'the terraform/ directory') points at globs.
- **D.** A slash command requires a human to invoke it, so it cannot fire automatically when Claude edits a file.
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.examTrick: 'Only when editing <file type>' = .claude/rules/ + paths frontmatter globs. No paths field = loads unconditionally.
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.chapterName: 3.9 Context Provisioning: @ References, CLAUDE.md Imports & Mechanism Selection

chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.question: Which glob pattern in a rule's paths field matches all TypeScript and TSX files under src/, plus all TypeScript under lib/?
options: paths: ["src/**/*.{ts,tsx}", "lib/**/*.ts"] — multiple patterns are allowed and brace expansion matches multiple extensions.
paths: "src/**/*.ts,tsx; lib/**/*.ts" — a single comma- and semicolon-delimited string.
paths: ["src/**/*.ts|tsx", "lib/**/*.ts"] — pipe alternation inside the extension.
paths: ["src/", "lib/"] with an extensions: ["ts","tsx"] sibling key.
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.answer: paths: ["src/**/*.{ts,tsx}", "lib/**/*.ts"] — multiple patterns are allowed and brace expansion matches multiple extensions.
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Memory: path-specific rules
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.explanation:
The docs show exactly this shape: a YAML list under paths, with brace expansion for multiple extensions. Documented pattern examples include **/*.ts (all TypeScript in any directory), src/**/* (all files under src/), *.md (markdown in the project root only), and src/components/*.tsx.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B, C, D.** None is valid glob or valid frontmatter for this field.

Two documented edge cases the exam can reach for: brace groups multiply, so a rule's whole paths list shares one budget of 1,000 expanded patterns and 4 MiB; a pattern exceeding the budget is used unexpanded and its literal braces match nothing. And glob treats [ as a bracket expression, so 'photos [2024/**' is invalid and matches nothing — escape it as 'photos \\[2024/**'.
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.examTrick: paths is a LIST of globs; braces expand. Budget: 1,000 expanded patterns / 4 MiB per rule.
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.chapterName: 3.9 Context Provisioning: @ References, CLAUDE.md Imports & Mechanism Selection

chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.question: How do user-level rules in ~/.claude/rules/ relate to project rules in .claude/rules/?
options: User-level rules are loaded before project rules, giving project rules higher priority.
User-level rules override project rules, since personal preferences are more specific.
User-level rules are ignored whenever a project defines any rules of its own.
The two directories are merged alphabetically by filename, regardless of scope.
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.answer: User-level rules are loaded before project rules, giving project rules higher priority.
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Memory: user-level rules
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.explanation:
'Personal rules in ~/.claude/rules/ apply to every project on your machine. Use them for preferences that aren't project-specific... User-level rules are loaded before project rules, giving project rules higher priority.' This mirrors the CLAUDE.md ordering principle: broader scope first, more specific scope read last.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** Reversed, and it would let a personal preference silently override a team convention.
- **C.** Both load; they are additive.
- **D.** Ordering is by scope, not filename.

Note that .claude/rules/ also supports symlinks, so you can maintain one shared rule set and link it into multiple projects; circular symlinks are detected and handled.
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.examTrick: Loaded FIRST = lower priority, because later content is read last. User rules before project rules.
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.chapterName: 3.9 Context Provisioning: @ References, CLAUDE.md Imports & Mechanism Selection

chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.question: Claude is not following an instruction in CLAUDE.md. Which command verifies whether the file actually loaded into the current session?
options: /context — check the list under 'Memory files'.
/memory — it lists locations, but does not show what loaded this session.
/doctor — it runs a configuration checkup.
/status — it shows which managed source applies.
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Memory: troubleshoot memory issues
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.explanation:
'Run /context and check the list under Memory files to verify your CLAUDE.md and CLAUDE.local.md files loaded. If a file is missing there, Claude can't see it.' The docs distinguish the two commands explicitly: /memory lists your CLAUDE.md, CLAUDE.local.md, and other memory file locations across user and project scopes, 'including user and project CLAUDE.md entries for files that don't exist yet' — but 'To check which files actually loaded into the current session, run /context.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** /memory is the browse-and-edit command; it lists locations including ones with no file.
- **C.** /doctor proposes trims for a checked-in CLAUDE.md and runs a broader checkup, not a per-session load list.
- **D.** /status surfaces which managed settings source applies.

For deeper debugging the docs suggest the InstructionsLoaded hook, which logs exactly which instruction files load, when, and why.
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.examTrick: /memory = where files COULD be. /context = what actually LOADED. The exam tests that distinction.
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.chapterName: 3.9 Context Provisioning: @ References, CLAUDE.md Imports & Mechanism Selection

chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.question: Why might an instruction in CLAUDE.md not be followed even when /context confirms the file loaded?
options: CLAUDE.md is delivered as a user message after the system prompt and is context rather than enforced configuration, so vague or conflicting instructions may not be followed strictly.
CLAUDE.md is only read on the first turn and is dropped from later requests.
CLAUDE.md instructions apply only to file edits, not to Bash commands or tool selection.
CLAUDE.md is loaded lazily and reaches the model only if Claude decides it is relevant.
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.answer: CLAUDE.md is delivered as a user message after the system prompt and is context rather than enforced configuration, so vague or conflicting instructions may not be followed strictly.
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Memory: Claude isn't following my CLAUDE.md
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.explanation:
'CLAUDE.md content is delivered as a user message after the system prompt, not as part of the system prompt itself. Claude reads it and tries to follow it, but there's no guarantee of strict compliance, especially for vague or conflicting instructions.' The documented remedies: make instructions more specific, look for conflicts across files, and — if it must run at a specific point — write it as a hook instead. For system-prompt-level instructions, use --append-system-prompt, though that must be passed every invocation.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** The context-cost table lists CLAUDE.md's cost as 'Every request'.
- **C.** No such scoping exists.
- **D.** That describes skills. CLAUDE.md loads eagerly at session start.
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.examTrick: CLAUDE.md = a user message after the system prompt = advisory. That single fact answers most 'why wasn't it followed' questions.
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.chapterName: 3.9 Context Provisioning: @ References, CLAUDE.md Imports & Mechanism Selection

chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.question: Which statement about auto memory is correct?
options: Claude writes it itself from your corrections and preferences; it is stored per repository at ~/.claude/projects/<project>/memory/ and is machine-local.
You write it manually and it is committed alongside CLAUDE.md.
It is synchronized across your machines and cloud sessions automatically.
It replaces CLAUDE.md; a project with auto memory enabled ignores CLAUDE.md.
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.answer: Claude writes it itself from your corrections and preferences; it is stored per repository at ~/.claude/projects/<project>/memory/ and is machine-local.
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Memory: auto memory
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.explanation:
The comparison table: CLAUDE.md is written by you and contains instructions and rules; auto memory is written by Claude and contains learnings and patterns, scoped 'Per repository, shared across worktrees'. 'Auto memory is machine-local... Files are not shared across machines or cloud environments.' The four memory types are user, feedback, project, and reference.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** You write CLAUDE.md; Claude writes auto memory.
- **C.** Explicitly machine-local.
- **D.** They are complementary and both load at the start of every conversation.

Also documented: Claude 'skips anything it can derive from the codebase, such as architecture, file paths, or debugging fixes. It also skips anything your CLAUDE.md files already say.'
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.examTrick: You write CLAUDE.md (rules). Claude writes auto memory (learnings). Both load every session; auto memory never leaves the machine.
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.chapterName: 3.9 Context Provisioning: @ References, CLAUDE.md Imports & Mechanism Selection

chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.question: How much of MEMORY.md is loaded at the start of every conversation, and what happens to the rest?
options: The first 200 lines or the first 25KB, whichever comes first; content beyond that threshold is not loaded at session start.
The entire file, however large, since it is the memory index.
Only the frontmatter; the body is read on demand.
The last 200 lines, so the most recent memories are always present.
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.answer: The first 200 lines or the first 25KB, whichever comes first; content beyond that threshold is not loaded at session start.
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Memory: how it works
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.explanation:
'The first 200 lines of MEMORY.md, or the first 25KB, whichever comes first, are loaded at the start of every conversation. Content beyond that threshold is not loaded at session start.' If the file is over a limit the write still succeeds, but Claude Code returns an error telling Claude to rewrite the index, 'because everything past the limit is dropped on the next load.' Topic files such as user_role.md are NOT loaded at startup; Claude reads them on demand.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** That is CLAUDE.md behaviour (full load up to 4 MiB), not MEMORY.md.
- **C.** MEMORY.md is an index of one-line pointers; its body is the point.
- **D.** It is the FIRST 200 lines, not the last — which is why Claude is instructed to keep the index short and move detail into topic files.
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.examTrick: MEMORY.md: first 200 lines OR 25KB, whichever first. Topic files load on demand, never at startup.
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows
chapter-09-context-provisioning-and-clau.chapterName: 3.9 Context Provisioning: @ References, CLAUDE.md Imports & Mechanism Selection

chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.question: A 'deploy' skill exists in both ~/.claude/skills/ and the project's .claude/skills/. Which one runs when you type /deploy?
options: The personal one in ~/.claude/skills/ — skill precedence is managed > user > project.
The project one in .claude/skills/, because project configuration is closest to the work.
Both load and their content is concatenated.
Claude Code refuses to run either and reports a name collision.
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.answer: The personal one in ~/.claude/skills/ — skill precedence is managed > user > project.
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Skills: where skills live
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.explanation:
The docs give this example directly: 'with a deploy skill in both ~/.claude/skills/ and your project's .claude/skills/, /deploy runs the personal one.' Skills override by name with priority managed > user > project.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** This is the intuitive answer and it is wrong for skills. Note the contrast with SUBAGENTS, where project outranks user. The two mechanisms order those tiers oppositely, which is exactly why the exam asks.
- **C.** Skills override by name; they do not merge. (CLAUDE.md files are the additive mechanism.)
- **D.** No error — one simply wins.

Plugin skills avoid the problem entirely because they are namespaced: my-plugin/skills/deploy/SKILL.md becomes /my-plugin:deploy and loads alongside a project deploy skill.
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.examTrick: Skills: managed > USER > project. Subagents: managed > --agents > PROJECT > user. Opposite middle order.
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.question: What is the relationship between .claude/commands/deploy.md and .claude/skills/deploy/SKILL.md?
options: Both create /deploy and work the same way; if both exist the skill takes precedence, and skills add a directory for supporting files plus invocation-control frontmatter.
Commands are deprecated and no longer load at all.
Commands create /deploy; skills can only be invoked automatically by Claude, never by typing.
They are unrelated features that happen to share a name.
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.answer: Both create /deploy and work the same way; if both exist the skill takes precedence, and skills add a directory for supporting files plus invocation-control frontmatter.
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Skills: custom commands merged into skills
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.explanation:
'Custom commands have been merged into skills. A file at .claude/commands/deploy.md and a skill at .claude/skills/deploy/SKILL.md both create /deploy and work the same way. Your existing .claude/commands/ files keep working. Skills add optional features: a directory for supporting files, frontmatter to control whether you or Claude invokes them, and the ability for Claude to load them automatically when relevant.' And: 'if a skill and a command share the same name, the skill takes precedence.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** Command files keep working.
- **C.** Skills are invocable by typing /name unless user-invocable is set to false.
- **D.** They are the same feature after the merge.

One detail: command files support the same frontmatter EXCEPT name and paths, which Claude Code ignores in a command file, and you invoke a command file by its file name.
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.examTrick: Commands merged into skills. Skill beats command on a name tie. Command files ignore the name and paths fields.
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.question: You have a deployment skill with real side effects and want only yourself to trigger it, never Claude automatically. Which frontmatter field?
options: disable-model-invocation: true
user-invocable: false
allowed-tools: none
context: fork
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.answer: disable-model-invocation: true
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Skills: control who invokes a skill
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.explanation:
'disable-model-invocation: Set to true to prevent Claude from automatically loading this skill. Use for workflows you want to trigger manually with /name.' The docs recommend it explicitly: 'Use disable-model-invocation: true for skills with side effects. This saves context and ensures only you trigger them.' It also prevents the skill from being preloaded into subagents and from running when a scheduled task fires with the skill as its prompt.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** user-invocable: false is the exact opposite — it hides the skill from the / menu so ONLY Claude can invoke it, used for background knowledge users should not trigger directly.
- **C.** allowed-tools pre-approves tools; 'none' is not a mechanism for invocation control.
- **D.** context: fork runs the skill in a forked subagent context.

These two fields are the exam's favourite pair because they are near-mirror images.
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.examTrick: disable-model-invocation: true = only YOU. user-invocable: false = only CLAUDE. Learn them as a pair.
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.question: There is no side-effect concern, but a skill contains background knowledge users should never invoke directly from the / menu. Which field?
options: user-invocable: false
disable-model-invocation: true
description: omitted
disallowed-tools: Skill
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.answer: user-invocable: false
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Skills: frontmatter reference
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.explanation:
'user-invocable: Set to false when only Claude should invoke the skill: Claude Code hides it from the / menu and doesn't run it when you type /name. Use for background knowledge users shouldn't invoke directly. Default: true.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** That blocks Claude, leaving only manual invocation — the reverse of the requirement.
- **C.** Omitting the description does not hide the skill; it just makes Claude 'use the first paragraph of markdown content' instead, which usually makes selection WORSE.
- **D.** Not a real mechanism.

If you want the same effect without editing someone else's skill file, the docs offer skillOverrides in settings, which can set a skill to 'user-invocable-only' from the outside.
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.examTrick: user-invocable: false hides it from you but keeps it available to Claude. skillOverrides does it from settings without editing the file.
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.question: What does the allowed-tools field in SKILL.md do, and how long does the grant last?
options: It lets Claude use the listed tools without asking permission during the turn that invokes the skill; the grant clears when you send your next message.
It permanently allowlists those tools in .claude/settings.local.json.
It restricts the skill to only those tools, blocking everything else.
It grants the tools for the remainder of the session.
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.answer: It lets Claude use the listed tools without asking permission during the turn that invokes the skill; the grant clears when you send your next message.
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Skills: frontmatter reference
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.explanation:
'allowed-tools: Tools Claude can use without asking permission during the turn that invokes this skill. The grant clears when you send your next message.' It accepts a space- or comma-separated string, or a YAML list.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** Nothing is written to settings; the grant is ephemeral by design.
- **C.** That is disallowed-tools, which removes tools from Claude's available pool while the skill is active — also clearing on your next message.
- **D.** Turn-scoped, not session-scoped. The single-turn lifetime is the safety property: a skill cannot silently widen your permissions for the rest of the session.

One limit worth knowing: like deny rules, disallowed-tools cannot remove EndConversation while any other tool remains.
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.examTrick: allowed-tools and disallowed-tools are both TURN-scoped and clear on your next message. Neither persists.
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.question: A skill's description and when_to_use text are long. What happens in the skill listing?
options: The combined description and when_to_use text is truncated at 1,536 characters, so the key use case must come first.
The full text always loads; only the skill body is deferred.
Descriptions over 200 characters are rejected at load time.
The text is summarized by a model before entering the listing.
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.answer: The combined description and when_to_use text is truncated at 1,536 characters, so the key use case must come first.
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Skills: frontmatter reference
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.explanation:
'Put the key use case first: the combined description and when_to_use text is truncated at 1,536 characters in the skill listing to reduce context usage.' when_to_use is 'Additional context for when Claude should invoke the skill, such as trigger phrases or example requests. Appended to description and counts toward the 1,536-character cap.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** Names always load, but descriptions are what get cut.
- **C.** No rejection occurs; it is silent truncation.
- **D.** Truncation, not summarization — which is why the ORDER of your words matters.

The large-codebase docs add the consequence: 'descriptions are shortened when there are many, which can strip the keywords Claude uses to decide whether a skill applies. Keep descriptions short and lead with words a request would contain.'
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.examTrick: 1,536-character cap on description + when_to_use combined, and it is TRUNCATION. Front-load the trigger words.
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.question: How does a skill run in an isolated context without you writing a separate subagent file?
options: Set context: fork in the skill's frontmatter, which runs it in a forked subagent context.
Set isolation: worktree in the skill's frontmatter.
Set model: inherit, which routes the skill through a subagent.
