It is not possible; only subagent files can create isolated context.
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.answer: Set context: fork in the skill's frontmatter, which runs it in a forked subagent context.
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Skills: run skills in a subagent
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.explanation:
'context: Set to fork to run in a forked subagent context.' The Extend Claude Code docs confirm the pairing from the other direction: 'A subagent can preload specific skills (skills: field). A skill can run in isolated context using context: fork.' With context: fork set, the skill's model field 'sets the forked subagent's model instead.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** isolation: worktree is SUBAGENT frontmatter, not skill frontmatter.
- **C.** model selects a model; it does not create isolation.
- **D.** Explicitly possible via context: fork.

This is the cheap way to get isolation: a task-content skill with 'context: fork' and 'disable-model-invocation: true' is a manually-triggered, isolated workflow in one file.
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.examTrick: context: fork is the skill-side route to isolation. skills: is the subagent-side route to shared content. They meet in the middle.
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.question: Where do project skills load from when you start Claude Code in a subdirectory of a repository?
options: From .claude/skills/ in the starting directory and in every parent directory up to the repository root.
From the starting directory's .claude/skills/ only.
From the repository root's .claude/skills/ only.
From every .claude/skills/ directory in the entire repository, loaded eagerly at startup.
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.answer: From .claude/skills/ in the starting directory and in every parent directory up to the repository root.
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Skills: where skills load from
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.explanation:
'Project skills load from .claude/skills/ in the directory where you start Claude Code and in every parent directory up to the repository root. Starting Claude in a subdirectory still picks up skills defined at the root.' Skills in NESTED directories below your starting directory are different: 'They load the first time Claude reads or edits a file inside that subdirectory, and stay available for the rest of the session. Until then, those skills don't appear in autocomplete and can't be invoked by name.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B, C.** Both halves of the upward walk are needed.
- **D.** Nested skills load lazily on first file access, not eagerly.

Note this differs from .claude/settings.json, which loads ONLY from the starting directory and is not inherited from parents.
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.examTrick: Skills walk UP to the repo root at startup, and load DOWNWARD lazily when Claude touches a file there. settings.json does neither.
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.question: Does the permissions.additionalDirectories setting load skills from the directories it grants access to?
options: No — it grants file access only. Only --add-dir and /add-dir load .claude/skills/ and .claude/commands/ from added directories.
Yes — any granted directory has its skills discovered automatically.
Yes, but only if CLAUDE_CODE_ADDITIONAL_DIRECTORIES_CLAUDE_MD is set.
No — neither mechanism loads skills from outside the project.
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.answer: No — it grants file access only. Only --add-dir and /add-dir load .claude/skills/ and .claude/commands/ from added directories.
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Skills: skills from added directories
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.explanation:
'The --add-dir flag and /add-dir command grant file access rather than configuration discovery, but skills and commands are an exception: Claude Code loads .claude/skills/ and .claude/commands/ from each added directory automatically. This exception applies only to --add-dir and /add-dir. The permissions.additionalDirectories setting in settings.json grants file access only and doesn't load skills, commands, or subagents.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** The setting and the flag behave differently, which is the whole point.
- **C.** That environment variable governs CLAUDE.md and rules loading from added directories, not skills. Skills load from --add-dir without it.
- **D.** --add-dir does load them.

Remember the full matrix: additionalDirectories = files only, ever. --add-dir = files + skills/commands always, + CLAUDE.md/rules only with the env var.
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.examTrick: additionalDirectories = files ONLY. --add-dir = files + skills/commands, and CLAUDE.md too if the env var is set.
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.question: You edit a skill file mid-session. Do you need to restart Claude Code?
options: No for an existing watched directory — Claude Code picks up adds, edits, and removals within the session; yes if you created a top-level skills directory that did not exist at startup.
Yes always; skills are read once at session start.
No; all skill changes including new top-level directories are picked up automatically.
Only plugin skills support live reloading.
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.answer: No for an existing watched directory — Claude Code picks up adds, edits, and removals within the session; yes if you created a top-level skills directory that did not exist at startup.
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Skills: live change detection
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.explanation:
'Claude Code watches skill directories for file changes. When you add, edit, or remove a skill under ~/.claude/skills/, the project .claude/skills/, or a .claude/skills/ inside an --add-dir directory, Claude Code picks up the change within the current session, without a restart. If you create a top-level skills directory that didn't exist when the session started, restart Claude Code so it can watch the new directory.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** Live detection is explicitly supported.
- **C.** The new-directory case is the documented exception.
- **D.** It applies to user, project, and --add-dir skills.

A related lifecycle detail: if you delete a skill, Claude Code drops it from /skills in the current session, but content from an invocation earlier in the session stays in context until the session ends.
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.examTrick: Live reload works inside already-watched directories. A brand-new top-level skills directory needs a restart.
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.question: How does a skill get the command name you type to invoke it?
options: From the directory name; the optional name field sets the display name shown in listings and defaults to the directory name.
From the name frontmatter field only; the directory name is ignored.
From the first markdown heading in the file body.
From the description field's first word.
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.answer: From the directory name; the optional name field sets the display name shown in listings and defaults to the directory name.
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Skills: create a skill; frontmatter reference
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.explanation:
'The directory name becomes the command you type.' The frontmatter reference lists name as not required: 'Display name shown in skill listings. Defaults to the directory name.' So ~/.claude/skills/summarize-changes/SKILL.md gives you /summarize-changes.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** name is optional and is a display name.
- **C, D.** Neither is used for naming.

Command files behave differently: 'You invoke a command file by its file name', and command files ignore the name and paths fields entirely.
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.examTrick: Skill: DIRECTORY name is the command. Command file: FILE name is the command. name: frontmatter is display only.
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.question: Which field sets the reasoning effort level while a skill is active?
options: effort, accepting low, medium, high, xhigh, or max, overriding the session effort level.
model, using an effort-suffixed alias.
maxTurns, which bounds reasoning depth.
context, set to deep.
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.answer: effort, accepting low, medium, high, xhigh, or max, overriding the session effort level.
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Skills: frontmatter reference
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.explanation:
'effort: Effort level when this skill is active. Overrides the session effort level. Default: inherits from session. Options: low, medium, high, xhigh, max; available levels depend on the model.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** model selects the model; it accepts the same values as /model or 'inherit'. Note its scoping detail: 'The override applies for the rest of the current turn and is not saved to settings; the session model resumes on your next prompt.'
- **C.** maxTurns is subagent frontmatter, not skill frontmatter.
- **D.** context accepts fork.

Both model and effort are turn-scoped overrides, matching the pattern of allowed-tools and disallowed-tools.
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.examTrick: Skill overrides (model, effort, allowed-tools, disallowed-tools) are all TURN-scoped and revert on your next prompt.
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.question: What happens if a skill omits the description field?
options: Claude Code uses the first paragraph of the markdown content as the description.
The skill fails to load and is reported as invalid.
The skill loads but can only be invoked manually, never by Claude.
The directory name is used as the description.
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.answer: Claude Code uses the first paragraph of the markdown content as the description.
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Skills: frontmatter reference
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.explanation:
The reference marks description as 'Recommended' rather than required: 'What the skill does and when to use it. Claude uses this to decide when to apply the skill. If omitted, uses the first paragraph of markdown content.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** It loads; description is recommended, not required.
- **C.** Model invocation is controlled by disable-model-invocation, not by whether a description exists.
- **D.** The directory name supplies the command name and the display name default, not the description.

The practical risk: an accidental first paragraph becomes your selection signal, and 'How Claude chooses skills' says that if descriptions are vague or overlap, 'Claude may load the wrong skill or miss one that would help.'
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.examTrick: No description = first markdown paragraph becomes it. That is a silent quality problem, not an error.
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.question: A project skill named 'code-review' is created. What happens to the bundled /code-review skill and its alias /review?
options: The project skill replaces the bundled /code-review, and typing the bundled alias /review never runs your skill.
Both remain available; the bundled one takes precedence because it ships with Claude Code.
Claude Code refuses to load a skill whose name collides with a bundled one.
The project skill replaces both /code-review and its alias /review.
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.answer: The project skill replaces the bundled /code-review, and typing the bundled alias /review never runs your skill.
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Skills: where skills live
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.explanation:
The docs give this exact example: 'a code-review skill in your project's .claude/skills/ replaces the bundled /code-review, and typing the bundled alias /review never runs your skill.' Aliases stay bound to the bundled skill.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** Your skill wins over the bundled one on the primary name.
- **C.** No refusal; overriding a bundled skill is supported.
- **D.** The alias is the exception, and that asymmetry is the testable detail — a teammate typing /review would silently get different behaviour from one typing /code-review.

Similarly, a skill enabled on claude.ai loses to a project skill of the same name.
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.examTrick: You can override a bundled skill by name, but NOT its aliases. The alias keeps running the bundled version.
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.question: Which frontmatter field scopes a skill so Claude loads it automatically only when working with matching files, without moving the skill into that directory?
options: paths, which takes glob patterns.
when_to_use, describing the file types.
context, set to the directory.
argument-hint, naming the file pattern.
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.answer: paths, which takes glob patterns.
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Large codebases: add per-directory skills; Skills frontmatter
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.explanation:
'You can also scope a skill by file pattern instead of by placement. The paths frontmatter field takes glob patterns, and Claude loads the skill automatically only when it works with matching files. Use this for a skill that lives in the repository root's .claude/skills/ but applies only to certain files wherever they appear, such as a database-migration skill scoped to **/migrations/**.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** when_to_use is prose appended to the description; it influences selection but enforces nothing.
- **C.** context accepts fork.
- **D.** argument-hint is autocomplete text such as [issue-number].

Note that command files in .claude/commands/ ignore the paths field entirely — another reason skills are recommended over command files.
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.examTrick: paths: globs scope a skill by FILE PATTERN, independent of where the skill file sits. Command files ignore paths.
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.question: Which pair of fields supports passing and substituting arguments in a skill?
options: argument-hint for autocomplete display, and arguments for named positional $name substitution in the skill content.
args and params.
$ARGUMENTS only; named arguments are not supported.
input-schema and defaults.
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.answer: argument-hint for autocomplete display, and arguments for named positional $name substitution in the skill content.
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Skills: frontmatter reference
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.explanation:
'argument-hint: Hint shown during autocomplete to indicate expected arguments. Example: [issue-number] or [filename] [format].' And 'arguments: Named positional arguments for $name substitution in the skill content. Accepts a space-separated string or a YAML list. Names map to argument positions in order.' The bundled example in the docs uses $ARGUMENTS in a fix-issue skill invoked as /fix-issue 1234.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B, D.** Not documented field names.
- **C.** $ARGUMENTS works, but named positional arguments via the arguments field are also supported — the claim that they are not is what makes this option wrong.
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.examTrick: argument-hint = what the user sees in autocomplete. arguments = named positional substitution. $ARGUMENTS = the whole string.
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.question: When is a skill the right mechanism rather than CLAUDE.md?
options: When the content is reference material needed only sometimes, or a multi-step procedure you trigger with /<name>.
When the content is a build command every session needs.
When the rule must hold every time regardless of what Claude decides.
When the instruction should apply only to files matching a glob.
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.answer: When the content is reference material needed only sometimes, or a multi-step procedure you trigger with /<name>.
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Skills; Extend Claude Code: CLAUDE.md vs Skill
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.explanation:
'Create a skill when you keep pasting the same instructions, checklist, or multi-step procedure into chat, or when a section of CLAUDE.md has grown into a procedure rather than a fact. Unlike CLAUDE.md content, a skill's body loads only when it's used, so long reference material costs almost nothing until you need it.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** Always-needed facts belong in CLAUDE.md.
- **C.** A must-hold-every-time rule is a hook or a permission rule; a skill is interpreted content.
- **D.** That is a .claude/rules/ file with paths frontmatter — though note a skill can also carry paths, the rules mechanism is the one for conventions that apply while editing matching files.

The distinguishing test is the shape of the content: a FACT belongs in CLAUDE.md, a PROCEDURE belongs in a skill.
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.examTrick: Fact every session = CLAUDE.md. Procedure or reference used sometimes = skill. Must-hold rule = hook.
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.question: What is the context cost of skills at session start?
options: Names and descriptions load at session start; full content loads only when the skill is used, so cost is low until then.
Full skill content loads at session start for every discovered skill.
Nothing loads until invocation, so the cost is exactly zero.
Only skills with paths frontmatter load anything at startup.
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.answer: Names and descriptions load at session start; full content loads only when the skill is used, so cost is low until then.
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Extend Claude Code: context cost by feature
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.explanation:
The context-cost table lists skills as loading at 'Session start + when used', with 'Descriptions at start, full content when used', giving 'Low (descriptions every request)'. The footnote adds: 'By default, skill descriptions load at session start so Claude can decide when to use them. Set disable-model-invocation: true in a skill's frontmatter to hide it from Claude entirely until you invoke it manually.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** That is CLAUDE.md behaviour.
- **C.** Zero cost applies to USER-ONLY skills (disable-model-invocation: true) and to hooks. Ordinary skills pay the description cost every request.
- **D.** All discovered skills contribute their descriptions.

This is why the 1,536-character description cap exists and why a sprawling skill library degrades selection.
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.examTrick: Skills cost DESCRIPTIONS every request. disable-model-invocation: true drops that to zero until you invoke it.
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.question: A routine (scheduled cloud run) invokes a skill that exists only in ~/.claude/skills/ on your machine. What happens?
options: Claude Code reports that the skill was not found, because each routine run starts as a fresh remote session that does not read your machine's user skills.
The skill is uploaded automatically at schedule time.
The routine falls back to the closest-matching skill by description.
The routine runs the skill from a cached copy of your last local session.
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.answer: Claude Code reports that the skill was not found, because each routine run starts as a fresh remote session that does not read your machine's user skills.
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Skills in Cowork and cloud sessions
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.explanation:
'Cowork sessions and cloud sessions, including routines, don't read ~/.claude/skills/ on your machine... If a skill exists only in ~/.claude/skills/ on your machine, Claude Code reports that the skill was not found when a routine invokes it, because each routine run starts as a fresh remote session.' The fixes: for cloud sessions, commit the skill to the repository's .claude/skills/, or ship it in a plugin declared in the repository's .claude/settings.json, since 'Repo-declared plugins install at session start; plugins enabled only in your user settings don't transfer.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B, D.** No upload or caching of local user skills occurs.
- **C.** There is no fuzzy fallback; a missing skill is reported as missing.
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.examTrick: Cloud/routine sessions see REPO skills, not your ~/.claude/skills/. Commit it or ship it in a repo-declared plugin.
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.question: Which statement about nested skills sharing a name with a root skill is correct?
options: Both stay available — a deploy skill at the project root and another in apps/web/.claude/skills/ coexist rather than one overriding the other.
The nested skill silently replaces the root skill for the whole session.
The root skill always wins and the nested one never loads.
Claude Code reports a collision and loads neither.
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.answer: Both stay available — a deploy skill at the project root and another in apps/web/.claude/skills/ coexist rather than one overriding the other.
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Skills: nested skills
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.explanation:
'If a nested skill shares a name with another skill, both stay available. For example, with a deploy skill at the project root and another in apps/web/.claude/skills/...' This is a deliberate exception to the usual override-by-name rule, so a monorepo package can provide its own version of a workflow without destroying the root one.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B, C.** Neither overrides the other.
- **D.** No error.

Remember the loading condition though: nested skills 'aren't loaded at startup. They load the first time Claude reads or edits a file inside that subdirectory.' So the nested one is invisible until Claude touches that package.
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.examTrick: Nested skills COEXIST with same-named root skills — an exception to override-by-name. But they load lazily.
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.question: An administrator wants to remove an enterprise skill. Where does it live?
options: In .claude/skills/ inside the managed settings directory, for example /etc/claude-code/.claude/skills/<skill-name>/ on Linux.
In ~/.claude/skills/synced/ on each user's machine.
In the project's .claude/skills/, deployed by MDM.
In managed-settings.json as an inline skills array.
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.answer: In .claude/skills/ inside the managed settings directory, for example /etc/claude-code/.claude/skills/<skill-name>/ on Linux.
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Skills: delete a skill
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.explanation:
'Enterprise skill: an administrator deletes the skill's directory from .claude/skills/ inside the managed settings directory, for example /etc/claude-code/.claude/skills/<skill-name>/ on Linux.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** ~/.claude/skills/synced/ is where skills you enable on claude.ai are downloaded when CLAUDE_CODE_SYNC_SKILLS is set. That folder name is reserved, and Claude Code skips a skill you author at that name.
- **C.** Project skills are the team-shared tier, not the enterprise tier.
- **D.** Skills are directories with SKILL.md files, not inline settings values. (claudeMd is the inline-content key, and it is for CLAUDE.md, not skills.)
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.examTrick: Enterprise skills live under the MANAGED SETTINGS directory. 'synced' is a reserved folder name for claude.ai skills.
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.question: Which trigger, per the documentation, means you should capture something as a skill rather than leaving it in chat?
options: You paste the same playbook or multi-step procedure into chat for the third time.
Claude gets a convention wrong twice.
You want something to happen every time without asking.
A side task floods your conversation with output you won't reference again.
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.answer: You paste the same playbook or multi-step procedure into chat for the third time.
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Extend Claude Code: build your setup over time
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.explanation:
The trigger table maps each symptom to a mechanism: 'You paste the same playbook or multi-step procedure into chat for the third time' → capture it as a skill. Also 'You keep typing the same prompt to start a task' → save it as a user-invocable skill.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** 'Claude gets a convention or command wrong twice' → add it to CLAUDE.md.
- **C.** 'You want something to happen every time without asking' → write a hook.
- **D.** 'A side task floods your conversation with output you won't reference again' → route it through a subagent.

Memorising this table answers a whole family of mechanism-selection questions, because each row states the observable symptom rather than the abstract principle.
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.examTrick: Learn the trigger table by SYMPTOM: wrong twice → CLAUDE.md; pasted thrice → skill; every time → hook; floods context → subagent.
chapter-10-skills-and-slash-commands.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.question: What is the config value of the mode labelled 'Manual' in the CLI, and why does it matter?
options: default — hooks and SDK integrations use the config value, and the CLI also accepts 'manual' as an alias.
manual — 'default' was renamed and is now deprecated.
review — Manual is the display name for the review mode.
ask — Manual maps to the ask permission rule type.
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.answer: default — hooks and SDK integrations use the config value, and the CLI also accepts 'manual' as an alias.
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Permission modes: available modes
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.explanation:
'The mode that reviews every action is named Manual in the CLI, in claude --help, in the VS Code and JetBrains extensions, and in the desktop app. Its config value is default, which is what hooks and SDK integrations use. The CLI accepts manual as an alias wherever you type the value, for example claude --permission-mode manual or "defaultMode": "manual".'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** default is the config value, not a deprecated name; manual is the alias.
- **C, D.** Neither is a mode name. Note that 'ask' is a permission RULE type, not a mode — rules and modes are two different layers.

The label-versus-value split matters because a settings file, a hook payload, and the UI can each show a different string for the same mode.
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.examTrick: Manual (label) = default (config value) = manual (CLI alias). Hooks and SDK see 'default'.
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.chapterName: 3.11 Permission Modes, Plan Mode & Unattended Execution

chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.question: In plan mode, what runs without asking?
options: Reads, plus classifier-approved commands when auto mode is available; Claude Code blocks edits until you approve a plan.
Reads and file edits, but no shell commands.
Nothing at all — plan mode prompts for every action including reads.
Everything, since plan mode is only about output formatting.
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.answer: Reads, plus classifier-approved commands when auto mode is available; Claude Code blocks edits until you approve a plan.
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Permission modes: available modes
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.explanation:
The mode table lists plan as allowing 'Reads, plus classifier-approved commands when auto mode is available', best for 'Exploring a codebase before changing it'. The mode-selection table adds: 'Explore before changing anything → claude --permission-mode plan → Claude Code blocks edits until you approve a plan.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** Blocking edits is the defining property of plan mode; allowing them would defeat it.
- **C.** Reads are permitted, which is what makes exploration possible.
- **D.** Plan mode is a permission mode with real enforcement, not a presentation setting.

Note the sandbox interaction: 'The Bash sandbox and auto mode work independently and combine, except in plan mode, where auto-allow doesn't widen approvals.'
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.examTrick: Plan mode = reads yes, edits blocked until the plan is approved. Sandbox auto-allow does NOT widen approvals in plan mode.
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.chapterName: 3.11 Permission Modes, Plan Mode & Unattended Execution

chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.question: How do you switch permission modes in a running CLI session, and what is the cycle from auto?
options: Press Shift+Tab; from auto the first press switches to default, then the cycle runs default → acceptEdits → plan → back to default.
Press Ctrl+P to open a mode picker; there is no cycle.
Modes can only be set at launch with --permission-mode.
Type /mode followed by the mode name; Shift+Tab only toggles plan mode.
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.answer: Press Shift+Tab; from auto the first press switches to default, then the cycle runs default → acceptEdits → plan → back to default.
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Permission modes: switch permission modes
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.explanation:
'During a session: press Shift+Tab to cycle permission modes. From auto, the first press switches to default, and the cycle then runs default → acceptEdits → plan → back to default. Optional modes slot in after plan.' The status bar shows the active mode as ⏸ manual mode on, ⏵⏵ accept edits on, ⏸ plan mode on, ⏵⏵ auto mode on, ⏵⏵ don't ask on, or ⏵⏵ bypass permissions on.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B, D.** Not the documented controls.
- **C.** Modes are changeable mid-session; the flag only sets the starting mode.

Optional modes have specific entry conditions: bypassPermissions 'appears after you start with --permission-mode bypassPermissions, --dangerously-skip-permissions, --allow-dangerously-skip-permissions, or permissions.defaultMode: "bypassPermissions"', and dontAsk 'never appears in the cycle; set it with --permission-mode dontAsk'.
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.examTrick: Shift+Tab cycles default → acceptEdits → plan. bypassPermissions only joins the cycle if you started with a flag enabling it. dontAsk never joins.
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.chapterName: 3.11 Permission Modes, Plan Mode & Unattended Execution

chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.question: Which statement about deny rules and permission modes is correct?
options: Deny rules block in every mode, including bypassPermissions; allow rules have no effect in bypassPermissions.
bypassPermissions overrides deny rules, which is why it is restricted to containers.
Deny rules apply only in Manual mode; other modes replace them.
Allow rules are the only rule type that survives a mode change.
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.answer: Deny rules block in every mode, including bypassPermissions; allow rules have no effect in bypassPermissions.
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Permission modes: available modes
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.explanation:
'Modes set the baseline. Layer permission rules on top to pre-approve or block specific tools. Deny rules block in every mode, including bypassPermissions. Deny and ask rules don't apply to EndConversation as long as Claude still has at least one other tool it can call. Allow rules have no effect in bypassPermissions.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** Deny survives bypassPermissions — this is the key safety property, and getting it backwards is a serious misunderstanding.
- **C.** Rules layer on top of every mode.
- **D.** Allow rules are the ones that become irrelevant in bypassPermissions, since nothing is being asked anyway.

The mental model: MODES decide what gets asked about; RULES decide what is permitted at all. Deny is the floor beneath every mode.
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.examTrick: Modes = baseline. Rules = layered on top. Deny holds in EVERY mode including bypass; allow is meaningless in bypass.
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.chapterName: 3.11 Permission Modes, Plan Mode & Unattended Execution

chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.question: Which writes are never auto-approved regardless of mode?
options: Writes to protected paths, except in bypassPermissions mode and in plan-mode sessions where bypass permissions are available.
Writes to any file outside the working directory, in every mode without exception.
Writes to files larger than a size threshold.
All writes; every mode prompts for file writes.
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.answer: Writes to protected paths, except in bypassPermissions mode and in plan-mode sessions where bypass permissions are available.
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Permission modes: protected paths
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.explanation:
'Writes to protected paths are never auto-approved except in bypassPermissions mode and in plan-mode sessions where bypass permissions are available, meaning sessions started in a way that puts bypassPermissions in the mode cycle.' The permissions docs identify protected paths as including .git and .claude — the directories that control the repository and Claude Code's own configuration.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** Directory scope is governed by working directories and additionalDirectories, a separate mechanism.
- **C.** Size is irrelevant.
- **D.** acceptEdits auto-approves ordinary file edits by design.

The reason .claude is protected is self-evident once you see it: a write there could rewrite the permission rules that constrain the session.
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.examTrick: Protected paths (.git, .claude) resist every mode except bypassPermissions. Self-modification of the permission system is the risk.
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.chapterName: 3.11 Permission Modes, Plan Mode & Unattended Execution

chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.question: A CI pipeline should run the test suite non-interactively with an exact allowlist. Which invocation matches the documented pattern?
options: claude -p "run the test suite" --permission-mode dontAsk --allowedTools "Bash(npm test)" "Read"
claude -p "run the test suite" --dangerously-skip-permissions
claude --permission-mode acceptEdits "run the test suite"
claude -p "run the test suite" --permission-mode plan
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.answer: claude -p "run the test suite" --permission-mode dontAsk --allowedTools "Bash(npm test)" "Read"
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Permission modes: choose a mode
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.explanation:
The mode-selection table gives this verbatim under 'Run in CI with an exact allowlist'. dontAsk plus a tight --allowedTools list is the CI pattern: nothing prompts, and nothing outside the allowlist runs. The caveat noted: 'Claude Code on the web ignores dontAsk from settings files.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** --dangerously-skip-permissions is the fully-unattended-in-a-container pattern and REQUIRES 'a container, VM, or the sandbox runtime'; on Linux and macOS it should run as a non-root user. It is far broader than a test run needs.
- **C.** acceptEdits still prompts for other actions and is not a headless pattern; also -p is missing.
- **D.** Plan mode blocks edits and produces a plan, not a test run.

The principle: in unattended contexts, narrow the TOOL surface rather than widening the permission mode.
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.examTrick: CI = -p + dontAsk + tight --allowedTools. Container-only = --dangerously-skip-permissions. Never confuse the two.
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.chapterName: 3.11 Permission Modes, Plan Mode & Unattended Execution

chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.question: Which is the correct precedence for deciding a session's starting permission mode?
options: The --permission-mode flag (or --dangerously-skip-permissions) outranks permissions.defaultMode in settings files.
permissions.defaultMode in managed settings outranks the --permission-mode flag.
The mode of the most recently resumed session always wins.
The VS Code extension setting outranks everything, including managed settings.
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.answer: The --permission-mode flag (or --dangerously-skip-permissions) outranks permissions.defaultMode in settings files.
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Permission modes: which mode a session starts in
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.explanation:
The documented order is: 1 the --permission-mode flag or --dangerously-skip-permissions, 2 permissions.defaultMode in a settings file. Within settings files, ordinary settings precedence applies, 'so a project or managed value outranks ~/.claude/settings.json'.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** Reversed for the starting mode specifically. Note that an organization CAN still remove auto mode entirely by setting permissions.disableAutoMode to "disable" — a capability lock, not a starting-mode preference.
- **C.** 'A session you resume keeps the permission mode it was in unless you pass --permission-mode or --dangerously-skip-permissions' — so the flag still wins.
- **D.** Managed settings are not overridden by an extension preference.

A quirk worth knowing: an "auto" value in .claude/settings.json or settings.local.json does not take effect, and Claude Code then uses the built-in default rather than a defaultMode from ~/.claude/settings.json.
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.examTrick: Flag beats settings for the STARTING mode. But capability locks (disableAutoMode, disableBypassPermissionsMode) at the managed tier beat everything.
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.chapterName: 3.11 Permission Modes, Plan Mode & Unattended Execution

chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.question: What distinguishes auto mode from acceptEdits?
options: In auto mode a classifier model reviews most actions instead of you, blocking risky ones; acceptEdits mechanically auto-approves reads, edits, and common filesystem commands with no review.
Auto mode approves everything; acceptEdits approves only reads.
They are the same mode under two names on different plans.
Auto mode is a plan-mode variant that auto-approves the plan.
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.answer: In auto mode a classifier model reviews most actions instead of you, blocking risky ones; acceptEdits mechanically auto-approves reads, edits, and common filesystem commands with no review.
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Permission modes: eliminate prompts with auto mode
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.explanation:
'In auto mode, a second model, the classifier, reviews actions instead of you.' The best-practices docs describe what it blocks: 'scope escalation, unknown infrastructure, and hostile-content-driven actions'. acceptEdits has no classifier — it 'Automatically accepts file edits and common filesystem commands such as mkdir, touch, mv, and cp for paths in the working directory or additionalDirectories.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** Auto mode blocks risky actions; it does not approve everything. bypassPermissions is the approve-everything mode.
- **C.** Different mechanisms. Auto mode is the built-in starting mode on Pro, Max, and Team plans, but it is a distinct mode.
- **D.** Unrelated to plan approval.

Auto mode also 'Requires a supported model, and your organization can turn auto mode off.'
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.examTrick: auto = a CLASSIFIER reviews. acceptEdits = mechanical rule, no review. bypass = no checks at all.
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.chapterName: 3.11 Permission Modes, Plan Mode & Unattended Execution

chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.question: A developer wants fewer prompts while iterating locally, without a classifier reviewing actions. What does the documentation suggest?
options: Manual mode plus the Bash sandbox in auto-allow mode — run /sandbox and select auto-allow, or set sandbox.enabled to true.
bypassPermissions mode, since local machines are trusted.
dontAsk mode with no allowlist.
Plan mode, which reduces prompts by blocking edits.
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.answer: Manual mode plus the Bash sandbox in auto-allow mode — run /sandbox and select auto-allow, or set sandbox.enabled to true.
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Permission modes: choose a mode
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.explanation:
The table row reads: 'Iterate locally with fewer prompts, without a classifier → Manual mode plus the Bash sandbox in auto-allow mode: claude --permission-mode default, then run /sandbox and select auto-allow.' The sandbox provides 'OS-level isolation that restricts filesystem and network access', available on macOS, Linux, and WSL2. Crucially: 'Deny rules still apply, and ask rules that name a command, such as Bash(git push *), still prompt.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** bypassPermissions is documented for 'Isolated containers and VMs only' — a developer machine is not that.
- **C.** dontAsk without an allowlist removes the prompts and the boundary at once.
- **D.** Plan mode blocks edits, which stops iteration entirely.

The principle: get safety from ISOLATION rather than from prompting, then keep your deny rules.
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.examTrick: Fewer prompts safely = sandbox (isolation), not a looser mode. Deny and command-specific ask rules still fire inside the sandbox.
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.chapterName: 3.11 Permission Modes, Plan Mode & Unattended Execution

chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.question: What happens to the few calls that would still prompt when a -p run uses --dangerously-skip-permissions?
options: They are denied instead of prompting, since a headless run cannot show a prompt.
They block the run indefinitely waiting for input.
They are auto-approved, since bypassPermissions approves everything.
They fall back to the classifier for a decision.
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.answer: They are denied instead of prompting, since a headless run cannot show a prompt.
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Permission modes: choose a mode
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.explanation:
The table row for 'Run fully unattended inside a container' notes: 'In this -p run, the few calls that would still prompt are denied instead.' Those are the actions no mode auto-approves — the list Claude Code never auto-approves 'in any mode, including bypassPermissions'.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** Hanging forever would make headless automation unusable; denial is the fail-safe.
- **C.** bypassPermissions skips prompts, but there remains a documented set of actions no mode auto-approves.
- **D.** The classifier belongs to auto mode, not bypassPermissions.

The general design principle: when a decision cannot be surfaced to a human, the safe default is refusal, not assumption.
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.examTrick: Headless + bypass: unpromptable calls are DENIED, never auto-approved. There is always a set no mode auto-approves.
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.chapterName: 3.11 Permission Modes, Plan Mode & Unattended Execution

chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.question: Plan mode adds overhead. According to the documentation, when should you skip it?
options: When the scope is clear and the fix is small — a typo, a log line, a rename — or if you could describe the diff in one sentence.
Whenever you are working in a language you know well.
Whenever the change is reversible with git.
Whenever you are the only person working on the repository.
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.answer: When the scope is clear and the fix is small — a typo, a log line, a rename — or if you could describe the diff in one sentence.
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Best practices: explore first, then plan, then code
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.explanation:
'Plan mode is useful, but also adds overhead. For tasks where the scope is clear and the fix is small (like fixing a typo, adding a log line, or renaming a variable) ask Claude to do it directly... If you could describe the diff in one sentence, skip the plan.' The inverse triggers are approach uncertainty, multi-file scope, and unfamiliar code.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** Your familiarity with the LANGUAGE is not the criterion; your familiarity with the CODE is.
- **C.** Reversibility is a reasonable engineering consideration but is not one of the documented criteria.
- **D.** Team size is not a criterion — though the exam objective does mention 'the need for stakeholder review before implementation', which is a reason TO plan, not to skip.

This objective scored 67% on the real exam, so the one-sentence-diff heuristic is worth memorising verbatim.
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.examTrick: The one-sentence-diff test decides it. Plan when: uncertain approach, multiple files, unfamiliar code, or stakeholders must review.
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.chapterName: 3.11 Permission Modes, Plan Mode & Unattended Execution

chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.question: How can you edit a plan before Claude implements it?
options: Press Ctrl+G to open the plan in your text editor before Claude proceeds.
Plans are immutable once generated; reject it and ask for a new one.
Run /compact with instructions to reshape the plan.
Edit the PLAN.md file after implementation begins.
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.answer: Press Ctrl+G to open the plan in your text editor before Claude proceeds.
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Best practices: explore first, then plan, then code
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.explanation:
In the Plan step: 'Press Ctrl+G to open the plan in your text editor for direct editing before Claude proceeds.' You then switch out of plan mode by approving the plan or pressing Shift+Tab.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** Direct editing is supported, which is faster than a regeneration round-trip.
- **C.** /compact summarizes conversation context; it is not a plan editor.
- **D.** Editing after implementation starts means the work already diverged from the plan.

The plan file is also what survives compaction: 'Claude Code re-injects the plan file after each compaction, so the plan survives where conversation history may not.'
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.examTrick: Ctrl+G edits the plan in your editor. Shift+Tab or approval exits plan mode. The plan file survives compaction by re-injection.
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.chapterName: 3.11 Permission Modes, Plan Mode & Unattended Execution

chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.question: An organization wants to remove auto mode so nobody can select it. What is the correct setting and tier?
options: permissions.disableAutoMode set to "disable" in managed settings.
permissions.defaultMode set to "default" in managed settings.
permissions.deny including "auto" in managed settings.
claudeCode.initialPermissionMode set to "default" in VS Code settings.
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.answer: permissions.disableAutoMode set to "disable" in managed settings.
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Permission modes: start in a different mode
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.explanation:
'Every terminal session in your organization → Set permissions.defaultMode in managed settings. Terminal sessions start in that mode and people can still switch to auto mode... To remove auto mode so nobody can select it, set permissions.disableAutoMode to "disable" instead.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** defaultMode sets where sessions START; users can still switch. The docs say so explicitly.
- **C.** deny rules name tools and patterns, not modes.
- **D.** A VS Code user setting is neither organization-wide nor a capability lock, and the extension setting does not even accept 'auto'.

The pattern generalises: a starting-mode preference is not an enforcement mechanism. To remove a capability you need the dedicated disable* key at the managed tier — the same distinction as disableBypassPermissionsMode.
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.examTrick: defaultMode = where you START. disableAutoMode / disableBypassPermissionsMode = capability REMOVED. Only the latter enforces.
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.chapterName: 3.11 Permission Modes, Plan Mode & Unattended Execution

chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.question: Which mode does a resumed session start in?
options: The mode it was in when it was suspended, unless you pass --permission-mode or --dangerously-skip-permissions.
Always the built-in default for the plan, regardless of prior mode.
Always Manual, as a safety measure on resume.
The mode set by permissions.defaultMode, which always overrides the saved mode.
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.answer: The mode it was in when it was suspended, unless you pass --permission-mode or --dangerously-skip-permissions.
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Permission modes: which mode a session starts in
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.explanation:
'A session you resume keeps the permission mode it was in unless you pass --permission-mode or --dangerously-skip-permissions.' The sessions documentation lists the exceptions under 'what a resumed session restores'.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B, D.** The saved session state takes priority over the default; only an explicit flag overrides it.
- **C.** No forced downgrade on resume.

This fits the broader session-resumption principle the exam tests: resumption restores accumulated state accurately rather than resetting it, so you do not have to re-establish your working context.
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.examTrick: Resume keeps the prior mode. Only an explicit flag changes it. Resumption restores state rather than resetting it.
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.chapterName: 3.11 Permission Modes, Plan Mode & Unattended Execution

chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.question: Which claim about the dontAsk mode is correct?
options: It never appears in the Shift+Tab cycle and must be set with --permission-mode dontAsk; Claude Code on the web ignores it from settings files.
It is the same as bypassPermissions under a friendlier name.
It appears in the cycle immediately after plan mode by default.
It disables deny rules so nothing can block a run.
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.answer: It never appears in the Shift+Tab cycle and must be set with --permission-mode dontAsk; Claude Code on the web ignores it from settings files.
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Permission modes: switch permission modes; choose a mode
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.explanation:
'dontAsk: never appears in the cycle; set it with --permission-mode dontAsk.' And in the CI row: 'Claude Code on the web ignores dontAsk from settings files.' The status bar shows it as ⏵⏵ don't ask on.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** They are distinct modes; dontAsk is paired with an exact --allowedTools list in the documented CI pattern, whereas bypassPermissions requires container isolation.
- **C.** Optional modes that DO slot in after plan are bypassPermissions (first) and auto (last); dontAsk is not among them.
- **D.** Deny rules block in every mode.

The design logic: dontAsk is meant for scripted contexts where you have already enumerated the permitted tools, so putting it one keystroke away in an interactive cycle would be a hazard.
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.examTrick: dontAsk is flag-only, never in the cycle. Optional cycle modes are bypassPermissions (first) and auto (last).
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.chapterName: 3.11 Permission Modes, Plan Mode & Unattended Execution

chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.question: Which combination gives defense in depth for a hands-off run?
options: auto mode with a classifier reviewing each action, plus a sandbox or container for isolation.
bypassPermissions with a long allow list.
acceptEdits plus a PostToolUse hook.
Manual mode with every tool pre-approved.
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.answer: auto mode with a classifier reviewing each action, plus a sandbox or container for isolation.
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Permission modes: choose a mode
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.explanation:
The table row: 'Work hands-off with a classifier reviewing each action → claude --permission-mode auto → None [required]; a sandbox or container adds defense in depth.' Two independent layers: a model-level review of each action and an OS-level restriction on what any action can reach.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** Allow rules have no effect in bypassPermissions, so the list does nothing — a subtle trap.
- **C.** A PostToolUse hook fires AFTER the tool ran, so it cannot prevent a harmful action; PreToolUse is the blocking event.
- **D.** Pre-approving everything converts Manual mode into an unreviewed mode while keeping its name.

Defense in depth means the layers must be INDEPENDENT — a second layer that the first can disable is not a second layer.
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.examTrick: auto (classifier) + sandbox (OS isolation) = independent layers. PostToolUse cannot prevent; only PreToolUse blocks.
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.chapterName: 3.11 Permission Modes, Plan Mode & Unattended Execution

chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.question: On which plans is auto mode the built-in starting permission mode for interactive terminal and VS Code sessions?
options: Pro, Max, and Team plans.
All plans, including the free tier.
Enterprise plans only.
No plan; auto mode always requires an explicit flag.
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.answer: Pro, Max, and Team plans.
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Permission modes: which mode a session starts in
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.explanation:
'On Pro, Max, and Team plans, the built-in starting permission mode is auto mode.' On other plans, Manual mode is the built-in starting mode. Auto mode also 'Requires a supported model, and your organization can turn auto mode off.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B, C, D.** Each misstates the plan set or the requirement.

A related behaviour: on those plans, if your ~/.claude/settings.json sets a defaultMode other than auto and no other settings file sets one, 'Claude Code asks once, in the terminal or in the VS Code extension, whether to change the setting to auto mode. If you decline, your setting stays as it is.'
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.examTrick: Pro/Max/Team start in auto. Other plans start in Manual. Auto needs a supported model and can be disabled by the org.
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.chapterName: 3.11 Permission Modes, Plan Mode & Unattended Execution

chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.question: Which best describes the layered mental model for Claude Code permissions?
options: Modes set the baseline of what is asked about; permission rules layer on top to pre-approve or block; hooks add deterministic programmatic decisions; sandboxing adds OS-level isolation.
Modes and rules are alternatives; you choose one system or the other.
Rules set the baseline and modes are exceptions to them.
Hooks replace permission rules once configured.
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.answer: Modes set the baseline of what is asked about; permission rules layer on top to pre-approve or block; hooks add deterministic programmatic decisions; sandboxing adds OS-level isolation.
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Permission modes; Permissions; Hooks
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.explanation:
'Modes set the baseline. Layer permission rules on top to pre-approve or block specific tools.' Hooks sit alongside as programmatic control — a PreToolUse hook can return permissionDecision allow, deny, or ask, and exit code 2 blocks regardless. Sandboxing is orthogonal: 'The Bash sandbox and auto mode work independently and combine.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** They compose by design.
- **C.** Modes are the baseline; rules layer on top. Reversing them predicts the wrong outcome for deny-in-bypassPermissions.
- **D.** Hooks and rules coexist; hooks merge from all sources and all registered hooks fire for matching events.

Holding this four-layer model straight answers most permission questions without memorising individual cases.
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.examTrick: Four layers: mode (baseline) → rules (allow/ask/deny) → hooks (programmatic) → sandbox (OS isolation). They compose, never replace.
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.chapterName: 3.11 Permission Modes, Plan Mode & Unattended Execution

chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.question: A --allow-dangerously-skip-permissions launch differs from --dangerously-skip-permissions how?
options: The --allow- variant adds bypassPermissions to the mode cycle without activating it.
The --allow- variant is the deprecated spelling of the same flag.
The --allow- variant activates bypass mode but logs every action.
The --allow- variant enables bypass only for read operations.
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.answer: The --allow- variant adds bypassPermissions to the mode cycle without activating it.
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Permission modes: switch permission modes
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.explanation:
'bypassPermissions: appears after you start with --permission-mode bypassPermissions, --dangerously-skip-permissions, --allow-dangerously-skip-permissions, or permissions.defaultMode: "bypassPermissions" in settings; the --allow- variant adds the permission mode to the cycle without activating it.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** Both are current, with different effects.
- **C, D.** Neither logging nor a read-only restriction is what distinguishes them.

The design is opt-in-then-choose: you declare at launch that this session MAY reach bypass mode, and then reach it deliberately with Shift+Tab rather than starting there. It also explains the plan-mode protected-path exception, which applies 'in plan-mode sessions where bypass permissions are available' — that is, sessions started with one of these flags.
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.examTrick: --allow-dangerously-skip-permissions puts bypass IN the cycle without starting there. That is what 'bypass available' means elsewhere.
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.chapterName: 3.11 Permission Modes, Plan Mode & Unattended Execution

chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.question: Where does the exam-relevant decision 'plan mode versus direct execution' ultimately turn?
options: Task scope, reversibility, architectural uncertainty, and whether stakeholders must review before implementation.
The size of the codebase alone.
Whether the session is interactive or headless.
Whether the repository has a CLAUDE.md.
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.answer: Task scope, reversibility, architectural uncertainty, and whether stakeholders must review before implementation.
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Best practices; CCAF objective wording
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.explanation:
These four factors are the decision axes. The documentation supplies the practical heuristics: plan when uncertain about the approach, when the change modifies multiple files, or when unfamiliar with the code; skip it when you could describe the diff in one sentence. Stakeholder review is the fourth axis — a plan is an artifact a human can read and edit with Ctrl+G before any code changes, which is exactly what a review gate needs.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** A large codebase with a one-line fix still does not need a plan.
- **C.** Plan mode works with -p as well; interactivity is not the axis.
- **D.** Unrelated.

This objective scored 67% on the real exam. The trap is treating change SIZE as the criterion when the documented criteria are uncertainty, spread, familiarity, and review need.
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.examTrick: Four axes: scope, reversibility, architectural uncertainty, stakeholder review. Size alone is a distractor.
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows
chapter-11-permission-modes-and-plan-mod.chapterName: 3.11 Permission Modes, Plan Mode & Unattended Execution

chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.question: What are the three values of --output-format, and what does each produce?
options: text (default, plain text), json (structured JSON with result, session ID, and metadata), and stream-json (newline-delimited JSON for real-time streaming).
plain, yaml, and json.
text, markdown, and json.
json, xml, and stream.
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.answer: text (default, plain text), json (structured JSON with result, session ID, and metadata), and stream-json (newline-delimited JSON for real-time streaming).
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Non-interactive mode: get structured output
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.explanation:
'text (default): plain text output. json: structured JSON with result, session ID, and metadata. stream-json: newline-delimited JSON for real-time streaming.' With stream-json, 'The last line of the stream is a result message with the final response text, cost, and session metadata.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B, C, D.** None matches the documented set.

A useful extra: with --output-format json 'the response payload includes total_cost_usd and a per-model cost breakdown, so scripted callers can track spend per invocation' — though both figures are client-side estimates that can differ from the actual bill.
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.examTrick: text / json / stream-json. json carries result + session_id + usage + total_cost_usd.
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.chapterName: 3.12 Non-Interactive Mode, CI/CD & the Agent SDK CLI

chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.question: What does --bare do, and why is it recommended for CI?
options: It skips auto-discovery of hooks, skills, custom commands, subagents, plugins, MCP servers, auto memory, and CLAUDE.md, so you get the same result on every machine.
It suppresses all output except the final result.
It disables all tools so only text generation runs.
It skips authentication so no API key is needed.
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.answer: It skips auto-discovery of hooks, skills, custom commands, subagents, plugins, MCP servers, auto memory, and CLAUDE.md, so you get the same result on every machine.
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Non-interactive mode: start faster with bare mode
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.explanation:
'Add --bare to reduce startup time by skipping auto-discovery of hooks, skills, custom commands, subagents, plugins, MCP servers, auto memory, and CLAUDE.md... Bare mode is useful for CI and scripts where you need the same result on every machine. A hook in a teammate's ~/.claude or an MCP server in the project's .mcp.json won't run, because bare mode never reads them.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** Output format controls that.
- **C.** 'In bare mode Claude has access to the Bash, file read, and file edit tools.'
- **D.** The opposite: 'In bare mode, Claude Code never reads OAuth credentials or the system keychain. For the Anthropic API, set ANTHROPIC_API_KEY in the environment.'

The docs note '--bare is the recommended mode for scripted and SDK calls, and will become the default for -p in a future release.'
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.examTrick: --bare = reproducibility. It skips repo and user configuration entirely, and requires ANTHROPIC_API_KEY rather than OAuth.

chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.question: Without --bare, what does a claude -p session do with repository content in an untrusted folder?
options: It runs the hooks in the project's .claude/settings.json and connects the servers in its .mcp.json, showing no workspace trust dialog and no per-server approval prompt.
It refuses to start until the folder is trusted interactively.
It loads settings but skips all hooks and MCP servers.
It prompts on stdin for trust approval.
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.answer: It runs the hooks in the project's .claude/settings.json and connects the servers in its .mcp.json, showing no workspace trust dialog and no per-server approval prompt.
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Non-interactive mode: start faster with bare mode
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.explanation:
'Without --bare, a -p session runs the hooks in a project's .claude/settings.json and connects the servers in its .mcp.json, even in a folder you've never trusted. A -p session shows no workspace trust dialog and no per-server approval prompt.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B, D.** A headless run cannot show a prompt, which is exactly why this behaviour exists and why it matters.
- **C.** They do run.

This is a genuine security consideration for CI on untrusted code: the safe pattern is --bare plus explicitly-passed configuration, so nothing from the checkout executes implicitly. It also connects to the MCP docs, which note that '-p runs, Agent SDK sessions, and cloud sessions can't show that prompt: Claude Code loads project-scoped servers there without asking.'
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.examTrick: -p without --bare EXECUTES repo hooks and MCP servers with no trust prompt. Use --bare on untrusted checkouts.

chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.question: Which permission mode does the documentation recommend for a locked-down CI run, and what does it do?
options: dontAsk — Claude Code denies anything not in your permissions.allow rules or the read-only command set.
acceptEdits — it approves file writes and common filesystem commands.
auto — a classifier reviews each action.
bypassPermissions — CI runners are already isolated.
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.answer: dontAsk — Claude Code denies anything not in your permissions.allow rules or the read-only command set.
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Non-interactive mode: auto-approve tools
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.explanation:
'dontAsk: Claude Code denies anything not in your permissions.allow rules or the read-only command set, which is useful for locked-down CI runs. AskUserQuestion, connector tools your organization set to ask, and MCP tools marked requiresUserInteraction are denied even when an allow rule matches.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** acceptEdits writes files without prompting, but 'Apart from the read-only command set, other shell commands and network requests still need an --allowedTools entry or a permissions.allow rule.' It is a baseline, not a lockdown.
- **C.** auto is hands-off with a classifier — useful, but it is permissive by design rather than locked down.
- **D.** bypassPermissions requires container isolation and skips checks entirely.

Also note: 'For -p, the built-in starting permission mode is Manual on every plan, so pass the permission mode you want.'
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.examTrick: Locked-down CI = dontAsk + an explicit allow list. -p always STARTS in Manual, on every plan.

chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.chapterName: 3.12 Non-Interactive Mode, CI/CD & the Agent SDK CLI

chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.question: How do you get output conforming to a specific JSON Schema from a headless run?
options: Use --output-format json with --json-schema; the structured output appears in the structured_output field.
Use --output-format schema-json with a schema file path.
Pass the schema in --append-system-prompt and parse the result field.
It is not supported; only free-form text and metadata are available.
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.answer: Use --output-format json with --json-schema; the structured output appears in the structured_output field.
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Non-interactive mode: get structured output
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.explanation:
'To get output conforming to a specific schema, use --output-format json with --json-schema and a JSON Schema definition. The response includes metadata about the request (session ID, usage, etc.) with the structured output in the structured_output field.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** No such format value.
- **C.** Prompt-based schema instruction is the weakest structured-output method and lands in result, not structured_output.
- **D.** It is supported.

Two behavioural details: an invalid schema now fails loudly — 'Error: --json-schema is not a valid JSON Schema' — where 'Before v2.1.205, Claude Code silently ignored an invalid schema and returned unstructured text.' And 'Claude Code accepts schemas that use the format keyword... but treats format as an annotation and doesn't enforce it.'
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.examTrick: --json-schema puts results in structured_output (not result). format is accepted but NOT enforced.

chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.chapterName: 3.12 Non-Interactive Mode, CI/CD & the Agent SDK CLI

chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.question: Which flags are needed to stream tokens as they are generated?
options: --output-format stream-json together with --verbose and --include-partial-messages.
--output-format stream-json alone.
--stream with --verbose.
--output-format json with --follow.
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.answer: --output-format stream-json together with --verbose and --include-partial-messages.
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Non-interactive mode: stream responses
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.explanation:
'Use --output-format stream-json with --verbose and --include-partial-messages to receive tokens as they're generated. Each line is a JSON object representing an event.' The documented jq filter selects .type == "stream_event" and .event.delta.type? == "text_delta".

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** Without --include-partial-messages you get message-level events, not token deltas.
- **C, D.** Not documented flags.

A robustness note: 'If your consumer reads the stream slowly, Claude Code waits for the queued output to drain before exiting, scaling the wait with how much is still queued, capped at 30 seconds.'
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.examTrick: Token streaming needs all three: stream-json + --verbose + --include-partial-messages.

chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.chapterName: 3.12 Non-Interactive Mode, CI/CD & the Agent SDK CLI

chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.question: In a stream-json output, how do you tell a subagent's messages from the main conversation's?
options: Subagent messages carry the spawning tool call's ID in parent_tool_use_id; main-conversation messages carry null.
Subagent messages have type "subagent".
Subagent messages appear only after the main conversation ends.
There is no way to distinguish them.
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.answer: Subagent messages carry the spawning tool call's ID in parent_tool_use_id; main-conversation messages carry null.
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Non-interactive mode: follow subagent messages
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.explanation:
'Messages from subagents appear in the stream as assistant and user messages whose parent_tool_use_id field is the ID of the tool call that spawned the subagent. Messages from the main conversation carry null in that field.' By default only subagent tool_use and tool_result blocks are emitted; pass --forward-subagent-text or set CLAUDE_CODE_FORWARD_SUBAGENT_TEXT to also emit subagent text and thinking blocks.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B, C, D.** None is the documented mechanism.

For nested agents: 'when a subagent spawns its own subagent, the nested subagent's messages carry the ID of the Agent tool call that spawned it in parent_tool_use_id, so you can rebuild the full nesting tree by following those IDs.'
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.examTrick: parent_tool_use_id identifies the spawning call; null = main conversation. Follow the IDs to rebuild the nesting tree.

chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.chapterName: 3.12 Non-Interactive Mode, CI/CD & the Agent SDK CLI

chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.question: How can a CI gate fail when an MCP server named in --mcp-config never loaded?
options: Check the mcp_server_errors array in the system/init event; the key is omitted when there are no errors, so a non-empty array can fail the build.
Check the process exit code, which is non-zero when a server fails validation.
Parse stderr for the startup warning, which is always printed.
There is no way to detect it; validation failures are silent.
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.answer: Check the mcp_server_errors array in the system/init event; the key is omitted when there are no errors, so a non-empty array can fail the build.
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Non-interactive mode: fail CI when a plugin or MCP server doesn't load
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.explanation:
'Claude Code validates each --mcp-config entry at startup and skips entries that fail validation... The run continues and exits cleanly, so check these fields to catch a server that never loaded.' mcp_server_errors carries name, type, and message per skipped entry, with skip categories like unknown_type, url_missing_type, invalid_config, or reserved_name. 'The key is omitted when there are no errors, so a CI gate can fail on a non-empty array.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** 'The run continues and exits cleanly' — the exit code will not catch it.
- **C.** The stderr warning appears only for interactive terminal use: 'When you redirect stderr, or when a program such as a CI runner or an SDK host captures it, Claude Code prints no warning.'
- **D.** It is detectable through the init event.

The same pattern applies to plugins via plugins and plugin_errors.
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.examTrick: Silent skips + clean exit. Gate CI on mcp_server_errors / plugin_errors in system/init, never on the exit code.
