chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.chapterName: 3.12 Non-Interactive Mode, CI/CD & the Agent SDK CLI

chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.question: How do you capture a session ID from one headless run and continue that specific conversation later?
options: session_id=$(claude -p "..." --output-format json | jq -r '.session_id') then claude -p "..." --resume "$session_id".
Use --continue, which always targets the correct session even with several running.
Read the newest file in ~/.claude/projects/ and parse its name.
Session IDs are not exposed to scripts.
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.answer: session_id=$(claude -p "..." --output-format json | jq -r '.session_id') then claude -p "..." --resume "$session_id".
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Non-interactive mode: continue conversations
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.explanation:
The documented pattern exactly: 'If you're running multiple conversations, capture the session ID to resume a specific one.' And: 'You can run the two commands from different directories: Claude Code finds the session by its ID in any project on this machine.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** --continue resumes the MOST RECENT conversation, which is ambiguous when several run in parallel — that is precisely why the docs show the capture pattern.
- **C.** Filesystem scraping depends on an internal layout the docs warn against relying on.
- **D.** session_id is a documented field of the json output.

Worth remembering: '--continue skips background sessions', and -p/SDK sessions are excluded from the interactive picker but resumable by ID.
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.examTrick: Parallel headless conversations = capture session_id from json and --resume it. --continue is only safe when there is one.

chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.chapterName: 3.12 Non-Interactive Mode, CI/CD & the Agent SDK CLI

chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.question: Which flag adds instructions while keeping Claude Code's default system prompt, and which replaces it entirely?
options: --append-system-prompt appends; --system-prompt fully replaces the default prompt.
--system-prompt appends; --append-system-prompt replaces.
Both append; there is no replacement flag.
--append-system-prompt appends only in interactive mode.
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.answer: --append-system-prompt appends; --system-prompt fully replaces the default prompt.
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Non-interactive mode: customize the system prompt
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.explanation:
'Use --append-system-prompt to add instructions while keeping Claude Code's default behavior... See system prompt flags for more options including --system-prompt to fully replace the default prompt.' There is also --append-system-prompt-file for loading from a file.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** Reversed.
- **C.** A replacement flag exists.
- **D.** It works in both modes.

The memory docs give the relevant use case: 'For instructions you want at the system prompt level, use --append-system-prompt. This must be passed every invocation, so it's better suited to scripts and automation than interactive use.' That is the key contrast with CLAUDE.md, which is delivered as a user message AFTER the system prompt.
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.examTrick: --append-system-prompt = system-prompt-level instructions, must be passed every run. CLAUDE.md is a user message after the system prompt.

chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.chapterName: 3.12 Non-Interactive Mode, CI/CD & the Agent SDK CLI

chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.question: What is the documented cap on piped stdin, and what should you do for larger inputs?
options: 10MB; write the content to a file and reference the file path in your prompt instead of piping it.
1MB; split the input into chunks and run several invocations.
100MB; no alternative is needed.
There is no cap; stdin is streamed.
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.answer: 10MB; write the content to a file and reference the file path in your prompt instead of piping it.
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Non-interactive mode: pipe data through Claude
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.explanation:
'Piped stdin is capped at 10MB. If you exceed the cap, Claude Code exits with a clear error and a non-zero status. To work with larger inputs, write the content to a file and reference the file path in your prompt instead of piping it.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B, C, D.** None matches the documented cap or remedy.

The file-reference approach is also better practice generally: Claude can read selectively rather than having the whole payload injected into context — the targeted-reading principle applied to headless input.
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.examTrick: 10MB stdin cap. Beyond that, pass a FILE PATH so Claude reads selectively instead of ingesting everything.

chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.chapterName: 3.12 Non-Interactive Mode, CI/CD & the Agent SDK CLI

chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.question: Do user-invoked skills and custom commands work in -p mode?
options: Yes — include /skill-name in the prompt string and Claude Code expands it before running; but terminal-only built-ins such as /login are unavailable.
No — slash commands require an interactive terminal.
Yes, all commands including /login work identically.
Only bundled skills work; custom ones are skipped.
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.answer: Yes — include /skill-name in the prompt string and Claude Code expands it before running; but terminal-only built-ins such as /login are unavailable.
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Non-interactive mode
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.explanation:
'User-invoked skills and custom commands work in -p mode: include /skill-name in the prompt string and Claude Code expands it before running. Built-in commands that only run in the terminal interface, such as /login, aren't available in -p mode.' Some accept arguments: '/model, /effort, /fast, /color, and /rename accept the value as an argument, for example /model sonnet', and '/config' takes key=value, for example '/config thinking=false'.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B, D.** Both understate support.
- **C.** Terminal-only built-ins are explicitly excluded.

Note the interaction with --bare: bare mode skips custom command discovery entirely, so a /my-command in a bare run will not resolve.
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.examTrick: /skill-name works inside a -p prompt string. But --bare skips command discovery, so they won't resolve there.

chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.chapterName: 3.12 Non-Interactive Mode, CI/CD & the Agent SDK CLI

chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.question: What happens to a background Bash task when a claude -p run finishes?
options: The shell is terminated about five seconds after Claude returns its final result and stdin has closed; background subagents and workflows are exempt and are waited for, capped at ten minutes by default.
Background tasks keep running indefinitely after the process exits.
Background tasks are killed immediately with no grace period.
The run refuses to exit until every background task completes, with no cap.
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.answer: The shell is terminated about five seconds after Claude returns its final result and stdin has closed; background subagents and workflows are exempt and are waited for, capped at ten minutes by default.
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Non-interactive mode: background tasks at exit
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.explanation:
'That shell is terminated about five seconds after Claude has returned its final result and stdin has closed. The grace period lets a task that finishes right after the result still deliver its output.' And: 'Background subagents and workflows are exempt from the five-second grace because their result is part of the final output, so claude -p waits for them to complete. From v2.1.182, that wait is capped at ten minutes by default so a stuck background agent cannot hold the process open indefinitely. Adjust the cap with CLAUDE_CODE_PRINT_BG_WAIT_CEILING_MS, or set it to 0 to wait without a limit.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** 'Before v2.1.163, a never-exiting background process would hold the claude -p invocation open indefinitely' — that was the old behaviour.
- **C.** There is a five-second grace.
- **D.** The wait is capped.

The design principle: results that are part of the output are waited for; side-effect processes are not.
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.examTrick: Background Bash: 5s grace then killed. Background subagents: waited for, 10-minute cap by default.
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.chapterName: 3.12 Non-Interactive Mode, CI/CD & the Agent SDK CLI

chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.question: A process supervisor sends SIGTERM to a claude -p run. What happens?
options: Claude Code exits with code 143, leaves the in-progress turn unfinished with no result recorded, terminates running Bash process trees, and runs SessionEnd hooks.
It exits 0 after finishing the current turn.
It ignores SIGTERM and must be killed with SIGKILL.
It finishes the turn and records the result before exiting.
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.answer: Claude Code exits with code 143, leaves the in-progress turn unfinished with no result recorded, terminates running Bash process trees, and runs SessionEnd hooks.
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Non-interactive mode: stop a run with SIGTERM
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.explanation:
'If you stop a claude -p run with SIGTERM... Claude Code exits with code 143. Claude Code leaves the turn that was in progress unfinished and records no result for it. To end the turn instead, send SIGINT, or call the Agent SDK's interrupt(), before you stop the process. On SIGTERM, Claude Code terminates the process tree of any Bash command that is still running. Claude Code then runs SessionEnd hooks and exits.' While exiting it 'starts no new tool call, sends no new model request, and runs no hook other than SessionEnd.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B, D.** The turn is left unfinished with no result.
- **C.** SIGTERM is handled.

The recovery path matters: 'When you resume the session, Claude Code continues the turn that SIGTERM left unfinished.' So an interrupted CI run is resumable rather than lost.
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.examTrick: SIGTERM = exit 143, turn unfinished but RESUMABLE, SessionEnd still runs. SIGINT ends the turn cleanly instead.
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.chapterName: 3.12 Non-Interactive Mode, CI/CD & the Agent SDK CLI

chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.question: Which --allowedTools entry correctly permits any command starting with 'git diff' and nothing broader?
options: Bash(git diff *) — the space before * enforces a word boundary, so it does not match git diff-index.
Bash(git diff*) — the tightest possible form.
Bash(git *) — scoped to git, which is equivalent.
Bash(command:git diff *) — the explicit field form.
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.answer: Bash(git diff *) — the space before * enforces a word boundary, so it does not match git diff-index.
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Non-interactive mode: create a commit
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.explanation:
'The --allowedTools flag uses permission rule syntax. The trailing " *" enables prefix matching, so Bash(git diff *) allows any command starting with git diff. The space before * is important: without it, Bash(git diff*) would also match git diff-index.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** Without the space it matches more, not less — the opposite of 'tightest'.
- **C.** Bash(git *) permits every git command including git push.
- **D.** Primary content fields cannot be matched this way; the rule would be ignored with a startup warning.

The documented commit example allows exactly four scoped git commands, which is the right shape for CI: enumerate what the task needs and nothing else.
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.examTrick: The SPACE before * is a word boundary. 'git diff *' ≠ 'git diff*'. --allowedTools uses full permission-rule syntax.

chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.chapterName: 3.12 Non-Interactive Mode, CI/CD & the Agent SDK CLI

chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.question: Which system event lets a script implement custom backoff around retryable API failures?
options: system/api_retry, carrying attempt, max_retries, retry_delay_ms, error_status, and an error category.
system/init, which reports the retry policy at startup.
system/error, emitted once per failed request.
There is no retry event; retries are invisible to consumers.
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.answer: system/api_retry, carrying attempt, max_retries, retry_delay_ms, error_status, and an error category.
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Non-interactive mode: handle API retries
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.explanation:
'When an API request fails with a retryable error, Claude Code emits a system/api_retry event before retrying. You can use this to surface retry progress or implement custom backoff logic.' The error field is a category: authentication_failed, oauth_org_not_allowed, billing_error, rate_limit, overloaded, invalid_request, model_not_found, server_error, max_output_tokens, or unknown.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** system/init reports session metadata — model, tools, MCP servers, plugins, and an optional capabilities array.
- **C, D.** Not documented.

The error categories are worth noting as an example of good structured error design: a consumer can distinguish rate_limit (retry with backoff) from billing_error (stop and alert a human) without parsing prose.
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.examTrick: system/api_retry gives attempt, max_retries, retry_delay_ms, and a typed error category — structured errors in practice.

chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.chapterName: 3.12 Non-Interactive Mode, CI/CD & the Agent SDK CLI

chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.question: How should a script feature-detect Claude Code protocol behaviours rather than comparing version strings?
options: Read the optional capabilities array in the system/init event and ignore values it does not recognize.
Parse the output of claude --version.
Attempt each behaviour and catch the failure.
Check the CLAUDE_CODE_VERSION environment variable.
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.answer: Read the optional capabilities array in the system/init event and ignore values it does not recognize.
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Non-interactive mode: read session metadata
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.explanation:
'The event also carries an optional capabilities array of strings naming the protocol behaviors this Claude Code version implements, such as interrupt_receipt_v1 or interrupt_cancel_queued_v1. Check it to feature-detect instead of comparing version strings, and ignore values you don't recognize. The field requires Claude Code v2.1.205 or later and is absent from earlier versions.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** Version comparison is explicitly what the capabilities array replaces.
- **C.** Trial-and-error is unreliable and has side effects.
- **D.** Not a documented variable for this.

'Ignore values you don't recognize' plus 'absent from earlier versions' is a well-designed capability protocol: forward-compatible and degrading gracefully.
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.examTrick: Feature-detect via the capabilities array in system/init. Never branch on version strings.

chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.chapterName: 3.12 Non-Interactive Mode, CI/CD & the Agent SDK CLI

chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.question: Which statement about exit codes from claude -p is correct?
options: Exit 0 on success and non-zero on failure; an invalid flag is reported to stderr before the run starts, while a failure inside the run is printed as the result on stdout.
Always exit 0; failures are only visible in the JSON payload.
Exit code equals the number of tool errors encountered.
Exit 1 whenever any tool call is denied.
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.answer: Exit 0 on success and non-zero on failure; an invalid flag is reported to stderr before the run starts, while a failure inside the run is printed as the result on stdout.
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Non-interactive mode: basic usage
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.explanation:
'Claude Code exits with code 0 on success and a non-zero code when the run fails, so your scripts can branch on the exit status. If you pass an invalid flag, Claude Code reports the error to stderr before the run starts. When a failure happens inside the run, such as missing authentication, Claude Code prints the failure as the result on stdout.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B, C, D.** None matches.

But note the important limit established earlier: config-level skips like an invalid --mcp-config entry or a failed plugin 'continue and exit cleanly'. So exit codes catch RUN failures, not CONFIGURATION problems — for those you must inspect system/init.
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.examTrick: Exit code catches run failures. Config skips (MCP, plugins) exit CLEANLY — gate on system/init fields instead.
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.chapterName: 3.12 Non-Interactive Mode, CI/CD & the Agent SDK CLI

chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.question: Which flags does --bare require you to pass explicitly to restore context it would otherwise auto-discover?
options: --append-system-prompt or --append-system-prompt-file, --settings, --mcp-config, --agents, and --plugin-dir or --plugin-url.
Only --settings; everything else is still discovered.
--allowedTools and --permission-mode only.
None; --bare cannot load any additional context.
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.answer: --append-system-prompt or --append-system-prompt-file, --settings, --mcp-config, --agents, and --plugin-dir or --plugin-url.
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Non-interactive mode: start faster with bare mode
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.explanation:
The 'To load / Use' table: system prompt additions via --append-system-prompt or --append-system-prompt-file; settings via --settings <file-or-json>; MCP servers via --mcp-config <file-or-json>; custom agents via --agents <json>; a plugin via --plugin-dir <path> or --plugin-url <url>.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B, C.** Bare mode skips all auto-discovery, so each piece must be passed.
- **D.** The whole point of the table is that context can be supplied explicitly.

One documented partial exception: 'A directory you name with --add-dir is a partial exception: bare mode loads skills from its .claude/skills/ folder, but still skips its .claude/commands/ and .claude/agents/ folders.'

The philosophy: bare mode makes configuration EXPLICIT rather than ambient, which is what reproducible CI requires.
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.examTrick: --bare = nothing ambient. Pass settings, MCP, agents, plugins, system prompt explicitly. --add-dir still loads its skills.
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.chapterName: 3.12 Non-Interactive Mode, CI/CD & the Agent SDK CLI

chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.question: Which pattern turns Claude Code into a project-specific linter inside a build script?
options: Pipe the diff into claude -p with a narrow instruction, for example: git diff main | claude -p "you are a typo linter..." as an npm script.
Run claude interactively from a pre-commit hook and parse the terminal output.
Install Claude Code as a PostToolUse hook in CI.
Use --output-format stream-json and grep for warnings.
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.answer: Pipe the diff into claude -p with a narrow instruction, for example: git diff main | claude -p "you are a typo linter..." as an npm script.
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Non-interactive mode: add Claude to a build script
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.explanation:
The documented example wraps exactly this in package.json: 'git diff main | claude -p "you are a typo linter. for each typo in this diff, report filename:line on one line and the issue on the next. return nothing else."' The docs note two design choices: 'Piping the diff means Claude doesn't need Bash permission to read it, and the escaped double quotes keep the script portable to Windows.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** Interactive mode cannot run unattended.
- **C.** Hooks run inside a Claude Code session; they are not a CI installation mechanism.
- **D.** Streaming is a transport choice, not a linting pattern.

Note how the prompt itself does the work: a precise output format ('filename:line', 'return nothing else') makes the output parseable without a schema.
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.examTrick: Pipe the input so no Bash permission is needed, and specify the output format precisely in the prompt.
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.chapterName: 3.12 Non-Interactive Mode, CI/CD & the Agent SDK CLI

chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.question: Which flags does claude -p reject or handle specially?
options: It rejects --bg, and rejects --cloud with a task description; --cloud with a session ID plus -p queues a message into that cloud session and exits.
It rejects --allowedTools, which is interactive-only.
It rejects --resume, which requires an interactive picker.
It accepts every CLI flag without exception.
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.answer: It rejects --bg, and rejects --cloud with a task description; --cloud with a session ID plus -p queues a message into that cloud session and exits.
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Non-interactive mode: basic usage
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.explanation:
'Not every CLI option combines with -p. Claude Code rejects --bg, and rejects --cloud with a task description, with an error naming the conflict; --cloud with a session ID and -p instead queues a message into that cloud session and exits.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B, C.** Both are among the flags most commonly used WITH -p; the docs list --continue, --allowedTools, and --output-format as the frequent combinations.
- **D.** Some flags conflict.

The useful part is that conflicts are reported by name rather than silently ignored — consistent with the --json-schema validation change, where silent acceptance of bad input was replaced by a clear error.
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.examTrick: -p rejects --bg and --cloud-with-a-task. --cloud + session ID + -p queues a follow-up into that cloud session.
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.chapterName: 3.12 Non-Interactive Mode, CI/CD & the Agent SDK CLI

chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.question: What is the relationship between claude -p and the Agent SDK?
options: The Agent SDK gives the same tools, agent loop, and context management that power Claude Code, available as a CLI for scripts and CI/CD or as Python and TypeScript packages for full programmatic control.
The Agent SDK is a separate product that does not share Claude Code's agent loop.
claude -p is a thin wrapper around the Messages API with no tools.
The Agent SDK replaces claude -p, which is deprecated.
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.answer: The Agent SDK gives the same tools, agent loop, and context management that power Claude Code, available as a CLI for scripts and CI/CD or as Python and TypeScript packages for full programmatic control.
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Run Claude Code programmatically
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.explanation:
'The Agent SDK gives you the same tools, agent loop, and context management that power Claude Code. It's available as a CLI for scripts and CI/CD, or as Python and TypeScript packages for full programmatic control.' The page frames claude -p as 'using the Agent SDK via the CLI'. The packages add 'structured outputs, tool approval callbacks, and native message objects'.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** They share the loop by design.
- **C.** -p has the full tool set and agent loop, not raw API access.
- **D.** Neither is deprecated.

The architectural point worth carrying into the exam: the agentic loop is one concept expressed at three levels — the raw Messages API round trip, the SDK, and the Claude Code CLI. Understanding stop_reason explains all three.
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.examTrick: -p IS the Agent SDK via the CLI. Same tools, same loop, same context management. Packages add callbacks and typed objects.
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows
chapter-12-headless-mode-and-cicd.chapterName: 3.12 Non-Interactive Mode, CI/CD & the Agent SDK CLI

chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.question: What does the Bash sandbox do, and who enforces the boundary?
options: You define which files and network domains commands can touch, and the operating system enforces that boundary for every Bash command and its child processes.
Claude is instructed to avoid restricted paths and complies voluntarily.
Claude Code inspects each command string and rejects unsafe ones before running.
Commands run in a remote container managed by Anthropic.
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.answer: You define which files and network domains commands can touch, and the operating system enforces that boundary for every Bash command and its child processes.
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.explanation:
'The Bash sandbox lets Claude run most shell commands without stopping to ask permission. Instead of approving each command, you define which files and network domains commands can touch, and the operating system enforces that boundary for every Bash command and its child processes.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** Voluntary compliance is what CLAUDE.md offers; the sandbox is OS-level enforcement — the strongest layer in the model.
- **C.** Pattern-based command inspection is what permission rules do, and the docs note such patterns are fragile.
- **D.** It is local: macOS uses the built-in Seatbelt framework; Linux and WSL2 use bubblewrap and socat.

The child-process clause matters: a permission rule matches the command STRING, but the sandbox constrains everything that command spawns.
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.examTrick: Sandbox = OS-enforced, covers child processes too. Permission rules match strings; the OS matches syscalls.
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.question: Which platforms support the sandbox, and what is required on each?
options: macOS, Linux, and WSL2 — nothing to install on macOS (built-in Seatbelt); Linux and WSL2 need bubblewrap and socat. Native Windows is not supported.
All platforms including native Windows, with no dependencies.
Linux only, using seccomp.
macOS and native Windows; Linux requires a container.
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.answer: macOS, Linux, and WSL2 — nothing to install on macOS (built-in Seatbelt); Linux and WSL2 need bubblewrap and socat. Native Windows is not supported.
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Sandboxing: get started
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.explanation:
'The sandbox is built into Claude Code and runs on macOS, Linux, and WSL2. Native Windows is not supported. On Windows, run Claude Code inside a WSL2 distribution. On macOS, there is nothing to install: sandboxing uses the built-in Seatbelt framework.' The Linux packages are bubblewrap ('the unprivileged sandboxing tool that enforces filesystem isolation') and socat ('the relay used to route network traffic through the sandbox proxy').

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B, C, D.** Each misstates platform support.

The /sandbox panel's Dependencies tab 'lists which of ripgrep, bubblewrap, socat, and the seccomp filter your platform lacks'. The seccomp filter is optional and 'adds Unix domain socket blocking', installed with npm install -g @anthropic-ai/sandbox-runtime. The dependency check runs at startup, so restart after installing.
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.examTrick: macOS = Seatbelt, nothing to install. Linux/WSL2 = bubblewrap + socat. Native Windows = unsupported, use WSL2.
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.question: What is the difference between the two sandbox modes?
options: Both enforce the same filesystem and network restrictions; auto-allow runs sandboxed commands without prompting, while regular permissions keeps the normal permission prompts even when commands are sandboxed.
Auto-allow disables the sandbox restrictions entirely.
Regular permissions applies filesystem isolation only; auto-allow adds network isolation.
Auto-allow works only in bypassPermissions mode.
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.answer: Both enforce the same filesystem and network restrictions; auto-allow runs sandboxed commands without prompting, while regular permissions keeps the normal permission prompts even when commands are sandboxed.
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Sandboxing: sandbox modes
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.explanation:
'Claude Code offers two sandbox modes. In both, the sandbox enforces the same filesystem and network restrictions; the difference is only in whether sandboxed commands are auto-approved or require explicit permission.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** The restrictions are identical in both modes.
- **C.** Both layers apply in both modes.
- **D.** 'Auto-allow mode works independently of your permission mode setting, with one exception: plan mode.'

The important consequence in auto-allow: 'sandboxed Bash commands run automatically when auto-allow is enabled. This means Bash commands that modify files within the sandbox boundaries execute without prompting, even in Manual mode, where the file edit tools would prompt.' And in plan mode, 'auto-allow doesn't widen approvals.'
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.examTrick: Same restrictions, different prompting. Auto-allow lets Bash write files without a prompt even in Manual mode — but not in plan mode.
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.question: By default, where can commands inside the sandbox write?
options: Only to the working directory and the session temp directory; the first time a command needs a new network domain, Claude Code prompts for approval.
Anywhere on the filesystem, with only network restricted.
Nowhere — the sandbox is read-only.
Only to a dedicated sandbox scratch directory outside the project.
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.answer: Only to the working directory and the session temp directory; the first time a command needs a new network domain, Claude Code prompts for approval.
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Sandboxing: get started
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.explanation:
'By default, commands inside the sandbox can write only to the working directory and the session temp directory. The first time a command needs a new network domain, Claude Code prompts for approval, or in auto mode sends the request to the classifier.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** That is what setting sandbox.filesystem.disabled to true produces, which is a deliberate opt-out rather than the default.
- **C.** Builds and test suites need to write.
- **D.** The working directory is writable, which is what makes ordinary development work.

The network default is the notable half: outbound domains are denied until approved, so a command that tries to reach an unexpected host surfaces rather than succeeding silently.
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.examTrick: Default writes: working directory + session temp. Network: deny-by-default, approved per domain on first use.
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.question: How do allowRead and denyRead interact in sandbox filesystem settings?
options: A narrower allow re-opens part of a denied region, and a deny holds inside a wider allow — so a broad allow cannot silently re-expose a secret, and wildcard denies hold the same way exact paths do.
Allow always wins over deny, since it is more specific.
Deny always wins and cannot be narrowed by any allow.
The last-listed rule wins.
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.answer: A narrower allow re-opens part of a denied region, and a deny holds inside a wider allow — so a broad allow cannot silently re-expose a secret, and wildcard denies hold the same way exact paths do.
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Sandboxing: filesystem isolation
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.explanation:
The documented cases: denyRead ['~/'] with allowRead ['~/projects'] means '~/projects is readable and the rest of the home directory stays blocked. The narrower allow re-opens that part of the denied region.' allowRead ['~/'] with denyRead ['~/.env'] means '~/.env stays blocked and the rest of the home directory is readable. The deny holds inside a wider allow, so a broad allow can't silently re-expose a secret.' And allowRead ['~/'] with denyRead ['~/**/.env'] blocks every .env under home — 'A wildcard deny holds inside a wider allow the same way an exact path does.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B, C.** Both are absolutes; the real rule is specificity-based in a way that preserves safety.
- **D.** Order does not decide.

Note this differs from PERMISSION rules, where 'a deny rule can't carry allowlist exceptions' and deny beats a narrower allow outright. Sandbox paths and permission rules resolve conflicts differently.
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.examTrick: Sandbox paths: narrower rule wins, but a deny inside a wider allow still holds. Permission RULES: deny always beats allow. Different systems.
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.question: How does a path with no prefix resolve in sandbox settings?
options: Relative to the project root for project settings, or to ~/.claude for user settings — so ./output in .claude/settings.json resolves to <project-root>/output.
Always relative to the filesystem root.
Always relative to the home directory.
Always relative to the current working directory regardless of the settings file.
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.answer: Relative to the project root for project settings, or to ~/.claude for user settings — so ./output in .claude/settings.json resolves to <project-root>/output.
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Sandboxing: path prefixes
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.explanation:
The prefix table: '/' is an absolute path from the filesystem root ('/tmp/build stays /tmp/build'); '~/' is relative to the home directory ('~/.kube becomes $HOME/.kube'); './' or no prefix is 'Relative to the project root for project settings, or to ~/.claude for user settings'.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B, C, D.** Each fixes one anchor, missing the settings-source dependency.

Compare with PERMISSION rules, which have four prefixes: // for filesystem root, ~/ for home, / for the settings source, and ./ or bare for the current directory. Sandbox paths use a SINGLE slash for filesystem root where permission rules use a double slash. Mixing them up silently anchors a rule in the wrong place.
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.examTrick: Sandbox: / = filesystem root. Permission rules: // = filesystem root, single / = settings source. Do not transfer the syntax.
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.question: What is the dangerouslyDisableSandbox escape hatch, and how is it disabled?
options: When a command fails because of sandbox restrictions, Claude analyzes the failure and may retry with dangerouslyDisableSandbox; set "allowUnsandboxedCommands": false to ignore the parameter entirely, shown as Strict sandbox mode.
It is a CLI flag that turns the sandbox off for a session.
It is a permission rule that exempts named commands.
It cannot be disabled once sandboxing is enabled.
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.answer: When a command fails because of sandbox restrictions, Claude analyzes the failure and may retry with dangerouslyDisableSandbox; set "allowUnsandboxedCommands": false to ignore the parameter entirely, shown as Strict sandbox mode.
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.explanation:
'When a command fails after the sandbox denied it access, Claude Code appends the violation details to the failed command's output, so Claude sees which file path or network host the sandbox blocked. Rather than failing the task or requiring you to turn sandboxing off, Claude Code includes an escape hatch: when a command fails because of sandbox restrictions, Claude analyzes the failure and may retry the command with the dangerouslyDisableSandbox parameter.' And: 'You can disable this escape hatch by setting "allowUnsandboxedCommands": false... When disabled, which the /sandbox Overrides tab shows as Strict sandbox mode, the dangerouslyDisableSandbox parameter is completely ignored and all commands must run sandboxed or be explicitly listed in excludedCommands.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B, C.** It is a per-call tool parameter, not a flag or a rule.
- **D.** allowUnsandboxedCommands: false disables it.

The violation-details feedback is itself good design: the failure tells Claude WHICH path or host was blocked, so it can react specifically rather than guessing.
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.examTrick: Sandbox failures append violation details so Claude can react. Strict sandbox mode = allowUnsandboxedCommands: false.
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.question: What does credential masking do that a deny entry does not?
options: The sandboxed command sees a per-session sentinel value, and the sandbox proxy swaps in the real value on outbound requests to hosts listed in injectHosts — so requests still authenticate while the command never holds the real credential.
It encrypts the credential file on disk.
It blocks the credential entirely, which is what deny also does.
It rotates the credential after each command.
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.answer: The sandboxed command sees a per-session sentinel value, and the sandbox proxy swaps in the real value on outbound requests to hosts listed in injectHosts — so requests still authenticate while the command never holds the real credential.
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Sandboxing: mask credentials
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.explanation:
'Masking goes further than a deny entry under Protect credentials. Instead of blocking a credential, Claude Code shows sandboxed commands a placeholder, the sentinel, and the sandbox proxy swaps in the real value on outbound requests to hosts you allow... With mask, the sandboxed command sees a per-session sentinel value instead of the real one. Each mask entry can list injectHosts, the hosts the real value is allowed to reach... The command and anything it logs never hold the real credential, but its requests still authenticate.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** No encryption at rest is involved.
- **C.** Deny blocks; mask substitutes — the whole point is that the command keeps working.
- **D.** No rotation occurs.

A platform caveat: 'For files, the substitution is Linux and WSL2 behavior; macOS blocks the file instead.'
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.examTrick: mask = sentinel to the command, real value injected by the proxy for injectHosts. macOS blocks masked FILES instead.
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.question: What is the documented risk of setting sandbox.filesystem.disabled to true while commands are auto-allowed?
options: A sandboxed command can write files that later commands run or read — shell startup files, executables on $PATH, or ~/.claude/settings.json — and use them to widen its own access on the next run.
Network isolation is also disabled, removing all boundaries.
Claude Code refuses to start.
Nothing; disabling filesystem isolation is equivalent to the default.
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.answer: A sandboxed command can write files that later commands run or read — shell startup files, executables on $PATH, or ~/.claude/settings.json — and use them to widen its own access on the next run.
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Sandboxing: filesystem isolation disabled
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.explanation:
'With filesystem isolation off and commands auto-allowed, a sandboxed command can write files that later commands run or read, such as shell startup files, executables on $PATH, or ~/.claude/settings.json, and use them to widen its own access on the next run. Set filesystem.disabled to true only for workloads you trust not to escalate their own access. Locking network domains with allowManagedDomainsOnly narrows the risk but doesn't remove it, since that lock applies only to commands running inside the sandbox.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** 'The sandbox has two independent layers' — network isolation survives.
- **C.** It is a supported configuration.
- **D.** The default restricts writes to the working directory and session temp.

The named self-escalation path through ~/.claude/settings.json is the sharpest example: writing your own permission rules is the ultimate privilege escalation, which is exactly why .claude is a protected path in the permission system.
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.examTrick: Writable config = self-escalation. That is why .claude and .git are protected paths under every permission mode.
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.question: Which statement about the sandbox and permission rules is correct?
options: Deny rules still apply inside the sandbox, and ask rules naming a command such as Bash(git push *) still prompt even in auto-allow mode.
The sandbox replaces permission rules; neither deny nor ask applies inside it.
Only allow rules apply inside the sandbox.
Permission rules apply only when the sandbox is unavailable.
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.answer: Deny rules still apply inside the sandbox, and ask rules naming a command such as Bash(git push *) still prompt even in auto-allow mode.
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Permission modes: choose a mode; Sandboxing
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.explanation:
The mode-selection table's row for Manual plus the sandbox in auto-allow notes: 'Deny rules still apply, and ask rules that name a command, such as Bash(git push *), still prompt.' Commands that cannot be sandboxed 'fall back to the regular permission flow, where Claude Code checks your permission rules and gates any command those rules do not already allow.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B, C.** The layers compose rather than replace.
- **D.** They apply alongside it.

This completes the four-layer model: permission MODES set the baseline for what is asked, RULES allow/ask/deny specific calls, HOOKS add programmatic decisions, and the SANDBOX adds OS-level isolation. Each layer is independent, and the strictest applicable constraint governs.
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.examTrick: Sandbox composes with rules. Deny and command-specific ask still fire inside auto-allow. Four layers, strictest wins.
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.question: Where does selecting a sandbox mode in the /sandbox panel save the setting, and how do you enable it more broadly?
options: To .claude/settings.local.json for the current project; set sandbox.enabled to true in ~/.claude/settings.json for all your projects, or use managed settings to enforce it organization-wide.
To .claude/settings.json, shared with the team by default.
To ~/.claude.json, alongside MCP local-scope servers.
It is session-only and not persisted anywhere.
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.answer: To .claude/settings.local.json for the current project; set sandbox.enabled to true in ~/.claude/settings.json for all your projects, or use managed settings to enforce it organization-wide.
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Sandboxing: get started
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.explanation:
'When you select a mode in the panel, Claude Code saves it to your project's local settings at .claude/settings.local.json, which apply to the current project. Claude Code adds that file to your global gitignore when it saves a setting there. To enable the sandbox across all of your projects, set sandbox.enabled to true in your user settings at ~/.claude/settings.json. To enforce sandboxing for every developer in an organization, use managed settings.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** The panel writes the LOCAL file, not the shared one — consistent with how permission approvals are saved.
- **C.** That is the MCP local-scope and project-state file.
- **D.** It persists.

The three tiers repeat the pattern seen everywhere: local for this project and you, user for all your projects, managed for the organization.
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.examTrick: Panel writes settings.local.json. sandbox.enabled in user settings = all your projects. Managed = enforced org-wide.
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.question: On WSL2, what governs whether a sandboxed command can launch a Windows binary such as powershell.exe?
options: The sandbox's Unix-socket settings — WSL hands the launch to the Windows host over a Unix socket, and the optional seccomp filter must be installed to block that socket at all.
The filesystem allow and deny rules for /mnt/c/.
The network allowedDomains list.
Windows binaries are always blocked inside the sandbox.
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.answer: The sandbox's Unix-socket settings — WSL hands the launch to the Windows host over a Unix socket, and the optional seccomp filter must be installed to block that socket at all.
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Sandboxing: WSL2 notes
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.explanation:
'On WSL2, WSL hands a launch of a Windows binary such as cmd.exe, powershell.exe, or anything under /mnt/c/ to the Windows host over a Unix socket, so whether a sandboxed command can launch one follows the sandbox's Unix-socket settings: the optional seccomp filter has to be installed to block the socket in the first place. To allow these launches, set allowAllUnixSockets; to keep them out of the sandbox entirely, add the command to excludedCommands.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B, C.** The mechanism is socket-based, not path- or domain-based.
- **D.** They are permitted unless the seccomp filter is installed and blocks the socket.

This is a genuine isolation gap worth understanding: without the optional seccomp filter, a WSL2 sandbox cannot prevent escape to the Windows host, because the escape route is a socket rather than a filesystem path.
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.examTrick: WSL2 Windows-binary launches go over a UNIX SOCKET. Without the optional seccomp filter, the sandbox cannot block them.
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.question: When is turning filesystem isolation off while keeping network isolation the right choice?
options: When you sandbox to control where commands connect rather than what they write — the two layers are independent, so network egress stays confined to allowed domains.
Never; both layers must be on together.
When you need faster command execution.
When commands need to reach any domain but must not write outside the project.
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.answer: When you sandbox to control where commands connect rather than what they write — the two layers are independent, so network egress stays confined to allowed domains.
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Sandboxing: filesystem isolation disabled
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.explanation:
'The sandbox has two independent layers: filesystem isolation controls which paths sandboxed commands can read and write, and network isolation controls which domains they can reach. With the filesystem layer off, sandboxed commands get unrestricted read and write access to the host filesystem, while their network egress stays confined to your allowed domains. Turn the layer off when you sandbox to control where commands connect rather than what they write.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** They are explicitly independent and separately configurable.
- **C.** Performance is not the documented rationale.
- **D.** That describes the DEFAULT configuration inverted — filesystem restricted, network open — which is not what disabling the filesystem layer produces.

Remember the paired warning: only do this 'for workloads you trust not to escalate their own access.'
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.examTrick: Two independent layers. Disable filesystem only when your goal is egress control, and only for trusted workloads.
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.question: How do the sandbox and auto mode relate?
options: They work independently and combine, except in plan mode where auto-allow does not widen approvals; a sandbox or container adds defense in depth to auto mode.
Auto mode replaces the sandbox, since the classifier reviews every action.
The sandbox only functions when auto mode is enabled.
They are mutually exclusive and cannot both be active.
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.answer: They work independently and combine, except in plan mode where auto-allow does not widen approvals; a sandbox or container adds defense in depth to auto mode.
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Permission modes; Sandboxing
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.explanation:
'The Bash sandbox and auto mode work independently and combine, except in plan mode, where auto-allow doesn't widen approvals.' And in the mode-selection table, working hands-off with a classifier notes 'a sandbox or container adds defense in depth.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** A model-based classifier and an OS-enforced boundary fail in different ways — that independence is exactly what makes them complementary.
- **C.** The sandbox works in any permission mode, including Manual.
- **D.** They are designed to combine.

Defense in depth requires INDEPENDENT layers: if the classifier misjudges a command, the OS boundary still holds, and if a command is within the sandbox boundary but strategically wrong, the classifier can still stop it.
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.examTrick: Classifier (model judgement) + sandbox (OS boundary) = independent failure modes = real defense in depth.
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.question: What happens to commands that cannot be sandboxed in auto-allow mode?
options: They fall back to the regular permission flow, where Claude Code checks your permission rules and gates anything not already allowed — a prompt in Manual mode, or the classifier in auto mode.
They are silently skipped.
They run unsandboxed without any check.
They cause the session to exit.
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.answer: They fall back to the regular permission flow, where Claude Code checks your permission rules and gates anything not already allowed — a prompt in Manual mode, or the classifier in auto mode.
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Sandboxing: auto-allow mode
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.explanation:
'When a command can be sandboxed, Claude Code runs it inside the sandbox and approves it automatically, without asking your permission. Commands that cannot be sandboxed, such as those needing network access to non-allowed hosts, fall back to the regular permission flow, where Claude Code checks your permission rules and gates any command those rules do not already allow, with a prompt in Manual mode or the classifier in auto mode.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B, C.** Silent skipping or unchecked execution would both be unsafe defaults.
- **D.** No session termination.

The design principle: the sandbox is an OPTIMISATION for the common case, not a replacement for the permission system. Anything it cannot cover falls back to the layer beneath it rather than through a gap.
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.examTrick: Non-sandboxable commands fall BACK to permission checks, never through a gap. Layers degrade safely.
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.question: Which sandbox setting keeps a specific command out of the sandbox entirely?
options: excludedCommands
allowUnsandboxedCommands
allowAllUnixSockets
filesystem.disabled
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.explanation:
excludedCommands lists commands that run outside the sandbox. The docs reference it twice: 'to keep them out of the sandbox entirely, add the command to excludedCommands', and under Strict sandbox mode 'all commands must run sandboxed or be explicitly listed in excludedCommands.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** allowUnsandboxedCommands: false disables the dangerouslyDisableSandbox escape hatch.
- **C.** allowAllUnixSockets governs Unix-socket access, relevant to WSL2 Windows-binary launches.
- **D.** filesystem.disabled turns off the filesystem layer while keeping network isolation.

The pairing matters: in Strict sandbox mode, excludedCommands becomes the ONLY route for a command that genuinely cannot be sandboxed — an explicit, reviewable list rather than a per-call model decision.
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.examTrick: excludedCommands = an explicit, reviewable exception list. In Strict mode it is the only escape route left.
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.question: A security team wants sandboxing on for every developer, with domain policy that developers cannot widen. What combination does the documentation point to?
options: Enforce sandboxing through managed settings, and lock the domain policy with allowManagedDomainsOnly — noting that lock applies only to commands running inside the sandbox.
Ask developers to set sandbox.enabled in their user settings.
Add a CLAUDE.md rule requiring sandbox use.
Set sandbox.enabled in the committed .claude/settings.json.
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.answer: Enforce sandboxing through managed settings, and lock the domain policy with allowManagedDomainsOnly — noting that lock applies only to commands running inside the sandbox.
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Sandboxing: enforce with managed settings; keep developers from widening the policy
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.explanation:
'To enforce sandboxing for every developer in an organization, use managed settings.' And on domain locking: 'Locking network domains with allowManagedDomainsOnly narrows the risk but doesn't remove it, since that lock applies only to commands running inside the sandbox.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** User settings are the developer's own file to change.
- **C.** CLAUDE.md is advisory context and cannot configure the sandbox at all.
- **D.** A committed project file is overridable by each developer's local settings, which sit higher in the precedence stack.

The caveat in the answer is the sophisticated part: a policy that binds only inside the sandbox does not bind a command that runs outside it, which is why Strict sandbox mode and a curated excludedCommands list matter alongside it.
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.examTrick: Managed settings enforce; allowManagedDomainsOnly locks domains — but only for commands INSIDE the sandbox.
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.question: Which describes the sandbox's place in the overall safety model?
options: It is the OS-level layer that makes autonomous execution safer by constraining what any command and its children can touch, complementing rather than replacing modes, rules, and hooks.
It is the primary permission mechanism, with rules and hooks as legacy fallbacks.
It is a debugging aid with no security guarantee.
It is only relevant for untrusted third-party code, not your own project.
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.answer: It is the OS-level layer that makes autonomous execution safer by constraining what any command and its children can touch, complementing rather than replacing modes, rules, and hooks.
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.explanation:
The docs frame it as providing 'filesystem and network isolation for safer, more autonomous agent execution', with the OS enforcing the boundary for every command and its child processes. Deny and command-specific ask rules continue to apply, and the sandbox composes with permission modes.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** Rules and hooks are current and complementary; the sandbox covers Bash specifically, while 'To reduce permission prompts for tools other than Bash, see permission modes.'
- **C.** OS-level enforcement is a real boundary, though not unconditional — the WSL2 socket case and the self-escalation risk with filesystem.disabled are documented limits.
- **D.** The documented purpose is enabling autonomous execution on your own work with fewer prompts.

The unifying idea for the exam: safety comes from LAYERS with different failure modes — advisory context, client-enforced rules, deterministic hooks, and OS isolation — not from any single mechanism.
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.examTrick: The sandbox covers BASH specifically. Other tools are governed by modes and rules. Layers, not a single mechanism.
chapter-13-sandboxing-and-isolation.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.question: When should you choose a plugin over standalone .claude/ configuration?
options: For sharing with teammates, distributing to the community, versioned releases, and reuse across projects; standalone suits personal workflows, project-specific customizations, and quick experiments.
Always — standalone configuration is deprecated.
Only when you need hooks, which standalone configuration cannot provide.
Only when publishing to the official marketplace.
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.answer: For sharing with teammates, distributing to the community, versioned releases, and reuse across projects; standalone suits personal workflows, project-specific customizations, and quick experiments.
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Create plugins: when to use plugins vs standalone
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.explanation:
The comparison table maps standalone (.claude/ directory, skill names like /hello) to 'Personal workflows, project-specific customizations, quick experiments', and plugins (skill names like /plugin-name:hello) to 'Sharing with teammates, distributing to the community, versioned releases, reusable across projects'. The recommended path: 'Start with standalone configuration in .claude/ for quick iteration, then convert to a plugin when you're ready to share.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** Standalone is the recommended starting point.
- **C.** Hooks work fine in settings.json.
- **D.** Private and team distribution are supported, including marketplaces in private repositories.

The decision axis is REACH: one project versus many, one person versus a team.
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.examTrick: One repo, quick iteration = standalone. Many repos, versioned, shared = plugin. Start standalone, convert later.
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.question: Which directory must plugin.json live in, and what is the common structural mistake?
options: .claude-plugin/plugin.json at the plugin root — and the common mistake is putting commands/, agents/, skills/, or hooks/ inside .claude-plugin/ instead of at the plugin root.
plugin.json at the plugin root, with all components inside .claude-plugin/.
.claude/plugin.json, matching the standalone layout.
Anywhere in the plugin; the file is located by name.
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.answer: .claude-plugin/plugin.json at the plugin root — and the common mistake is putting commands/, agents/, skills/, or hooks/ inside .claude-plugin/ instead of at the plugin root.
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Create plugins: plugin structure overview
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.explanation:
The warning states it plainly: 'Common mistake: Don't put commands/, agents/, skills/, or hooks/ inside the .claude-plugin/ directory. Only plugin.json goes inside .claude-plugin/. All other directories must be at the plugin root level.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** Exactly inverted.
- **C, D.** Neither matches.

The docs also clarify what 'plugin root' means: 'the individual plugin's own directory: the one you pass to --plugin-dir or that contains .claude-plugin/plugin.json. It is never ~/.claude/. For example, Claude Code doesn't read a .mcp.json placed at ~/.claude/.mcp.json.'
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.examTrick: ONLY plugin.json goes in .claude-plugin/. Everything else sits at the plugin root.
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.question: What does the name field in plugin.json control besides identity?
options: The skill namespace — skills are prefixed with it, so a hello skill in my-first-plugin becomes /my-first-plugin:hello.
The install directory under ~/.claude/plugins/.
The marketplace category the plugin appears in.
The order in which plugin hooks fire.
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.answer: The skill namespace — skills are prefixed with it, so a hello skill in my-first-plugin becomes /my-first-plugin:hello.
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Create plugins: create the plugin manifest
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.explanation:
'name: Unique identifier and skill namespace. Skills are prefixed with this (e.g., /my-first-plugin:hello).' And: 'Plugin skills are always namespaced (like /my-first-plugin:hello) to prevent conflicts when multiple plugins have skills with the same name. To change the namespace prefix, update the name field in plugin.json.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B, C, D.** None is a documented function of the field.

Namespacing is what makes plugins composable: many plugins can each ship a deploy skill without colliding, and a plugin skill 'loads alongside a deploy skill in your project's .claude/skills/' rather than one overriding the other.
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.examTrick: plugin.json name = the namespace. Namespacing is why plugin components never collide with project ones.
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.question: What happens if the version field is omitted from plugin.json?
options: The version comes from the next source in version management; when set, users only receive updates when you bump it, except for a command source.
The plugin fails to load.
The plugin is treated as version 0.0.0 and never updates.
Users receive updates on every push regardless.
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.answer: The version comes from the next source in version management; when set, users only receive updates when you bump it, except for a command source.
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Create plugins: manifest fields
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.explanation:
'version: Optional. If set, users only receive updates when you bump this field, except for a command source. If omitted, the version comes from the next source in version management.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** Only name and description are meaningful for basic operation; the manifest itself is 'optional if components use default locations'.
- **C, D.** Neither matches the fallback behaviour.

The practical consequence for a plugin author: an explicit version gives you release control — nobody gets a change until you bump it — while omitting it delegates that to the source. Choosing between them is a documented step in sharing a plugin: 'Choose a versioning strategy.'
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.examTrick: Explicit version = you control when users get updates. Omitted = the source decides.
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.question: Which components can a plugin bundle?
options: skills/, commands/, agents/, hooks/hooks.json, .mcp.json, .lsp.json, monitors/, bin/, and settings.json.
Only skills and commands.
Only hooks and MCP servers.
Only skills, since everything else is per-project.
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.answer: skills/, commands/, agents/, hooks/hooks.json, .mcp.json, .lsp.json, monitors/, bin/, and settings.json.
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Create plugins: plugin structure overview
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.explanation:
The directory table lists all of these at the plugin root: skills/ (as <name>/SKILL.md directories), commands/ (flat markdown files, with 'Use skills/ for new plugins'), agents/, hooks/ (event handlers in hooks.json), .mcp.json, .lsp.json (LSP servers for code intelligence), monitors/ (background monitor configurations), bin/ (executables added to the Bash tool's PATH while the plugin is enabled), and settings.json (default settings applied when enabled). Workflows can also ship in a workflows/ directory.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B, C, D.** Each is far narrower than the documented set.

A convenience for the simplest case: 'A plugin that ships exactly one skill can place SKILL.md directly at the plugin root instead of creating a skills/ directory.'
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.examTrick: Plugins bundle nearly the whole extension surface: skills, agents, hooks, MCP, LSP, monitors, bin, settings, workflows.
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.question: How do you test a plugin during development without installing it?
options: Launch with claude --plugin-dir ./my-plugin, which also accepts a .zip archive and can be repeated for multiple plugins.
Copy it into ~/.claude/plugins/ and restart.
Publish it to a private marketplace and install from there.
Set enabledPlugins in settings.json pointing at the local path.
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.answer: Launch with claude --plugin-dir ./my-plugin, which also accepts a .zip archive and can be repeated for multiple plugins.
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Create plugins: test your plugins locally
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.explanation:
'Use the --plugin-dir flag to test plugins during development. This loads your plugin directly without requiring installation.' It accepts a directory or a .zip archive, and 'You can load multiple plugins at once by specifying the flag multiple times.' There is also --plugin-url to fetch a hosted .zip for one session.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B, C, D.** None is the documented development flow.

A useful override rule: 'When a --plugin-dir plugin has the same name as an installed marketplace plugin, the local copy takes precedence for that session' — so you can test changes without uninstalling. 'The exception is plugins that managed settings force-enable or force-disable: --plugin-dir cannot override those.'
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.examTrick: --plugin-dir for local dev (dir or .zip, repeatable). It overrides an installed copy — except managed force-enabled ones.
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.question: After editing a plugin mid-session, what reloads its components?
options: /reload-plugins, which reloads plugins, skills, agents, hooks, plugin MCP servers, and plugin LSP servers.
Nothing is needed; plugin changes are always live.
/clear, which reinitializes the session.
Restarting Claude Code is the only option.
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.answer: /reload-plugins, which reloads plugins, skills, agents, hooks, plugin MCP servers, and plugin LSP servers.
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Create plugins: test your plugins locally
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.explanation:
'As you make changes to your plugin, run /reload-plugins to pick up the updates without restarting. This reloads plugins, skills, agents, hooks, plugin MCP servers, and plugin LSP servers.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** Live detection covers standalone skill directories (~/.claude/skills/, project .claude/skills/, and --add-dir ones); plugins need the reload command.
- **C.** /clear resets conversation context, not configuration.
- **D.** A restart works but is unnecessary.

A quirk worth knowing from the quickstart: after /reload-plugins 'The skills count in the summary covers only commands/ directories, so it can report 0 skills even though the skill you just edited reloaded.'
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.examTrick: /reload-plugins for plugin changes. Standalone skill directories live-reload on their own.
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.question: You migrate a project agent into a plugin but the plugin version never takes effect. Why?
options: Project and user .claude/agents/ definitions override same-named plugin agents, so the originals must be removed first.
Plugin agents require an explicit enabledPlugins entry per agent.
Plugin agents are namespaced and cannot be invoked.
Agents cannot be distributed in plugins.
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.answer: Project and user .claude/agents/ definitions override same-named plugin agents, so the originals must be removed first.
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Create plugins: what changes when migrating
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.explanation:
'After migrating, remove the original files from .claude/ to avoid duplicates. Project and user .claude/agents/ definitions override same-named plugin agents, so the plugin version only takes effect once the originals are removed.' This matches the subagent precedence chain: managed > --agents > project > user > plugin, with plugin lowest.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B, C, D.** None is documented; agents/ is a supported plugin directory.

The contrast in the same note is the exam-relevant detail: 'Plugin skills are namespaced as /plugin-name:skill-name, so the original /skill-name and the plugin copy both remain available rather than one overriding the other.' Agents OVERRIDE by name; skills COEXIST via namespacing.
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.examTrick: Plugin AGENTS are overridden by project/user ones. Plugin SKILLS coexist because they're namespaced. Different behaviours.
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.question: Where do hooks live when migrating from standalone configuration to a plugin?
options: In hooks/hooks.json at the plugin root — the format is the same, so you copy the hooks object from settings.json.
In .claude-plugin/hooks.json.
In settings.json at the plugin root.
Hooks cannot be bundled; they stay in settings.json.
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.answer: In hooks/hooks.json at the plugin root — the format is the same, so you copy the hooks object from settings.json.
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Create plugins: migrate hooks
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.explanation:
'Create my-plugin/hooks/hooks.json with your hooks configuration. Copy the hooks object from your .claude/settings.json or settings.local.json, since the format is the same.' The migration table confirms: 'Hooks in settings.json' becomes 'Hooks in hooks/hooks.json'.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** Only plugin.json belongs in .claude-plugin/.
- **C.** A plugin's settings.json supports only the agent and subagentStatusLine keys.
- **D.** hooks/ is a supported plugin directory, and plugin hooks merge with all others.

Remember that hooks MERGE across sources: 'all registered hooks fire for their matching events regardless of source', so a plugin hook does not replace a project one.
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.examTrick: hooks/hooks.json at the plugin root, same object format as settings.json. Plugin hooks MERGE with project ones.
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.question: Which keys does a plugin's settings.json currently support?
options: Only agent and subagentStatusLine; unknown keys are silently ignored.
Every settings key, applied at the managed tier.
Only permissions, so a plugin can ship its own allowlist.
None; plugins cannot ship settings.
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.answer: Only agent and subagentStatusLine; unknown keys are silently ignored.
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Create plugins: ship default settings
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.explanation:
'Plugins can include a settings.json file at the plugin root to apply default configuration when the plugin is enabled. Currently, only the agent and subagentStatusLine keys are supported... Settings from settings.json take priority over settings declared in plugin.json. Unknown keys are silently ignored.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** A plugin cannot apply arbitrary settings, and certainly not at the managed tier.
- **C.** Permissions are not among the supported keys — an important safety property, since a plugin that could grant itself permissions would be a serious escalation path.
- **D.** The file is supported for those two keys.

The agent key is powerful: 'Setting agent activates one of the plugin's custom agents as the main thread, applying its system prompt, tool restrictions, and model. This lets a plugin change how Claude Code behaves by default when enabled.'
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.examTrick: Plugin settings.json = agent and subagentStatusLine ONLY. A plugin cannot grant itself permissions.
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.question: What does the bin/ directory in a plugin do, and what is its distribution restriction?
options: It adds executables to the Bash tool's PATH while the plugin is enabled; you cannot include it in a plugin distributed through claude.ai organization settings.
It stores compiled hook binaries and is required for hooks to run.
It holds the plugin's installer script.
It is a build output directory ignored at load time.
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.answer: It adds executables to the Bash tool's PATH while the plugin is enabled; you cannot include it in a plugin distributed through claude.ai organization settings.
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Create plugins: plugin structure overview
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.explanation:
'bin/: Executables added to the Bash tool's PATH while the plugin is enabled. You can't include this directory in a plugin you distribute through claude.ai organization settings.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B, C, D.** None is documented; hooks reference commands by path or name.

The restriction is a sensible security boundary: a plugin distributed centrally to an organization that could place arbitrary executables on PATH would let any command name be silently shadowed. Keeping bin/ out of that channel limits what a centrally-pushed plugin can do.
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.examTrick: bin/ puts executables on PATH — and is barred from claude.ai org distribution for exactly that reason.
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.question: What is a skills-directory plugin, and how is one created?
options: A plugin kept inside your skills directory that loads automatically — claude plugin init my-tool scaffolds ~/.claude/skills/my-tool/ with a manifest and starter SKILL.md, loading as my-tool@skills-dir with no marketplace or install step.
A plugin that contains only skills and no other components.
A plugin installed into ~/.claude/plugins/ from a marketplace.
A plugin loaded with --plugin-dir pointing at a skills folder.
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.answer: A plugin kept inside your skills directory that loads automatically — claude plugin init my-tool scaffolds ~/.claude/skills/my-tool/ with a manifest and starter SKILL.md, loading as my-tool@skills-dir with no marketplace or install step.
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Create plugins: develop a plugin in your skills directory
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.explanation:
'Instead of passing --plugin-dir on every launch, you can keep a plugin in your skills directory and have Claude Code load it automatically. claude plugin init my-tool scaffolds one... This creates ~/.claude/skills/my-tool/ with a .claude-plugin/plugin.json manifest and a starter SKILL.md. On the next session it loads as my-tool@skills-dir with no marketplace or install step.'

**Why the others are wrong**
