- **B.** Component mix is not what defines it; LOCATION is.
- **C, D.** Neither matches.

The skills documentation adds the mechanism from the other side: 'Add a .claude-plugin/plugin.json to a skill folder and it loads as a plugin named <name>@skills-dir, so it can bundle agents, hooks, and MCP servers. In a project's .claude/skills/, this requires accepting the workspace trust dialog first.'
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.examTrick: A manifest inside a skill folder turns it into a <name>@skills-dir plugin. In a PROJECT skills dir it needs workspace trust.
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.question: Which command validates a plugin before submission, and what does --strict change?
options: claude plugin validate ./your-plugin; --strict treats warnings as errors, since warnings do not fail validation by default.
claude plugin test ./your-plugin; --strict enables verbose output.
claude plugin lint; --strict checks the marketplace manifest too.
There is no validation command; submission runs the checks.
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.answer: claude plugin validate ./your-plugin; --strict treats warnings as errors, since warnings do not fail validation by default.
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Create plugins: submit your plugin
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.explanation:
'Run claude plugin validate ./your-plugin locally before you submit... The review pipeline runs the same check on every submission, along with automated safety screening. When validation passes, Claude Code prints ✔ Validation passed, or ✔ Validation passed with warnings if there are warnings. Warnings don't fail validation; add --strict to treat them as errors.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B, C.** Not documented commands.
- **D.** Local validation exists and runs the same check as the pipeline.

Running the same check locally that CI runs is the general pattern worth noting — it is the fast feedback loop that stops you discovering a problem only after submission.
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.examTrick: claude plugin validate runs the SAME check as the review pipeline. --strict makes warnings fail.
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.question: What are the two public Anthropic marketplaces, and how do they differ?
options: claude-plugins-official is a curated set maintained by Anthropic and registered automatically on first interactive start; claude-community is the public community marketplace where third-party submissions land after review.
Both are community-submitted; official is simply the older name.
Only claude-plugins-official exists; community plugins are hosted individually.
Both require a Team or Enterprise plan to access.
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.answer: claude-plugins-official is a curated set maintained by Anthropic and registered automatically on first interactive start; claude-community is the public community marketplace where third-party submissions land after review.
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Create plugins: submit your plugin to the community marketplace
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.explanation:
'claude-plugins-official: a curated set of plugins maintained by Anthropic. Claude Code registers it automatically the first time you start Claude Code interactively.' 'claude-community: the public community marketplace where third-party submissions land after review. Users add it with /plugin marketplace add anthropics/claude-plugins-community and install from it as @claude-community.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B, C.** Both exist with different curation models.
- **D.** The claude.ai SUBMISSION form requires a Team or Enterprise organization, but 'Individual authors who aren't part of a Team or Enterprise organization can use the Console form instead.' Access to the marketplaces is not plan-gated.

Note the official marketplace 'is curated separately. Anthropic decides which plugins to include at its discretion. There is no application process.'
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.examTrick: official = curated by Anthropic, auto-registered, no application. community = submitted and reviewed, added manually.
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.question: How can a team keep a plugin internal rather than public?
options: Host the marketplace in a private repository.
Omit the version field so it is not indexed.
Distribute the plugin directory by email and load it with --plugin-dir.
It is not possible; all marketplaces are public.
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.answer: Host the marketplace in a private repository.
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Create plugins: share your plugins
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.explanation:
'To keep a plugin internal to your team, host the marketplace in a private repository.' The docs also point to configuring team marketplaces at the repository level.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** Version has nothing to do with visibility.
- **C.** --plugin-dir is a development and testing flag requiring the flag on every launch; it is not a distribution channel.
- **D.** Private repositories are explicitly supported.

The large-codebase guidance connects here: when per-directory CLAUDE.md files stop scaling, the recommended move is 'A plugin in an internal marketplace' owned by a platform team, so conventions are versioned and centrally maintained rather than drifting per directory.
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.examTrick: Private marketplace = internal distribution. --plugin-dir is dev-only, not a distribution channel.
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.question: A plugin ships an LSP server that fails to start. Where do you look?
options: The /plugin manager's Errors tab, which shows failures such as 'Executable not found in $PATH'; an entry with invalid configuration is skipped instead, and claude --debug shows why.
The /mcp panel, which lists all server statuses.
The /context output under Custom Agents.
The session transcript, which records all startup failures.
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.answer: The /plugin manager's Errors tab, which shows failures such as 'Executable not found in $PATH'; an entry with invalid configuration is skipped instead, and claude --debug shows why.
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Create plugins: add LSP servers
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.explanation:
'To confirm the server starts, launch Claude Code with the plugin enabled and check the /plugin Errors tab: a language server that fails to start appears there, for example with Executable not found in $PATH when the binary isn't installed. An entry with an invalid configuration is skipped instead; run claude --debug to see why.' Users installing an LSP plugin 'must have the language server binary installed on their machine.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** /mcp covers MCP servers.
- **C.** /context shows loaded context including Custom Agents.
- **D.** The transcript is the conversation.

The two-tier failure handling repeats a pattern seen elsewhere: a runtime failure is REPORTED, while an invalid configuration is SKIPPED — the same distinction as MCP's mcp_server_errors versus a connection failure.
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.examTrick: Runtime failure = reported in the Errors tab. Invalid config = silently skipped; use --debug. Same split as MCP.
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.question: What do background monitors in a plugin do?
options: They watch logs, files, or external status and deliver each stdout line from their command to Claude as a notification, starting automatically when the plugin is active.
They poll the model for status updates on long-running tasks.
They track token usage and warn when limits approach.
They restart failed MCP servers.
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.answer: They watch logs, files, or external status and deliver each stdout line from their command to Claude as a notification, starting automatically when the plugin is active.
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Create plugins: add background monitors
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.explanation:
'Background monitors let your plugin watch logs, files, or external status in the background and notify Claude as events arrive. Claude Code starts each monitor automatically when the plugin is active, so you don't need to instruct Claude to start the watch.' Configuration lives in monitors/monitors.json as an array of entries with name, command, and description; 'Each stdout line from command is delivered to Claude as a notification during the session.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B, C, D.** None is documented.

Monitors are a push-based context source, complementing the pull-based tools: instead of Claude polling a log, the log pushes lines to Claude. That has a context cost, so the command should be narrow — tail -F on an error log rather than everything.
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.examTrick: monitors/monitors.json pushes stdout lines to Claude as notifications. Keep the command narrow — every line costs context.
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.question: Which statement about plugin skills and the commands/ directory is correct?
options: skills/ holds <name>/SKILL.md directories and is recommended for new plugins; commands/ holds flat markdown files and is the older form.
commands/ is required and skills/ is optional.
Both are equivalent with no recommendation either way.
commands/ is no longer loaded at all.
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.answer: skills/ holds <name>/SKILL.md directories and is recommended for new plugins; commands/ holds flat markdown files and is the older form.
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Create plugins: plugin structure overview
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.explanation:
The directory table: 'skills/: Skills as <name>/SKILL.md directories' and 'commands/: Skills as flat Markdown files. Use skills/ for new plugins.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** Neither is required, and skills/ is preferred.
- **C.** There is an explicit recommendation.
- **D.** Command files keep working — 'Your existing .claude/commands/ files keep working.'

The skills documentation gives the reason to prefer skills/: 'Skills are recommended since they support additional features like supporting files', plus frontmatter for invocation control and automatic model invocation. Command files also ignore the name and paths frontmatter fields.
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.examTrick: skills/ = directories with SKILL.md, full frontmatter. commands/ = flat files, ignores name and paths. Prefer skills/.
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.question: Which layering rule applies to plugin components, and how does it differ across component types?
options: Skills and subagents override by name with plugins lowest in priority, MCP servers override by name with plugins fourth in the chain, and hooks merge so plugin hooks always fire alongside others.
All plugin components merge with project ones.
All plugin components override project ones.
Plugin components load only when no project equivalent exists.
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.answer: Skills and subagents override by name with plugins lowest in priority, MCP servers override by name with plugins fourth in the chain, and hooks merge so plugin hooks always fire alongside others.
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Extend Claude Code: understand how features layer
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.explanation:
'Skills and subagents override by name: when the same name exists at multiple levels, one definition wins based on priority (managed > user > project for skills; managed > CLI flag > project > user > plugin for subagents). Plugin skills are namespaced to avoid conflicts.' 'MCP servers override by name: local > project > user', with plugin-provided servers fourth and claude.ai connectors fifth. 'Hooks merge: all registered hooks fire for their matching events regardless of source.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B, C, D.** Each applies one rule uniformly, and the whole point is that the rules DIFFER by component type.

Four distinct behaviours to hold: CLAUDE.md is additive, hooks merge, skills and subagents and MCP servers override by name, and plugin skills sidestep collisions entirely through namespacing.
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.examTrick: Four layering rules: CLAUDE.md additive, hooks merge, skills/agents/MCP override by name, plugin skills namespaced.
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.question: Which trigger, per the setup-evolution table, means it is time to package your configuration as a plugin?
options: A second repository needs the same setup.
Claude gets a convention wrong twice.
You paste the same playbook into chat for the third time.
A side task floods your conversation with output.
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.answer: A second repository needs the same setup.
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Extend Claude Code: build your setup over time
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.explanation:
The trigger table's final row: 'A second repository needs the same setup → Package it as a plugin.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** 'Claude gets a convention or command wrong twice' → add it to CLAUDE.md.
- **C.** 'You paste the same playbook or multi-step procedure into chat for the third time' → capture it as a skill.
- **D.** 'A side task floods your conversation with output you won't reference again' → route it through a subagent.

The table is worth memorising whole, because it states each trigger as an OBSERVABLE SYMPTOM rather than an abstract principle — which is exactly how exam scenarios present them. The plugin row's symptom is specifically about crossing a REPOSITORY boundary.
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.examTrick: Crossing a repo boundary is the plugin trigger. Wrong twice = CLAUDE.md. Pasted thrice = skill. Every time = hook.
chapter-14-plugins-and-distribution.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.question: Claude is ignoring an instruction you believe is in CLAUDE.md. Which command tells you whether the file actually loaded into this session?
options: /context — check the list under Memory files.
/memory — it lists file locations across user and project scopes.
/doctor — it runs a configuration checkup.
/status — it shows which managed source applies.
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.answer: /context — check the list under Memory files.
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Memory: troubleshoot memory issues
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.explanation:
'Run /context and check the list under Memory files to verify your CLAUDE.md and CLAUDE.local.md files loaded. If a file is missing there, Claude can't see it.' The docs draw the contrast explicitly: /memory lists locations 'including user and project CLAUDE.md entries for files that don't exist yet', but 'To check which files actually loaded into the current session, run /context.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** /memory answers 'where could files be', not 'what loaded'.
- **C.** /doctor runs a checkup and proposes trims for a checked-in CLAUDE.md.
- **D.** /status surfaces the applicable managed settings source.

The general diagnostic instinct: separate 'what is configured' from 'what actually loaded'. Most configuration confusion lives in that gap.
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.examTrick: /context = what LOADED. /memory = where files could be. The gap between them is where most confusion lives.
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.question: Which command shows how many tokens each loaded MCP tool is consuming?
options: /context all
/mcp
/usage
/insights
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.answer: /context all
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — MCP: context cost
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.explanation:
'Run /mcp to see each server's connection status. Run /context all to see how many tokens each loaded MCP tool uses.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** /mcp shows connection status per server and lets you authenticate or disconnect.
- **C.** /usage shows session token statistics and, on paid plans, attribution by skill, subagent, plugin, and MCP server as percentages — useful but at a different granularity.
- **D.** /insights reports on how you work rather than token counts.

The three tools answer three different questions: /mcp is 'is it connected', /context all is 'what is it costing right now', /usage is 'what share of recent usage did it account for'.
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.examTrick: /mcp = connected? /context all = per-tool tokens now. /usage = share of recent usage.
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.question: What does /doctor do for a checked-in CLAUDE.md?
options: It proposes trims — cutting content Claude can derive from the codebase such as directory layouts, dependency lists, and architecture overviews, while keeping pitfalls, rationale, and conventions that differ from tool defaults.
It rewrites the file automatically to fit 200 lines.
It validates the file's markdown syntax.
It reports which instructions Claude followed during the session.
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.answer: It proposes trims — cutting content Claude can derive from the codebase such as directory layouts, dependency lists, and architecture overviews, while keeping pitfalls, rationale, and conventions that differ from tool defaults.
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Memory: my CLAUDE.md is too large
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.explanation:
'The /doctor checkup proposes trims for a checked-in CLAUDE.md: it cuts content Claude can derive from the codebase, such as directory layouts, dependency lists, and architecture overviews, and keeps pitfalls, rationale, and conventions that differ from tool defaults.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** It proposes rather than rewrites.
- **C.** Markdown validity is not the concern.
- **D.** Per-instruction adherence is not reported; the InstructionsLoaded hook logs which files load.

What it keeps versus cuts encodes the whole CLAUDE.md philosophy: derivable facts are waste, while non-obvious pitfalls and deviations from defaults are exactly what Claude cannot infer.
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.examTrick: /doctor cuts what Claude can DERIVE and keeps what it cannot infer: pitfalls, rationale, deviations from defaults.
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.question: Which bundled skill reviews the current diff for bugs in a fresh subagent context?
options: /code-review
/verify
/debug
/insights
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.answer: /code-review
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Best practices: add an adversarial review step
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.explanation:
'For a correctness check, run the bundled /code-review skill, which reviews the current diff for bugs in a fresh subagent and returns findings to the session.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** /verify builds and runs your app 'to confirm a code change does what it should, without falling back to tests or type checks'.
- **C.** /debug is a bundled skill for debugging.
- **D.** /insights analyses your working patterns.

One caveat from the skills documentation: a project skill named code-review 'replaces the bundled /code-review, and typing the bundled alias /review never runs your skill' — so a teammate typing the alias would silently get different behaviour.
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.examTrick: /code-review = diff correctness in a fresh subagent. Overriding it does NOT capture its /review alias.
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.question: Which pair of bundled skills records a per-project recipe for building and launching your app?
options: /run-skill-generator records the recipe as .claude/skills/run-<name>/, and /verify can record its own at .claude/skills/verify/SKILL.md.
/init and /doctor.
/debug and /code-review.
/batch and /loop.
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.answer: /run-skill-generator records the recipe as .claude/skills/run-<name>/, and /verify can record its own at .claude/skills/verify/SKILL.md.
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Skills: bundled skills
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.explanation:
'/run-skill-generator records the recipe instead. It gets your app running from a clean environment, captures what worked (the install commands, the env vars, the launch script), and commits it as a per-project skill at .claude/skills/run-<name>/. After that, /run, /verify, and any other agent in the repo follow the recorded recipe instead of rediscovering it.' And: '/verify can also record its own recipe... it writes what worked to .claude/skills/verify/SKILL.md at the repo root, or in the touched package directory in a monorepo... At the repo root, the recorded skill replaces the bundled /verify.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B, C, D.** None records a launch recipe.

The pattern is a feedback loop over your own configuration: discover once, record as a skill, and every later run and every other agent reuses it instead of re-deriving.
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.examTrick: Discover once, record as a skill, reuse forever. /run-skill-generator and /verify both write recipes to disk.
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.question: Which command asks a side question whose answer never enters conversation history?
options: /btw
/compact
/clear
/subtask
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.answer: /btw
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Best practices: manage context aggressively
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.explanation:
'For questions that don't need to stay in context, use /btw. The answer never enters conversation history, so you can check a detail without growing context.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** /compact summarizes what is already present.
- **C.** /clear resets the whole context.
- **D.** /subtask creates a fork, which inherits the parent conversation and returns its result as a message.

The three isolation mechanisms differ in what returns: /btw returns an answer that is not retained, a subagent returns a summary into your context, and a fork inherits everything and returns a message. Choose by whether the RESULT should persist.
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.examTrick: /btw = answer not retained. Subagent = summary returns. Fork = inherits everything. Choose by what should persist.
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.question: Which command splits a change across 5 to 30 subagents, each in its own worktree opening a pull request?
options: /batch <instruction>, available in a git repository.
/loop <instruction>.
/workflows.
/deep-research.
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.answer: /batch <instruction>, available in a git repository.
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Best practices: fan out across files
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.explanation:
'In a git repository, run /batch <instruction> to have Claude split the change across 5 to 30 subagents. Each subagent works in its own worktree and opens a pull request.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** /loop runs a prompt repeatedly on an interval.
- **C.** /workflows lists and manages dynamic workflow runs rather than starting one from an instruction.
- **D.** /deep-research is the bundled research workflow.

The distinction from a dynamic workflow is worth holding: /batch fans one change across worktrees with a PR each, while a workflow runs a script Claude wrote that orchestrates dozens to hundreds of agents and returns one result.
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.examTrick: /batch = 5-30 subagents, worktree each, PR each. Workflow = a script, one result. Different shapes of fan-out.
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.question: Which command relocates a session to a different directory's project storage?
options: /cd — from v2.1.169 it relocates the session so it appears in the new directory's picker afterward.
/add-dir, which moves the working directory.
/branch, which creates a copy in the new location.
/resume, which re-anchors the session on selection.
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.answer: /cd — from v2.1.169 it relocates the session so it appears in the new directory's picker afterward.
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Sessions: where the session picker looks
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.explanation:
'From v2.1.169, moving a session with /cd relocates it to the new directory's project storage, so it appears in that directory's picker afterward. As of v2.1.196, a moved session stays out of the old directory's picker even after a crash or forced exit.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** /add-dir grants access to an additional directory; it does not move the session. Sessions that added a directory that way do appear in that directory's picker.
- **C.** /branch copies the conversation and switches the process into it, within the same storage.
- **D.** /resume selects an existing session.

The cross-project resume lookup handles moved sessions too: claude --resume <session-id> 'looks for the ID in the current project directory and its git worktrees first, then in every other project on this machine, so it finds a session that started elsewhere or moved with /cd.'
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.examTrick: /cd MOVES a session's storage. --resume <id> searches across projects, so a moved session is still findable.
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.question: How do you set a verification condition that a separate evaluator re-checks after every turn?
options: Set it as a /goal condition — Claude keeps working until the goal resolves, and if it stalls Claude Code eventually stops the run with the goal still set.
Set it as a PostToolUse hook.
State it in CLAUDE.md as an always-on rule.
Pass it with --append-system-prompt.
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.answer: Set it as a /goal condition — Claude keeps working until the goal resolves, and if it stalls Claude Code eventually stops the run with the goal still set.
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Best practices: how hard the check gates the stop
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.explanation:
'Across a session: set the check as a /goal condition. A separate evaluator re-checks it after every turn and Claude keeps working until the goal resolves. If Claude stalls, Claude Code eventually stops the run with the goal still set.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** PostToolUse fires per tool call and cannot gate the turn ending — the Stop hook is the deterministic gate.
- **C.** CLAUDE.md is advisory and has no evaluator.
- **D.** A system prompt addition is also advisory.

/goal sits in the middle of the gating ladder: a prompt instruction is weakest, /goal re-checks every turn, and a Stop hook blocks the turn from ending (until it gives up after 8 consecutive blocks). Two cost notes: a goal survives session resume with its counters reset, and idle goal check-ins send your full context, controllable with CLAUDE_CODE_GOAL_CHECKIN_MINUTES.
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.examTrick: Gating ladder: prompt < /goal (re-checked per turn) < Stop hook (blocks the turn, 8-block cap).
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.question: Which command brings another coding agent's configuration into Claude Code, including MCP servers, commands, subagents, and skills?
options: /import, which appends a one-time copy of instruction files such as AGENTS.md to the matching CLAUDE.md and carries over the other components.
/init, which reads other agents' rule files and generates a CLAUDE.md.
/config, which merges external configuration.
/plugin, which installs the other agent as a plugin.
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.answer: /import, which appends a one-time copy of instruction files such as AGENTS.md to the matching CLAUDE.md and carries over the other components.
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Memory: AGENTS.md
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.explanation:
'You can also run /import to bring a supported coding agent's configuration into Claude Code, which appends a one-time copy of instruction files such as AGENTS.md to the matching CLAUDE.md and carries over MCP servers, commands, subagents, and skills. Requires Claude Code v2.1.213 or later.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** /init generates a starting CLAUDE.md and does read Cursor and Copilot rules — and with CLAUDE_CODE_NEW_INIT=1 also AGENTS.md, .devin/rules/, .windsurf/rules/, and .clinerules — but it does not carry over MCP servers or subagents.
- **C, D.** Neither is documented for this.

Note the word 'one-time': /import COPIES, so later changes to AGENTS.md do not propagate. For an ongoing link, the documented alternative is a CLAUDE.md containing @AGENTS.md, which re-reads the file every session.
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.examTrick: /import = one-time COPY of another agent's config. @AGENTS.md = a living link that re-reads every session.
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.question: Which flag set makes a headless run reproducible across machines?
options: --bare plus explicitly passed --settings, --mcp-config, --agents, --plugin-dir, and --append-system-prompt.
--verbose plus --output-format json.
--permission-mode dontAsk plus --allowedTools.
--no-session-persistence plus --continue.
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.answer: --bare plus explicitly passed --settings, --mcp-config, --agents, --plugin-dir, and --append-system-prompt.
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Non-interactive mode: start faster with bare mode
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.explanation:
'Bare mode is useful for CI and scripts where you need the same result on every machine. A hook in a teammate's ~/.claude or an MCP server in the project's .mcp.json won't run, because bare mode never reads them.' The 'To load / Use' table then lists the flags for supplying each piece explicitly.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** Output formatting does not affect what configuration loads.
- **C.** That is the permission posture for CI — important, but orthogonal to reproducibility.
- **D.** Session persistence is unrelated.

Reproducibility comes from making configuration EXPLICIT rather than ambient. Note also that bare mode 'never reads OAuth credentials or the system keychain', so ANTHROPIC_API_KEY must be set.
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.examTrick: Reproducibility = --bare + explicit flags. Ambient configuration is what makes runs differ between machines.

chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.question: Which flag suppresses transcript writes for a single non-interactive run, and which suppresses them in all modes?
options: --no-session-persistence for one -p run; CLAUDE_CODE_SKIP_PROMPT_HISTORY as an environment variable for all modes.
--no-transcript for one run; cleanupPeriodDays: 0 for all modes.
--bare for one run; sandbox.enabled for all modes.
--ephemeral for one run; CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR for all modes.
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.answer: --no-session-persistence for one -p run; CLAUDE_CODE_SKIP_PROMPT_HISTORY as an environment variable for all modes.
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Sessions: where transcripts are stored
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.explanation:
The configuration table lists 'Suppress transcript writes in all modes → CLAUDE_CODE_SKIP_PROMPT_HISTORY → Environment variable' and 'Suppress writes for one non-interactive run → --no-session-persistence → CLI flag with claude -p'. The same table covers CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR to move storage off ~/.claude, CLAUDE_CODE_PROJECT_DIR_NAME to name the project directory, and cleanupPeriodDays to change the 30-day retention.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B, C, D.** None matches; cleanupPeriodDays controls retention rather than whether writes happen, and CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR relocates storage rather than disabling it.

Note the interaction: '-p runs still create a resumable session unless you pass --no-session-persistence', which is why -p and SDK sessions are resumable by ID even though they are excluded from the picker.
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.examTrick: --no-session-persistence = one -p run. CLAUDE_CODE_SKIP_PROMPT_HISTORY = all modes. Retention is a separate knob.

chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.question: How do you change a setting from within a -p invocation?
options: Pass key=value to /config in the prompt, for example /config thinking=false.
Use --set key=value.
It is not possible; settings must be edited in a file.
Use --settings with a JSON fragment, which is the only route.
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.answer: Pass key=value to /config in the prompt, for example /config thinking=false.
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Non-interactive mode
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.explanation:
'To change a setting from a -p invocation, pass key=value to /config, for example /config thinking=false.' The same note covers other commands that accept a value as an argument in -p: '/model, /effort, /fast, /color, and /rename accept the value as an argument, for example /model sonnet, and /mcp with no argument prints a text summary of server status.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** Not a documented flag.
- **C.** It is possible via /config.
- **D.** --settings works too — 'Settings via --settings <file-or-json>' — so calling it the ONLY route is what makes this option wrong.

The general point: user-invoked skills and commands work inside a -p prompt string because 'Claude Code expands it before running'. Only terminal-interface built-ins such as /login are unavailable.
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.examTrick: Slash commands work inside a -p prompt string. /config key=value changes a setting; only terminal-only built-ins are excluded.

chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.question: Which command lets you inspect and stop a running dynamic workflow?
options: /workflows — select a run to open its progress view, where p pauses or resumes, x stops an agent or the whole run, r restarts a running agent, and s saves the script as a command.
/agents, which lists all running agents.
/tasks, which shows background work.
/context, which shows what each agent is consuming.
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.answer: /workflows — select a run to open its progress view, where p pauses or resumes, x stops an agent or the whole run, r restarts a running agent, and s saves the script as a command.
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Workflows: watch the run
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.explanation:
'Run /workflows at any time to list running and completed workflows, then select one to open its progress view. The progress view shows each phase with its agent counts, token totals, and elapsed time.' The key table lists Enter or → to drill in, Esc or ← to back out, j/k to scroll, f to filter by status, p to pause or resume, x to stop, and r to restart a running agent.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B, C.** Neither is the documented workflow view. (Progress also appears in the task panel below the input box, expandable with the down arrow then Enter.)
- **D.** /context reports the main session's context usage, not per-agent workflow progress.

This is also where the cost signals appear: per-agent token usage as the run progresses, and the 'Large workflow' warning pointing you here to stop a run.
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.examTrick: /workflows is the control surface: p pause, x stop, r restart, s save, f filter. Cost signals appear here too.
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.question: A hook seems to work when you run its script by hand, but Claude never reacts to its output. What is the most likely cause?
options: The script writes to stdout and exits 0 — plain stdout on exit 0 goes to the debug log, not the transcript; use additionalContext JSON or exit 2 with stderr.
The matcher is a glob, which hooks do not support.
Hooks cannot return output to Claude at all.
The hook needs a timeout value to deliver output.
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.answer: The script writes to stdout and exits 0 — plain stdout on exit 0 goes to the debug log, not the transcript; use additionalContext JSON or exit 2 with stderr.
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Context window: hooks
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.explanation:
'Output reaches Claude via additionalContext JSON. Exit code 2 surfaces stderr to Claude. Plain stdout on exit 0 goes to the debug log, not the transcript.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** Matchers are exact strings or REGEX (not globs) — a real gotcha, but it would stop the hook firing at all rather than producing invisible output.
- **C.** Hook output does reach Claude; a linting PostToolUse hook depends on it.
- **D.** timeout bounds execution, not delivery.

The diagnostic path: '/hooks to browse what's configured', and 'Claude Code records which hooks matched, their exit codes, and their output in the debug log' viewable with claude --debug. SessionStart is the documented exception where plain stdout text is added to context before the first prompt.
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.examTrick: Hook runs but Claude ignores it? Plain stdout + exit 0 goes to the DEBUG LOG. Use additionalContext or exit 2.
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.question: Which flag lets you inspect the plan or a workflow script in your editor before it runs?
options: Ctrl+G — it opens the plan in your text editor in plan mode, and opens the script from a workflow's approval prompt.
Ctrl+E, which opens the last file Claude edited.
Ctrl+R, which opens the run configuration.
Shift+Tab, which cycles to an editing mode.
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.answer: Ctrl+G — it opens the plan in your text editor in plan mode, and opens the script from a workflow's approval prompt.
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Best practices: plan; Workflows: approve the plan before it runs
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.explanation:
In plan mode: 'Press Ctrl+G to open the plan in your text editor for direct editing before Claude proceeds.' In the workflow launch prompt: 'Ctrl+G opens the script in your editor. Tab lets you adjust the prompt before the run starts.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** Not documented.
- **C.** Ctrl+R renames the highlighted session in the session picker.
- **D.** Shift+Tab cycles permission modes.

The consistent affordance is worth noting: before a consequential automated action, Claude Code offers to show you the artifact — the plan or the script — in your own editor. Reviewing the plan is cheaper than reviewing the diff it produces.
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.examTrick: Ctrl+G inspects the artifact before it runs — plan or workflow script. Review the plan, not just the diff.
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.question: Which command reduces prompts safely by enabling OS-level isolation rather than loosening the permission mode?
options: /sandbox, selecting auto-allow on the Mode tab.
/permissions, adding broad allow rules.
/config, setting defaultMode to bypassPermissions.
/hooks, adding an allow-everything PreToolUse hook.
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.answer: /sandbox, selecting auto-allow on the Mode tab.
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Permission modes: choose a mode; Sandboxing
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.explanation:
The mode-selection table: 'Iterate locally with fewer prompts, without a classifier → Manual mode plus the Bash sandbox in auto-allow mode: claude --permission-mode default, then run /sandbox and select auto-allow.' Deny rules still apply, and ask rules naming a command still prompt.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** Broad allow rules remove the prompt AND the boundary.
- **C.** bypassPermissions is documented for 'Isolated containers and VMs only'.
- **D.** A blanket-allow hook is the same mistake expressed programmatically.

The principle: get safety from ISOLATION, not from asking. The prompt is a proxy for a boundary; the sandbox is the boundary itself, so you can drop the proxy without dropping the protection.
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.examTrick: Fewer prompts safely = isolation, not looser rules. The prompt is a proxy; the sandbox is the actual boundary.
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.question: Which command controls how full the context window gets before automatic compaction runs?
options: /autocompact with a token count, such as /autocompact 500k.
/compact with a token count.
/context set, with a threshold.
/config compactAt=500k.
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.answer: /autocompact with a token count, such as /autocompact 500k.
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Context window: when your context fills up
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.explanation:
'Compact earlier: run /autocompact with a token count, like /autocompact 500k, to set how full the context window gets before the automatic pass runs.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** /compact runs one pass now, optionally with focus instructions such as '/compact Focus on the API changes'.
- **C, D.** Neither is documented.

Why compact earlier: performance degrades as context fills, so compacting before the ceiling can produce better output than running right up against it. And a cost note that argues the other way — '/compact reads the conversation it summarizes, so compacting a large context is itself a large request', while '/clear costs nothing'. Compact earlier for quality; clear instead when you do not need continuity.
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.examTrick: /autocompact sets the THRESHOLD; /compact runs one pass NOW; /clear is free. Three different operations.
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.question: You want a status line that continuously shows context usage. What does the documentation point to?
options: A custom status line, which can display context window usage and receives data including transcript_path and session_name.
/usage, which must be re-run manually.
/context, which refreshes automatically once opened.
The task panel below the input box.
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.answer: A custom status line, which can display context window usage and receives data including transcript_path and session_name.
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Costs: manage context proactively; Sessions
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.explanation:
'Use /usage to check your current token usage, or configure your status line to display it continuously.' The best-practices guidance says the same: 'Track context usage continuously with a custom status line.' Status line commands receive input data including the transcript_path field that hooks also get, and a session_name field that shows the AI-generated session title when no name is set.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B, C.** Both are point-in-time checks.
- **D.** The task panel shows background task progress, including a workflow's one-line progress summary.

The distinction: /context and /usage answer 'where am I now'; the status line makes context pressure ambient so you notice it before it becomes a problem.
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.examTrick: Status line = CONTINUOUS context visibility. /context and /usage are point-in-time checks.
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.question: Which command shows which managed settings source applies when your setting is being overridden?
options: /status.
/config.
/doctor.
/context.
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.answer: /status.
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Settings: precedence examples
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.explanation:
In the scenario where a managed source overrides your value: 'You can't get your value back. Run /status to see which managed source applies, and ask your administrator if the policy should change.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** /config changes settings and shows options; it does not attribute a managed override.
- **C.** /doctor is a broader checkup.
- **D.** /context reports loaded context.

The diagnostic sequence for a setting that will not take effect is worth memorising: check whether a higher LEVEL sets it (the precedence stack, with /status for managed sources), whether the key WAITS FOR TRUST (allow rules, additionalDirectories, extraKnownMarketplaces and most env values do), whether an environment variable or flag overrides it per-key, and whether the file has a JSON syntax error reported as a Settings Error.
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.examTrick: Setting not applying? Check: higher level (/status), waiting for trust, env/flag override, or a Settings Error.
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.question: Which command runs a prompt or slash command repeatedly on an interval, and what is its documented side effect on the session picker?
options: /loop — a session whose FIRST prompt was /loop does not appear in the picker and is skipped by claude --continue, though running /loop later does not hide the session.
/schedule — scheduled sessions are always hidden from the picker.
/batch — batched sessions are hidden until their PRs are opened.
/monitor — monitored sessions appear only in the task panel.
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.answer: /loop — a session whose FIRST prompt was /loop does not appear in the picker and is skipped by claude --continue, though running /loop later does not hide the session.
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Sessions: where the session picker looks
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.explanation:
'Sessions whose first prompt was a /loop command don't appear in the picker, and claude --continue skips them too. Running /loop later in a conversation doesn't hide the session. Before v2.1.211, a /loop run early in a conversation hid the session from the picker permanently.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B, C, D.** None matches the documented behaviour.

Note the mode asymmetry: interactive --continue skips -p, SDK, background, and /loop sessions, but 'When you run claude -p --continue, Claude Code includes -p, SDK, and /loop sessions and still skips background sessions.' Each mode continues its own kind of work.

The cost angle: '/usage' shows Loops rows for the heaviest scheduled tasks, because 'a scheduled task fires on its interval even while the session is idle, sending your full context each time.'
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.examTrick: /loop as the FIRST prompt hides the session from the picker. Loops send full context on every fire — check /usage Loops rows.
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.question: Which sequence best diagnoses 'my project rule is not being applied' in a monorepo session started in a subdirectory?
options: Run /context to see what loaded, remember that .claude/settings.json loads only from the starting directory while CLAUDE.md walks up, check whether the rule is path-scoped and has not matched a file yet, and verify no claudeMdExcludes pattern skips it.
Run /doctor and accept its proposed trims.
Run /clear and try again.
Run /config and re-enter the rule.
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.answer: Run /context to see what loaded, remember that .claude/settings.json loads only from the starting directory while CLAUDE.md walks up, check whether the rule is path-scoped and has not matched a file yet, and verify no claudeMdExcludes pattern skips it.
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Memory troubleshooting; Large codebases; Settings
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.explanation:
Four documented causes combine here. /context shows what actually loaded under Memory files. Project settings 'load only from your starting directory and are not inherited from parent directories the way CLAUDE.md files are.' Path-scoped rules 'trigger when Claude reads files matching the pattern, not on every tool use', so a rule can be present and simply not yet active. And claudeMdExcludes can skip a file by absolute-path glob.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** /doctor proposes trims — it would cut content, not explain absence.
- **C.** Clearing loses context without diagnosing anything, and re-triggers the same loading rules.
- **D.** Re-entering a rule that is already present changes nothing.

The diagnostic discipline the exam rewards: distinguish NOT LOADED (wrong directory, excluded) from LOADED BUT NOT YET TRIGGERED (path-scoped, awaiting a matching file) from LOADED BUT ADVISORY (CLAUDE.md is a user message after the system prompt, with no guarantee of compliance). Three different causes, three different fixes.
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.examTrick: Three failure classes: not loaded, loaded-but-untriggered, loaded-but-advisory. Diagnose which before changing anything.
chapter-15-commands-cli-and-diagnostics.subject: Claude CCAF: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

chapter-01-context-preservation-and-comp.question: An agent loop appends tool results to history; after 20 iterations the context window approaches its limit. How do you manage conversation history in long-running loops?
options: Increase context window size to accommodate all iterations without truncation.
Clear conversation history periodically, restarting the agent with fresh context.
Implement a sliding window maintaining context relevance, summarizing older content.
Truncate the oldest tool results, keeping only recent results.
chapter-01-context-preservation-and-comp.answer: Implement a sliding window maintaining context relevance, summarizing older content.
chapter-01-context-preservation-and-comp.source: Context windows and compaction · Effective context engineering for AI agents ---
chapter-01-context-preservation-and-comp.explanation:
A sliding window **with summarisation** bounds growth while preserving the causal chain: recent turns stay verbatim (where detail matters most), older material is condensed into what still bears on the remaining work, and nothing is silently dropped. This is the pattern behind both server-side compaction and `/compact`.

Why distractors fail:
- **A** — Buys headroom without changing the growth rate; any unbounded loop fills any window.
- **B** — Clearing discards the task definition and everything learned, so the agent restarts from nothing.
- **D** — Truncating the oldest results removes the earliest turns, which typically hold the goal and constraints — the highest-value tokens present.

chapter-01-context-preservation-and-comp.question: Long-document extraction shows the "lost in the middle" effect — middle content is missed despite being within the context window. How do you address attention dilution?
options: Use extended thinking, giving the model more time for complete analysis.
Explicit instructions directing attention to middle sections.
Increase context window size, reducing the "middle" proportion of the document.
Split the document into focused chunks, processing each independently with overlap.
chapter-01-context-preservation-and-comp.answer: Split the document into focused chunks, processing each independently with overlap.
chapter-01-context-preservation-and-comp.source: Long context prompting tips · Context windows ---
chapter-01-context-preservation-and-comp.explanation:
Chunking **eliminates the middle**: in a small enough chunk, every position is effectively a high-attention position. The overlap matters too — it ensures information spanning a boundary appears intact in at least one chunk, so nothing is lost at the seams.

Why distractors fail:
- **C** — The stem already says the content is *within* the window; a larger window leaves the same proportion in the middle, just of a bigger document.
- **A** — Thinking time does not change where attention falls across a long input.
- **B** — "Pay attention to the middle" is an instruction against an architectural effect; it cannot reliably override it.

chapter-01-context-preservation-and-comp.question: A 47-turn support conversation approaches the context limit; earlier turns contain critical account details needed for the current issue. How do you preserve critical information?

Increase context window to maximum, accommodating the complete history.
Sliding window approach with structured summarization preserving critical details.
Restart the conversation with fresh context when approaching the limit.

chapter-01-context-preservation-and-comp.source: Effective context engineering for AI agents · Context windows ---
chapter-01-context-preservation-and-comp.explanation:
The requirement is explicitly to **preserve the critical details**, and structured summarisation is what distinguishes this from ordinary compaction: account numbers, balances, and decisions are lifted into a durable structured form, while the conversational padding around them is condensed.

Why distractors fail:

- **D** — Restarting discards them entirely, and the customer must repeat everything.
- **B** — Delays the limit without preserving anything, and the conversation will reach it again.

chapter-01-context-preservation-and-comp.question: Web-search output (85K tokens **including page content**) plus document-analysis output (70K **including chains of thought**) totals 155K, but the synthesis agent performs best under 50K. Most effective solution?
options: Have the synthesis agent process findings in sequential batches, maintaining state between calls.
Modify upstream agents to return structured data (key facts, quotes, relevance scores) instead of verbose content and reasoning.
Store findings in a vector database and give synthesis search tools to query during its work.
Add an intermediate summarization agent that condenses findings before synthesis.
chapter-01-context-preservation-and-comp.answer: Modify upstream agents to return structured data (key facts, quotes, relevance scores) instead of verbose content and reasoning.
chapter-01-context-preservation-and-comp.source: Effective context engineering for AI agents · Multi-agent research system ---
chapter-01-context-preservation-and-comp.explanation:
The stem tells you what the bulk *is*: raw page content and reasoning traces — material the synthesis agent does not need. **Fixing the contract at the source** eliminates the tokens rather than compressing them later, and structured output (facts, quotes, scores) is more useful to synthesis than prose ever was. It also costs nothing extra: no additional agent, no additional call.

Why distractors fail:
- **D** — The closest alternative, and it works — but it adds a whole agent and a pass over 155K tokens to discard material that should never have been produced.
- **A** — Batching means synthesis never sees all findings together, which is exactly what synthesis requires.
- **C** — Retrieval is lossy and non-deterministic for a task that needs *all* findings; a missed query silently drops a source.

Why distractors fail:
- **B** — Caches content that changes next request, so it is never read back.
- **A** — Exceeds the breakpoint limit, and breakpoints inside the volatile region are wasted.

chapter-01-context-preservation-and-comp.question: 8K system prompt, 5 tool definitions at 2K each, user messages averaging 500 tokens, responses up to 4K, on a 200K model. Approximately how many turns before hitting the limit?
options: About 180 turns · **B.** About 20 turns · **C.** About 40 turns · **D.** Unlimited, because old messages are truncated automatically
chapter-01-context-preservation-and-comp.answer: About 180 turns · **B.** About 20 turns · **C.** About 40 turns · **D.** Unlimited, because old messages are truncated automatically
chapter-01-context-preservation-and-comp.source: Context windows · Token counting ---
chapter-01-context-preservation-and-comp.explanation:
The arithmetic:
| Component | Tokens |
|---|---|
| System prompt | 8,000 |
| 5 tools × 2,000 | 10,000 |
| **Fixed overhead** | **18,000** |
| Remaining budget | 200,000 − 18,000 = **182,000** |
| Per turn (500 user + 4,000 response) | **4,500** |
| Turns | 182,000 ÷ 4,500 ≈ **40** |
The key insight is that the fixed overhead is paid **once**, while each turn's tokens **accumulate** in history and are re-sent on every subsequent request.

Why distractors fail:
- **A** — ~180 would follow from counting only the 500-token user messages, ignoring the 4K responses that dominate.
- **B** — ~20 would follow from charging the 18K overhead per turn rather than once.
- **D** — Nothing truncates automatically; exceeding the window is an error unless you implement compaction.

- **C** — The plausible runner-up, and worth doing — but instructions to a summariser are probabilistic, so values will still be lost sometimes. "Prevents" requires the structural guarantee.

The context window overflowed, causing hallucinated class names.
Claude Code cached module 3's source and served the stale version instead of the updated file.
The model confused similar class names because too many modules were processed in one session.

It traces the exact failure path. Module 3's summary — recorded before the rename — carried the old names. Module 12's summary was *supposed* to record the rename, but summarisation compressed away the specific old→new mapping. chapter-03-error-propagation-and-recover.question: A docs pipeline reads source comments, wiki pages, and API schemas. Wiki retrieval times out; the other two succeed. The pipeline currently halts entirely on any source failure. Best error handling strategy?
options: Retry the wiki three times with exponential backoff; if all retries fail, halt to prevent incomplete documentation.
Return structured error context for the wiki failure, proceed with available sources, and mark the gaps that lack wiki content.
Silently skip the wiki source and generate from the remaining two without noting the omission.
Use the source comments to infer what the wiki pages would have contained.
chapter-03-error-propagation-and-recover.answer: Return structured error context for the wiki failure, proceed with available sources, and mark the gaps that lack wiki content.
chapter-03-error-propagation-and-recover.source: UD5-036 | Multi-agent research system — partial results · Building effective agents
chapter-03-error-propagation-and-recover.explanation: Graceful degradation with disclosure: continue pipeline execution with the successful sources (comments + schemas) while explicitly annotating sections missing wiki data.
chapter-03-error-propagation-and-recover.examTrick: Partial pipeline source outage = Graceful degradation with explicit gap annotations.
chapter-03-error-propagation-and-recover.subject: Claude CCAF: Context Management & Reliability

chapter-04-large-codebase-context-manage.question: Adding error-handling wrappers across 120 files in three phases: (1) discover call sites, (2) collaboratively design the approach, (3) implement consistently. Phase 1's output fills the context window before discovery finishes. Most effective approach?
options: Define the pattern in CLAUDE.md, then process files in batches across multiple sessions relying on the shared memory file for consistency.
Use an Explore subagent for Phase 1 to isolate verbose discovery output and return a summary, then continue Phases 2–3 in the main conversation.
Switch to headless mode with --continue, passing explicit context summaries between batch calls.
Do all phases in the main conversation, periodically using /compact.
chapter-04-large-codebase-context-manage.answer: Use an Explore subagent for Phase 1 to isolate verbose discovery output and return a summary, then continue Phases 2–3 in the main conversation.
chapter-04-large-codebase-context-manage.source: UD5-017 | Claude Code subagents · Effective context engineering
chapter-04-large-codebase-context-manage.explanation: Phase 1 discovery is verbose and exploratory. Delegating it to an Explore subagent confines raw search outputs to a disposable context, returning a clean summary for collaborative design.
chapter-04-large-codebase-context-manage.examTrick: Large discovery phase = Explore subagent -> returns summary -> design/edit in main session.
chapter-04-large-codebase-context-manage.subject: Claude CCAF: Context Management & Reliability

chapter-04-large-codebase-context-manage.question: Repeated lookup_order calls return 40+ fields each; tool outputs now dominate the conversation, and the customer mentions two more orders. Most effective approach before making additional lookups?
options: Extract only return-relevant fields (items, purchase date, return window, status) from each existing order response, removing verbose details.
Have the model generate a natural language summary of each order, replacing structured responses with prose.
Move all tool responses to a vector database with semantic indexing, retrieving relevant portions as the conversation continues.
Proceed with additional lookups without modifying the existing context.
chapter-04-large-codebase-context-manage.answer: Extract only return-relevant fields (items, purchase date, return window, status) from each existing order response, removing verbose details.
chapter-04-large-codebase-context-manage.source: CS5-001 (§5.4) | Effective context engineering · Writing tools for agents
chapter-04-large-codebase-context-manage.explanation: Payload projection: prune 40+ fields down to the 4 return-relevant fields (items, date, window, status), reclaiming context while retaining structured precision.
chapter-04-large-codebase-context-manage.examTrick: Context bloat from repeated tool results = Project payloads to task-relevant fields only.
chapter-04-large-codebase-context-manage.subject: Claude CCAF: Context Management & Reliability

chapter-05-human-review-and-confidence-c.question: Confidence thresholds calibrated over three months; >90% auto-approves. A new client submits contracts in an unusual two-column format the system has never seen, and the system reports 92% confidence. Appropriate safeguard?
options: Maintain stratified random sampling of high-confidence extractions across document types to catch the new format's error rate.
Trust the calibrated threshold, since 92% exceeds 90%.
Raise the threshold from 90% to 98% for all document types.
Add a document format classifier that flags unknown formats for mandatory human review before any auto-approval.
chapter-05-human-review-and-confidence-c.answer: Add a document format classifier that flags unknown formats for mandatory human review before any auto-approval.
chapter-05-human-review-and-confidence-c.explanation: Confidence calibration is only valid within the distribution on which it was trained. Out-of-distribution formats must be flagged by a format classifier for mandatory human review.
chapter-05-human-review-and-confidence-c.examTrick: Novel / unseen format = Flag for mandatory human review (confidence calibration is invalid out-of-distribution).
chapter-05-human-review-and-confidence-c.subject: Claude CCAF: Context Management & Reliability

chapter-05-human-review-and-confidence-c.question: An agent emits confidence scores 0–1; confidence 0.9 and 0.5 produce wrong code at similar rates. MOST important step before relying on these scores?
options: Calibrate the confidence scores against a labeled validation set so 0.9 maps to actual 90% accuracy.
Trust the raw scores as-is.
Drop confidence scoring and gate auto-merge purely on whether the code compiles.
Train the model further on edge cases until confidence becomes reliable.
chapter-05-human-review-and-confidence-c.answer: Calibrate the confidence scores against a labeled validation set so 0.9 maps to actual 90% accuracy.
chapter-05-human-review-and-confidence-c.explanation: Raw self-reported confidence is uncalibrated. Calibration against labeled golden datasets maps raw model scores to actual empirical accuracy probabilities.
chapter-05-human-review-and-confidence-c.examTrick: Raw confidence scores MUST be calibrated against labeled validation datasets before gating automation.
chapter-05-human-review-and-confidence-c.subject: Claude CCAF: Context Management & Reliability

chapter-05-human-review-and-confidence-c.question: Three months at 100% human review; extractions with confidence >90% show 97% accuracy overall. Before automating high-confidence extractions, what validation step is most critical?
options: Analyze accuracy by document type and field to verify high-confidence extractions perform consistently across all segments, not just in aggregate.
Compare accuracy at 85%, 90%, and 95% thresholds to find the optimal cutoff.
Run a two-week pilot routing 25% of high-confidence extractions to downstream systems and monitor error reports.
Verify that 97% accuracy meets requirements for all downstream systems.
chapter-05-human-review-and-confidence-c.answer: Analyze accuracy by document type and field to verify high-confidence extractions perform consistently across all segments, not just in aggregate.
chapter-05-human-review-and-confidence-c.explanation: Aggregate accuracy masks segment-level failures (e.g. 99% on standard invoices but 70% on tables). Validate by segment and field before removing human review.
chapter-05-human-review-and-confidence-c.examTrick: Before automating high-confidence approvals: Segment accuracy by document type and field (Simpson's paradox).
chapter-05-human-review-and-confidence-c.subject: Claude CCAF: Context Management & Reliability

chapter-06-provenance-and-uncertainty.question: Batch API processing 50 documents; results must be matched to original documents and the batch returns them unordered. How do you correlate?
options: Use the custom_id field in batch requests to correlate results with document IDs.
Sequential processing with the real-time API for guaranteed ordering.
Results return in submission order, enabling positional array correlation.
Store batch request IDs in a database for post-processing correlation.
chapter-06-provenance-and-uncertainty.answer: Use the custom_id field in batch requests to correlate results with document IDs.
chapter-06-provenance-and-uncertainty.source: UD5-001 | Batch processing · Message Batches API
chapter-06-provenance-and-uncertainty.explanation: custom_id round-trips through the Batch API, enabling order-independent, deterministic correlation between submitted documents and returned results.
chapter-06-provenance-and-uncertainty.examTrick: Batch API result correlation = Match via custom_id parameter.
chapter-06-provenance-and-uncertainty.subject: Claude CCAF: Context Management & Reliability

chapter-06-provenance-and-uncertainty.question: A synthesis report attributes some claims to the wrong sources; provenance tracking failed. How do you maintain provenance in multi-agent synthesis?
options: The coordinator tracks which subagent produced which information.
Natural language source attribution in subagent responses is sufficient.
A separate provenance tracking subagent logging all information sources.
Subagents emit structured claim-source mappings in results passed to the coordinator.
chapter-06-provenance-and-uncertainty.answer: Subagents emit structured claim-source mappings in results passed to the coordinator.
chapter-06-provenance-and-uncertainty.source: UD5-003 | Multi-agent research system — citations · Citations
chapter-06-provenance-and-uncertainty.explanation: Provenance must be bound at extraction time. Structured claim-source mappings ({claim, source_url, location}) survive synthesis merging and rewriting without misattribution.
chapter-06-provenance-and-uncertainty.examTrick: Preserve multi-agent provenance = Subagents emit structured claim-source mappings.
chapter-06-provenance-and-uncertainty.subject: Claude CCAF: Context Management & Reliability

chapter-06-provenance-and-uncertainty.question: Web search returns "2024: 35% adoption"; document analysis returns "2022: 18% adoption". The synthesis agent flags these as contradictory rather than recognising growth over time. What change best enables correct interpretation?
options: Require subagents to include publication or data collection dates in their structured outputs.
Add a conflict resolution agent that automatically discards older data when newer data exists.
Configure the web search agent to only return results from the past 6 months.
Instruct the synthesis agent to always treat the most recent data as authoritative and place older findings in a historical appendix.
chapter-06-provenance-and-uncertainty.answer: Require subagents to include publication or data collection dates in their structured outputs.
chapter-06-provenance-and-uncertainty.source: CS5-002 (§5.6) | Multi-agent research system · Structured outputs
chapter-06-provenance-and-uncertainty.explanation: Attaching publication/collection dates to structured findings transforms apparent contradictions into recognized time-series trends (growth from 18% in 2022 to 35% in 2024).
chapter-06-provenance-and-uncertainty.examTrick: Reconcile metric discrepancies over time = Require dates in structured findings.
chapter-06-provenance-and-uncertainty.subject: Claude CCAF: Context Management & Reliability

chapter-06-provenance-and-uncertainty.question: Contracts frequently include amendments (original "30-day payment terms", Amendment 1 changes it to "45 days"); the model inconsistently extracts one value or the other with no indication of which applies. Most effective approach?
options: Redesign the schema so amended fields capture multiple values, each with source location and effective date.
Prompt instructions to always extract the most recent amendment and ignore superseded original terms.
Preprocess documents with a classifier that identifies and removes superseded sections before extraction.
Post-extraction validation using pattern matching to detect amendments and flag them for manual review.
chapter-06-provenance-and-uncertainty.answer: Redesign the schema so amended fields capture multiple values, each with source location and effective date.
chapter-06-provenance-and-uncertainty.explanation: Contracts with amendments contain multiple valid terms over different effective periods. Structuring the schema as an array of entries with source location and effective date captures full legal provenance.
chapter-06-provenance-and-uncertainty.examTrick: Contract amendments = Schema with array of {value, source_clause, effective_date}.
chapter-06-provenance-and-uncertainty.subject: Claude CCAF: Context Management & Reliability

chapter-07-codebase-exploration-and-cont.question: A developer asks Claude to 'investigate how authentication works' in an unfamiliar 400k-line repository, with no further scoping. Claude reads hundreds of files and the context window fills before any implementation starts. Which documented failure pattern is this, and what is the fix?
options: The infinite exploration — scope investigations narrowly, or route them through subagents so the exploration doesn't consume the main context.
The kitchen sink session — run /clear between unrelated tasks.
The trust-then-verify gap — always provide tests or scripts Claude can run.
The over-specified CLAUDE.md — ruthlessly prune the instruction file.
chapter-07-codebase-exploration-and-cont.answer: The infinite exploration — scope investigations narrowly, or route them through subagents so the exploration doesn't consume the main context.
chapter-07-codebase-exploration-and-cont.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Best practices: avoid common failure patterns
chapter-07-codebase-exploration-and-cont.explanation:
The docs name this pattern exactly: 'The infinite exploration. You ask Claude to investigate something without scoping it. Claude reads hundreds of files, filling the context. Fix: Scope investigations narrowly or use subagents so the exploration doesn't consume your main context.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** The kitchen sink session is about mixing UNRELATED tasks in one session, not one unscoped task.
- **C.** The trust-then-verify gap is about plausible-looking implementations that miss edge cases — a verification problem, not a context problem.
- **D.** Nothing here concerns the size of CLAUDE.md.
chapter-07-codebase-exploration-and-cont.examTrick: Unscoped 'investigate X' + context blowout = infinite exploration. Fix = narrow the scope OR delegate to a subagent.
chapter-07-codebase-exploration-and-cont.subject: Claude CCAF: Context Management & Reliability

chapter-07-codebase-exploration-and-cont.question: Why does delegating codebase research to a subagent preserve the main conversation's context?
options: Subagents run in separate context windows with their own input and output tokens, and report back only a summary.
Subagents compress every file they read before adding it to the shared context window.
Subagents run with a smaller model, so their reads cost proportionally fewer tokens.
Subagents write everything they read to disk instead of into any context window.
chapter-07-codebase-exploration-and-cont.answer: Subagents run in separate context windows with their own input and output tokens, and report back only a summary.
chapter-07-codebase-exploration-and-cont.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Best practices: use subagents for investigation; Extend Claude Code
chapter-07-codebase-exploration-and-cont.explanation:
'Since context is your fundamental constraint, subagents are one of the most powerful tools available. When Claude researches a codebase it reads lots of files, all of which consume your context. Subagents run in separate context windows and report back summaries.' The comparison table lists the subagent's key benefit as 'Context isolation. Work happens separately, only summary returns.'

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** There is no shared context window to compress into; the isolation is the mechanism, not compression.
- **C.** A subagent's model is configurable, but model size is not why the main context is preserved.
- **D.** Subagents do have context windows; they simply are not yours.
chapter-07-codebase-exploration-and-cont.examTrick: Subagent = separate context window, summary returns. That is the whole benefit. Not compression, not a smaller model.
chapter-07-codebase-exploration-and-cont.subject: Claude CCAF: Context Management & Reliability

chapter-07-codebase-exploration-and-cont.question: When should you use /clear rather than /compact?
options: /clear resets context entirely between unrelated tasks; /compact summarizes and preserves what matters when you are continuing the same work.
/clear is for when the context is full; /compact is for when it is nearly empty.
/clear summarizes the conversation into a shorter form; /compact deletes it outright.
They are aliases; /compact is the newer name and /clear is retained for compatibility.
chapter-07-codebase-exploration-and-cont.answer: /clear resets context entirely between unrelated tasks; /compact summarizes and preserves what matters when you are continuing the same work.
chapter-07-codebase-exploration-and-cont.source: NEW | Claude Code docs — Best practices: manage context aggressively
chapter-07-codebase-exploration-and-cont.explanation:
The docs advise 'Use /clear frequently between tasks to reset the context window entirely' and describe compaction as: 'When auto compaction triggers, Claude summarizes what matters most, including code patterns, file states, and key decisions.' For more control, run /compact <instructions>, like '/compact Focus on the API changes'.

**Why the others are wrong**

- **B.** Fullness is not the deciding factor; task continuity is. You /clear when moving to unrelated work even if there is room left.
- **C.** Exactly backwards — /compact summarizes, /clear resets.
- **D.** They are distinct commands with different effects.
chapter-07-codebase-exploration-and-cont.examTrick: Unrelated next task = /clear. Same task, running long = /compact (optionally with focus instructions).
chapter-07-codebase-exploration-and-cont.subject: Claude CCAF: Context Management & Reliability

chapter-07-codebase-exploration-and-cont.question: You have corrected Claude three times on the same issue in one session and it is still wrong. What does the documentation recommend?
